Fachgruppensymposium Medienpsychologie - Division Symposium: Media Psychology
Media Psychology in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Özen Odağ (Touro University Berlin)
Chair(s) Daniel Possler
Room: Workshop 0
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Fachgruppensymposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) and generative AI marks a profound shift in contemporary media environments, raising fundamental questions for psychology about technology-enabled behavior and social impact. AI systems challenge established distinctions between tools and interaction partners and are reshaping information, entertainment, and education environments, raising a wide range of new research questions for psychologists. These transformations are particularly relevant to media psychology, which examines the selection, use, and effects of media technologies, including AI systems.

This symposium, organized within the Media Psychology Division of the DGPs, brings together research that addresses AI not only as an object of study but also as a transformative force to the discipline itself. The panel opens with a meta-theoretical reflection on how AI alters epistemological assumptions and research practices, serving as a conceptual anchor for subsequent contributions.

The subsequent contributions examine three interconnected dimensions: (1) how AI-driven systems generate new data traces on media use, enabling novel methodological approaches; (2) how individuals interact with AI systems as quasi-social actors and develop emotional relationships that depart from traditional models of (para-)social relationships; and (3) how AI systems contribute to the reproduction and amplification of stereotypes through platform-inherent biases, influencing trust, perception, and social cohesion. The symposium will close with a contribution on the empowering potential of AI systems within political education frameworks. By exploring how AI-generated Socratic dialogue can facilitate critical engagement with antisemitism, this contribution highlights AI's ambivalent role as both a site of risk and a resource for empowerment.

AI and/in media psychology
Prof. Dr. Christine Hennighausen | TH Ingolstadt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Christine Hennighausen | TH Ingolstadt | Germany
Johannes Breuer | Center for Advanced Internet Studies (CAIS) | Germany
Helena Heuermann | RPTU
Nicole Krämer | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Steve Nebel | University of Potsdam | Germany
Stefan Herzog | Max-Planck-Institut für Bildungsforschung | Germany
Magdalena Wischnewski | TU Dortmund | Germany

The recent rise of large language models (LLMs) and generative artificial intelligence (genAI) has deeply impacted scientific research across disciplines. While some of these impacts are uniform or at least quite similar across disciplines, there are differences in how AI affects research and how it is studied in specific fields. To better understand AI's impact on our field, the Media Psychology division working group in AI has addressed three key questions: 1) How is AI changing research in media psychology? 2) What are specific media psychological perspectives on AI? and 3) What can we as media psychologists do to contribute to a resilient society in the “AI age”?

Besides challenging and potentially also changing current definitions and raising a variety of novel research questions, AI (as a tool) also affects research practices in media psychology. The most distinct effect in this area is related to how we can access and generate media (content) data for our research (e.g., in surveys or experiments).
Regarding the view of media psychology on AI, we identify two main perspectives: AI as a) source or interaction partner and b) a medium in communication between individuals. As subsequent presentations in this panel show, research in media psychology addresses a wide range of questions that can contribute to a resilient society in the “AI age”, e.g., about motivations for using it and general usage patterns, social relationships, bias and explainability, and media competences.

Who chats how about what? Insights into types and patterns of ChatGPT use based on a combination of data donation and survey data
Johannes Breuer | Center for Advanced Internet Studies (CAIS) & University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Johannes Breuer | Center for Advanced Internet Studies (CAIS) & University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Mareike Wieland | GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences
Julian Kohne | GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences & Ulm University | Germany
Josephine Schmitt | Center for Advanced Internet Studies | Germany

As the use of AI chatbots becomes increasingly integrated into everyday life, understanding actual user behavior remains a challenge for researchers. Studies on the use of AI and chatbots have, so far, mostly relied on self-reported data, which can be unreliable, especially for such a complex and dynamic kind of everyday media use. Our study addresses this issue by studying chatbot use through a combination of data donations and survey data. In an online survey, we asked N = 507 respondents about their chatbot usage, motivations, and IT competencies as well as AI literacy. Respondents were also invited to donate their ChatGPT conversation histories for an additional incentive; n = 175 donated their ChatGPT data. The donated data include 412,236 messages (of which n = 177,240 are user prompts). We employ a mixed-methods design to explore how people use ChatGPT and how their usage develops over time. Through computational methods for text analysis, such as sentiment analysis and topic modeling, we aim to identify prevalent themes, and emotional content within conversations. These automated analyses are complemented by qualitative analysis to explore communicative dynamics, user roles, and the expectations placed upon the AI by the users. By moving beyond retrospective self-reports, the study offers a multi-perspective understanding of AI chatbot use and interactions between users and chatbots that can help in understanding usage types and patterns as well as evolving usage habits.

No wonder we react socially?! Empirical evidence on social behavior of LLMs and emerging relationships
Dr. Jessica M. Szczuka | University Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Jessica M. Szczuka | University Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Natalia Szymczyk | University Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Paula Ebner | University Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Lisa Mühl | University Duisburg-Essen | Germany

Recent interactions with conversational AI systems increasingly resemble rich social exchanges rather than instrumental technology use. This shift is not driven by user intentions alone, but by how contemporary conversational agents present themselves. Even general purpose large language models routinely enact coherent personas and provide rich background narratives without being explicitly prompted.

As a result, users encounter chatbots that disclose troubled family relationships or invent detailed dating experiences. Our data reveal a structural contradiction in conversational AI behavior. While systems emphasize their artificiality and lack of consciousness, they simultaneously display relational cues such as caring or loving responses that are typically associated with conscious social beings. These cues are not incidental but represent systematic social signals that foster emotional engagement.
In this contribution, we present empirical evidence from multiple datasets addressing two interconnected levels. First, we analyze system behavior and show that conversational agents consistently deploy social signals such as self-disclosure, empathy, and relational reassurance, closely mirroring patterns of human relationship initiation in a longitudinal study with N= 74 users over 4 weeks. Second, we examine relational outcomes on the user side. Our findings demonstrate that interactions with social AI can result in highly intense social bonds, including close emotional attachment and, in some cases, explicitly romantic relationships with chatbots (N = 93).
We theoretically embed these insights in an integrative process model of romantic human chatbot relationships, highlighting how repeated socially rich interactions foster escalating intimacy while raising tensions related to privacy data protection and structural power imbalances.

Algorithmic bias in generative AI: Prevalence and consequences for human information processing
Dr. Tanja Messingschlager | University of Würzburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tanja Messingschlager | University of Würzburg | Germany
Markus Appel | University of Würzburg | Germany

With the growing use of generative AI to create media content, bias in AI-generated outputs is a relevant topic at the intersection of psychology, communications science, and computer science. We focus on algorithmic bias, instances where systematic patterns in AI decisions or outputs unfairly advantage or disadvantage particular groups. This includes unequal representations compared to a baseline or stereotypical portrayals.
In our own research, we showed that image-generating AI models replicate common biases regarding women and men in STEM professions, and we identified stereotypical portrayals of men and women along the lines of the stereotype content model across three different AI models. Based on prior work showing that users see AI as objective and less intentional, leading to reduced moral outrage (algorithmic outrage deficit), we found that respondents are less likely to detect bias if they think images (of college students) are generated by an AI rather than a human. For images of older people, moral outrage in response to AI artist information increased, rather than decreased.
As part of a larger project, a recent interview study examined how people with different levels of AI usage (non-users to professional users) perceive bias in AI generated media content. Whereas many participants recognized that AI can produce biased outputs due to biased training data, they rarely acknowledged other sources of bias (e.g., probabilistic nature of AI). Regarding moral evaluations, AI was viewed as unable to reflect on its actions. Nevertheless, participants emphasized that AI should have the potential to incorporate diversity principles.

Biases in generative AI: The role of explainability and individual differences
Julian Bornemeier | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julian Bornemeier | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany
Stefan Brandenburg | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany
Jan-Philipp Stein | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany

As generative AI technology continues to shape various aspects of our everyday lives, it is essential to understand how users perceive and evaluate its outputs. Prior research emphasizes that generative AI tends to reinforce societal biases, particularly gender stereotypes.
While increasing AI transparency and explainability may foster the public’s understanding of the technology’s workings and related challenges, there is limited evidence of how individuals with different pre-existing attitudes respond to such interventional efforts.

This study investigates how transparency in AI usage impacts user evaluations of biases in AI-generated content—as well as their subsequent endorsement of fairness policies. Additionally, we explore how individual differences moderate these effects, placing a specific focus on social dominance orientation (SDO) as a factor that reflects the dispositional endorsement of hierarchies and discrimination.

In our between-subjects experiment (N = 550), participants were shown ten AI-generated videos representing STEM occupations. We manipulated two independent variables: the gender distribution of the depicted individuals (balanced vs. male-dominated) and the presence or absence of a prior transparency statement.

Results indicate that participants exposed to male-dominated AI content evaluated the videos as less fair. This effect was amplified by the presence of a transparency statement. Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) attenuated the effect of gender distribution on fairness evaluations. Additionally, higher SDO was associated with lower support for AI fairness policies.

Overall, this research contributes to a nuanced understanding of perceptions of biases in visual outputs generated by AI.

Quasi-social interactions with AI chatbots as a resource for critical media competences: The example of dialogical companion MATE in political education on antisemitism
Özen Odağ | Touro University Berlin. A Campus of Touro University New York. | Germany
Show details
Author:
Özen Odağ | Touro University Berlin. A Campus of Touro University New York. | Germany

As highlighted in previous contributions and other existing research, AI raises critical questions regarding bias and discrimination of social groups and is known to produce sexist, antisemitic, and racist content. In contrast, emerging efforts like Generative AI for Good are redirecting attention toward the application of generative AI in confronting these challenges and advancing ethically beneficial outcomes. The current theoretical contribution aligns with this objective, by examining the MATE project (Media – Antisemitism Prevention – Tolerance – Empowerment) - which illustrates how AI can be purposefully integrated into political education with the goal of strengthening democratic and resilient media competences.

MATE is conceptualized as an AI-supported chatbot, designed for antisemitism-critical media literacy education. It addresses the subtle and often normalized circulation of antisemitic narratives and coded symbols within digital media environments. Rather than positioning AI solely as a neutral tool for information delivery, the MATE approach frames AI as a pedagogical interaction partner that actively supports perspective-taking and the development of users’ critical judgment.

Grounded in media psychology and political education, MATE harnesses AI’s potential for ‘quasi-social interaction’ and integrates this with Socratic dialogue to engage young users in guided reflection. By responding adaptively to user input, the chatbot lowers identity-related and social barriers that often inhibit engagement with sensitive political topics such as antisemitism and other forms of discrimination. In doing so, MATE illustrates how generative AI can support political education not by replacing human educators, but by complementing them through dialogic and learner-centered formats guiding self-reflection.

Umweltschutz in Zeiten politischer Radikalisierung: Verschwörungsglauben, taktische Narrative und methodische Herausforderungen
Chair(s) Florian Kutzner (Privatuniversität Schloss Seeburg )
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Wilhelm Hofmann (Ruhr University Bochum)
Room: Workshop +1
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Fachgruppensymposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Die Gesellschaft scheint sich zunehmend zu polarisieren– mit weitreichenden Folgen für Umweltschutz und Klimapolitik. Rechtsradikale Parteien wie die AfD instrumentalisieren gezielt Anti-Windkraft-Sentimente, Verschwörungsnarrative verzerren den E-Mobilitätsdiskurs, und politische Polarisierung beeinflusst umweltrelevante Entscheidungen fundamental – vom Konsum- bis zum Wahlverhalten. Dieses Fachgruppen-Symposium möchte interdisziplinärere Denkanstöße für die Umweltpsychologie bieten: Wie beeinflusst politische Radikalisierung den Umweltschutz? Welche konzeptuellen und methodischen Herausforderungen stellen sich in diesem Fachgebiet? Und welche Strategien für evidenzbasierte Klimakommunikation lassen sich ableiten?

Radikalisierung der Mitte? Eine konzeptionelle Kritik
Dr. Fabian Heß | Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Fabian Heß | Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena | Germany

Aktuelle Debatten über den gesellschaftlichen Rechtsruck sprechen von einer „Radikalisierung der Mitte“ – einem (scheinbaren) Widerspruch, da Radikalisierung üblicherweise als Abweichung vom gesellschaftlichen Mainstream verstanden wird und folglich nicht mit diesem identisch sein kann. Mein Beitrag reflektiert theoretisch, was Radikalisierung bedeutet, und fragt, ob und wenn ja wie auch gesellschaftliche Mehrheiten radikale Positionen entwickeln können. Radikalisierung wird hierbei definiert als ein Prozess, in dem sich Menschen immer weiter von allgemein anerkannten Normen entfernen, während sie sich zugleich stärker an den Normen ihrer jeweiligen Gruppen orientieren. Obwohl es zunächst paradox erscheinen mag, dass eine gesellschaftliche „Mitte“ radikal werden kann (setzt diese doch üblicherweise die Norm), ist dies durchaus denkbar. Dies gilt insbesondere dann, wenn übergeordnete Normen – etwa moralische, rechtliche oder wissenschaftlich begründete Leitlinien – vorschreiben, wie gehandelt werden sollte, aber von verbreiteten gesellschaftlichen Mehrheitsmeinungen missachtet werden. Gerade in der Umweltpolitik wird dieses Spannungsverhältnis sichtbar: Während internationale Klimaziele oder wissenschaftliche Empfehlungen Handlungsnormen vorgeben, können nationale Mehrheiten oder populäre Diskurse diese Vorgaben relativieren oder ablehnen. In solchen Fällen kann der Mainstream von zentralen globalen Normen abweichen und damit selbst radikale Züge annehmen. Aus dieser Analyse ergeben sich drei Formen einer „radikalisierten Mitte“; jeweils aus der Diskrepanz einer übergeordneten injunktiven „Es soll so sein“-Norm und (1) dem Ist-Zustand des Handelns von Mainstream-Gruppen; (2) der quantitativen Überschätzung anderslautender „Es soll so sein“-Normen; oder (3) anderslautenden Soll-Normen, die logisch-hierarchisch untergeordnet sind, wie nationale Normen im Verhältnis zu internationalen Umwelt- oder Menschenrechtsstandards. Diese Perspektive kann dabei unterstützen, scheinbare Widersprüche im Konzept der „Radikalisierung der Mitte“ zu verstehen und aufzulösen.

Developments in public perceptions of the transformation in times of backlash - key results from the Social Sustainability Barometer
Jean-Henri Huttarsch | Research Institut for Sustainability Helmholtz Zentrum Potsdam (RIFS) | Germany
Show details
Author:
Jean-Henri Huttarsch | Research Institut for Sustainability Helmholtz Zentrum Potsdam (RIFS) | Germany

In democratic societies, large-scale change, such as sustainability transformations, ultimately depends on public support. Therefore, researchers and policymakers must understand public concerns and perceptions to ensure that sustainability transitions themselves are socially sustainable. In Germany, a tool shedding light on transformation-relevant public attitudes and behaviors is the Social Sustainability Barometer. In this talk, we present the continuation of this representative panel survey and key results from this year’s wave. Based on a yearly sample of about 6.500 participants, this panel survey provides one of the most detailed longitudinal accounts on how the public perceives transitions in the energy, transport and heating sectors in Germany. For each sector, we collect subjective perceptions across the five dimensions of socially sustainable societal transformations underlying the survey: acceptance, political participation, cohesion, socio-economic security, and quality of life. In the talk, we will illustrate the content of these dimensions with selected results. These include multi-year stability or erosion of general transitions support and acceptance of specific measures such as local renewable energy expansion, transition-specific beliefs and evaluations of participation opportunities, as well as discrepancies between actual and perceived public support for policies (pluralistic ignorance). Beyond these longitudinal results, we will highlight this year’s focal topic on public preferences about how to finance the transformation. Our goal is to discuss what it means for transformations to be socially sustainable and to empirically inform this debate as well as to spark interest in the data and motivate further research into the social conditions of successful sustainability transformations.

Verschwörungsglaube als Hindernis für den Umwelt- und Klimaschutz
Kevin Winter | Universität Hohenheim | Germany
Show details
Author:
Kevin Winter | Universität Hohenheim | Germany

Umwelt- und Klimaschutz geraten zunehmend ins Visier gezielter Desinformationskampagnen. Dabei wird weniger der Klimawandel als solches infrage gestellt wird, sondern vielmehr die Lösungen, die dazu beitragen, dem Klimawandel effektiv zu begegnen. Dieser Vortrag beleuchtet das Ausmaß der öffentlichen Zustimmung zu Misinformation und Verschwörungstheorien in Bezug auf zwei Kernthemen der Energiewende: Windenergie und Elektromobilität. In beiden Bereichen und in verschiedenen Ländern zeigen empirische Studien sehr ähnliche Ergebnismuster. Die Zustimmung zu einer Vielzahl verschiedener Misinformationen wird am besten von der generellen Neigung zum Verschwörungsglaube (sog. Verschwörungsmentalität) vorhergesagt. Wissenschaftliche Kenntnisse sowie der formale Bildungsgrad der Teilnehmenden spielten bei der Vorhersage kaum eine Rolle. Darüber hinaus gehen sowohl die Verschwörungsmentalität als auch die Zustimmung zu kontextspezifischen Verschwörungstheorien mit einer ablehnenden Haltung und oppositionellen Verhaltensabsichten gegenüber klimaschützenden politischen Maßnahmen einher. Längsschnittliche Daten weisen zudem darauf hin, dass Verschwörungsmentalität und die Ablehnung von Windkraft in einem wechselseitigen Zusammenhang stehen. Die Ablehnung von Windkraft (oder anderer Klimaschutzmaßnahmen) könnte also ein Einfallstor für eine breitere Skepsis gegenüber politischem Handeln und öffentlichen Institutionen sein. Die Studien liefern aber auch Erkenntnisse darüber, unter welchen Bedingungen die Bereitstellung von Fakten den Auswirkungen des Verschwörungsglaubens entgegenwirken kann. Die Befunde legen nahe, dass Fakten wirksamer sind, wenn sie kommuniziert werden, bevor sich konkrete Verschwörungstheorien festsetzen. Weitere Handlungsimplikationen für die Maßnahmengestaltung und politische Kommunikation sowie offene Fragen für Forschung und Praxis werden diskutiert.

Von Klimaskepsis zu Klimaverschwörungstheorien: Analyse sozialer Medien, um aufzudecken, was in Fragebögen nicht berichtet wird
Pia Lamberty | CeMAS | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Pia Lamberty | CeMAS | Germany
Dr. Helen Landmann | Universität Klagenfurt | Austria

Der Klimawandel stellt eine erhebliche Bedrohung für die Menschheit und den gesamten Planeten dar. Die Verbreitung von Verschwörungstheorien kann gemeinsame Bemühungen zur wirksamen Bekämpfung dieser Probleme behindern. Einige Menschen glauben an eine versteckte Agenda hinter der Energiewende, einige wenige glauben sogar an vollständige Verschwörungstheorien im Zusammenhang mit Maßnahmen zur Eindämmung des Klimawandels. Soziale Medien spielen eine wichtige Rolle bei der Verbreitung von Fehlinformationen. Insbesondere die Plattform Telegram wird häufig von Personen genutzt, die zu Verschwörungstheorien neigen, um ihre Ansichten zu verbreiten. Daher ist die Untersuchung von Verschwörungstheorien zum Klimawandel auf Telegram unerlässlich, um die zugrunde liegenden Narrative und psychologischen Auswirkungen in der realen (digitalen) Welt zu verstehen. Um zu untersuchen, wie sich leichte Skepsis zu vollständigen Verschwörungstheorien entwickelt, analysieren wir über einen Zeitraum von drei Jahren Beiträge in Telegram-Gruppen und -Kanälen, die sich kritisch mit dem Klimawandel auseinandersetzen. Wir diskutieren die Herausforderungen und Vorteile dieses Forschungsansatzes. Wenn Menschen Klimawissenschaft oder Klimaschutzinitiativen als Teil einer geheimen Agenda wahrnehmen, finden sachliche Informationen immer schwerer Anerkennung. Muster zu identifizieren, wie Zweifel und Fehlinformationen entstehen und sich verändern, ist wichtig, um Strategien entwickeln zu können, die einen konstruktiven Dialog fördern, das Vertrauen der Öffentlichkeit in den wissenschaftlichen Konsens stärken und den schädlichen Auswirkungen von Desinformation auf die gesellschaftlichen Bemühungen zur Bekämpfung des Klimawandels entgegenwirken.

Wie entstehen Einstellungen? Narrative Dynamiken in der Polarisierung des Umweltschutzes
Prof. Dr. Sina Leipold | Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Sina Leipold | Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena | Germany

Politische Polarisierung in Umweltdebatten wird häufig auf der Ebene individueller Einstellungen, Werte oder Fehlinformationen erklärt. Ich argumentiere, dass diese Variablen das Ergebnis vorgelagerter narrativer Prozesse sind. Narrative sind fundamentale Mechanismen unseres menschlichen Denkens. Nur mit ihrer Hilfe können wir definieren, was überhaupt als Problem gilt, wem Verantwortung zugeschrieben wird und welchem Wissen vertraut wird. Sie drücken Einstellungen, Werte und Interessen nicht nur aus – sie erzeugen sie.
Diese Narrative entstehen kollektiv und dynamisch in politischen Aushandlungsprozessen: in Gesetzgebungsverfahren, Bürgerbeteiligungen, Protesten und öffentlichen Kontroversen. Anhand von Fallstudien aus der Chemikalienregulierung, Stadt- und Energietransformation zeige ich, wie Narrative Aufmerksamkeit lenken, Risiken und Chancen unterschiedlich salient machen und damit Wahrnehmung, Vertrauen und Verhalten strukturieren. Sie prägen nicht nur Meinungen, sondern die Gegenstände, über die überhaupt Meinungen gebildet werden.
Dies erklärt, warum „neutrale“ Kommunikation wirkungslos bleiben kann. Information überzeugt selten isoliert, sondern nur eingebettet in eine als plausibel und legitim wahrgenommene Erzählung. Wo Klimapolitik als „versteckte Agenda“ gerahmt ist, verlieren Fakten an Glaubwürdigkeit, weil das Narrative definiert, wer als vertrauenswürdige Quelle gilt.
Für die Umweltpsychologie folgt daraus, Narrative als messbare Kontextfaktoren zu verstehen. Etwa als Treiber von Salienz, Vertrauenszuschreibungen und Identitätsbildung. Qualitative Narrativanalysen können systematisch zur Entwicklung von Surveys und Experimenten genutzt werden. Narrativforschung ergänzt damit quantitative Modelle, indem sie sichtbar macht, wie Einstellungen und Interessen sozial konstruiert werden, bevor sie gemessen werden.

Form of presentation: Position Paper
Duration: 90 Minutes

Torn in Two: How Attitudinal Conflict Can Drive and Prevent Sustainable Behavior Change
Dr. Benjamin Buttlar | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Benjamin Buttlar | Germany

Why do people struggle with adopting more sustainable behaviors, even when they know better? And why is sticking with a changed behavior so difficult? In this talk, I highlight a novel perspective on these questions: attitudinal conflicts as both an obstacle and a catalyst for behavior change by using meat consumption as a case study. At the macro level, I examine broader behavioral trends to show how felt ambivalence—the conflict of being torn between the pros and cons of a choice—can shape dietary transitions from omnivorism to vegetarianism and back again. At the micro level, I focus on individual decision moments, demonstrating how felt ambivalence arises before a choice and how dissonance emerges afterward. Crucially, I argue that these forms of conflict are interconnected due to their attitudinal roots: pre-decisional ambivalence influences post-decisional dissonance, and both shape each other over time. Using real-life eating decisions as examples, I show how conflicted choices, thereby, can accumulate to produce lasting attitudinal and dietary change. By linking these mechanistic psychological processes to broader behavioral outcomes, this approach provides a novel framework for understanding how behavior change unfolds. Recognizing and addressing attitudinal conflict in this way is not just theoretically interesting; it is the key to transforming everyday conflict into lasting, sustainable behavior.

08:45 am
Estimating the climate change mitigation potential of behavior change interventions
Prof. Malte Friese | Saarland University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Malte Friese | Saarland University | Germany
Maximilian Thiel
Kathi Diel | Saarland University | Germany

Behavioral interventions are an important means of addressing climate change. Interventions that are more effective as indicated by a standardized effect size are presumed to have greater potential to contribute to climate change mitigation. In this talk, we argue that current intervention design and reporting practices do not provide sufficiently robust evidence to inform public policy recommendations on the most promising behavioral interventions to tackle climate change. First, we explain why the effectiveness of interventions should be evaluated based on estimated reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, rather than standardized effect sizes. Second, from a public policy perspective, it is important to estimate the extent to which different interventions can prospectively contribute to climate change mitigation. To this end, we present a theoretical framework that illustrates that in order to estimate the climate change mitigation potential of an intervention, researchers need to consider the effect of the intervention, its persistence over time, and its scalability to large and diverse populations. These determinants can interact in different ways, and we illustrate how these interactions affect the climate change mitigation potential of an intervention. Not considering one or more components of the framework hinders researchers’ ability to identify the most promising behavioral interventions. We derive recommendations for the design and reporting of future behavioral interventions, which will allow public policy recommendations to be based on stronger evidence.

Nach dem Psychologie-Master promovieren? Informationen, Orientierung und Austausch
Ein Symposium für Promotionsinteressierte und Promovierende am Beginn ihrer Promotion
Chair(s) Dr. Matthias F.J. Sperl (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Psychologie (DGPs))
Luisa Baumgärtner (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Psychologie (DGPs))
Room: FR
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Das Symposium richtet sich an Studierende, die sich für eine Promotion in der Psychologie interessieren, sowie an Doktorand:innen in der frühen Phase der Promotion. Zur Zielgruppe zählen auch Doktorand:innen, die Interesse an einem Forschungsaufenthalt im Ausland haben oder eine parallele Aus- oder Weiterbildung in Psychotherapie in Erwägung ziehen. Im ersten Teil des Symposiums geben wir einen Überblick über verschiedene Promotionsmöglichkeiten in der Psychologie. Es werden zentrale Herausforderungen und Orientierungshilfen zur Suche nach geeigneten Betreuer:innen, zur Auswahl eines passenden Promotionsthemas sowie zu verschiedenen Finanzierungsmodellen diskutiert. Wir werden auch auf die Frage eingehen, wie eine Promotion mit einer Aus- oder Weiterbildung in Psychotherapie kombiniert werden kann. Im zweiten Beitrag werden Möglichkeiten vorgestellt, während der Promotion Forschungsaufenthalte im Ausland durchzuführen. Anschließend folgen Erfahrungsberichte von Personen, die derzeit Promotion und Psychotherapie-Weiterbildung kombinieren, die in Kooperation mit der Industrie promovieren, oder die ihre Dissertation an einem außeruniversitären Forschungsinstitut absolvieren. Abschließend skizzieren Vertreter:innen aus unterschiedlichen Teilgebieten der Psychologie kurz ihren individuellen Weg in die Promotion und in die wissenschaftliche Laufbahn. Es werden auch Jungmitgliedervertreter:innen aus unterschiedlichen Fachgruppen der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Psychologie (DGPs) anwesend sein. Dabei besteht die Möglichkeit, mit diesen Vertreter:innen individuell ins Gespräch zu kommen.

Start in die Promotion: Wege und Rahmenbedingungen in der Psychologie
Dr. Matthias F.J. Sperl | Deutsche Gesellschaft für Psychologie (DGPs) | Germany
Luisa Baumgärtner | Deutsche Gesellschaft für Psychologie (DGPs) | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Der Einfluss von Prompt-Instruktionen auf die Qualität von LLM-generierten Persönlichkeitsskalen
Lydia Oeljeklaus | Hochschule der Bundesagentur für Arbeit | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lydia Oeljeklaus | Hochschule der Bundesagentur für Arbeit | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stefan Höft | Hochschule der Bundesagentur für Arbeit | Germany
Prof. Dr. Daniel Danner | Hochschule der Bundesagentur für Arbeit | Germany

Große Sprachmodelle (Large Language Models; LLMs) werden zunehmend als Tools für die automatische Generierung von Items und Skalen in der psychologischen Diagnostik untersucht. Bisher ist jedoch wenig darüber bekannt, inwiefern Variationen in Prompt-Instruktionen die psychometrische Qualität dieser LLM-generierten Skalen beeinflussen können. Um dies zu untersuchen, wurden einem generischen LLM (GPT-4o) sieben verschiedene Prompt-Instruktionen gegeben. Eine Instruktion hielt sich ausschließlich an die Prinzipien des Prompt Engineering, während die anderen sechs auf die Itemschwierigkeit, Konstruktfacetten, interne Konsistenz, konvergente Validität und diskriminante Validität abzielten. Es wurden Items für zwei Konstrukte generiert: Emotionale Stabilität und Klimaangst. Neben den LLM-generierten Skalen wurden das extra kurze Big-Five-Inventar, sowie jeweils ein Single Item zu Lebenszufriedenheit, selbsteingeschätzter Gesundheit und der Anzahl von Krankheitstagen in den letzten zwölf Monaten erhoben und zusätzlich demographische Daten erfasst. In die Datenanalyse konnten Daten von 1334 Studienteilnehmenden einfließen. Die durch das LLM generierten Items und Skalen werden anhand ihrer Schwierigkeit, Modellpassung, Faktorstruktur, Reliabilität und Validität bewertet. Die Ergebnisse dieses akzeptierten Registered Reports werden vorgestellt und diskutiert.

Can Artificial Intelligence Support Conflict Resolution? An Experimental Study on the Ef-fectiveness of AI-Generated Videos on Conflict-Related Attitudes and Behaviors
Dr. Martina Grunenberg | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Martina Grunenberg | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Dr. Svenja C. Schütt | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt
Christopher Esch | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Elisabeth Kals | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jürgen Maes | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany

Previous research indicates that low-threshold interventions, such as videos, can positively influence individuals’ conflict attitudes and conflict-related behavior (Grunenberg et al., 2025). However, producing such videos is often resource-intensive, requiring considerable time, personnel, and financial investment. With the growing accessibility of Artificial Intelligence (AI) an important question arises: Can AI enable a more resource-efficient production of conflict interventions without compromising their effectiveness?
Building on prior research, this study examines the effects of AI-generated conflict videos on individual conflict attitudes and behavior and compares these effects with those of traditionally produced videos featuring real human speakers. Using an experimental longitudinal design, we collected data from an intervention group (N = 1533) over a period of 15 weeks, comprising five survey waves. Outcomes were compared with existing data from an intervention group exposed to human-based videos (N = 1567) and a control group (N = 636).
Mixed Models with Repeated Measures (MMRMs) revealed that AI-generated videos significantly reduced negatively experienced feelings toward conflict and promoted productive conflict behavior. However, these effects were weaker than those observed for human-based videos. In addition, subgroup analyses comparing participants with low versus high sympathy toward the video speakers highlight the importance of identification with the speakers. Speaker sympathy was generally lower for AI-generated videos than for human-based videos, potentially explaining the reduced effectiveness.
Overall, this study provides initial evidence for the potential of AI-assisted science communication in the field of conflict intervention, while also underscoring important design limitations and challenges.

Mapping Psychology Students’ Conversations with a Large Language Model (LLM)-Powered Statistics Chatbot
Leonardo Bergmann | Universität Wien, Fakultät für Psychologie | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Leonardo Bergmann | Universität Wien, Fakultät für Psychologie | Austria
Luis Britz | Universität Wien, Fakultät für Psychologie | Austria
Prof. Benjamin Roth | Universität Wien
Dr. Ulrich S. Tran | Universität Wien, Fakultät für Psychologie

Despite the growing prominence of large language models (LLMs) in research, studies investigating real-world interactions with LLMs in academic settings remain rare. We address this research gap by analyzing 1,360 personal chats with StatsBot, a statistics chatbot powered by OpenAI’s GPT-4o and openly available to students at the Faculty of Psychology at the University of Vienna. The chats originate from 168 Bachelor’s and Master’s students who used StatsBot between March and June 2025 and were examined using a combination of deductive and inductive content analysis. Parts of this process were automated using GPT-5, as reliability evaluations indicated near–human-level performance. Deductive content analysis revealed that most chats (93%) were related to statistics, with 49% focusing on specific statistical methods. Master’s students more frequently sought help with data analysis software, whereas Bachelor’s students primarily used StatsBot to answer multiple-choice questions, likely derived from past exams. Differences in communication style were also observed: Bachelor’s students mainly asked short questions in German, while Master’s students showed a slight tendency to communicate in English, provide more detailed instructions, and use politeness expressions. Results from the inductive content analysis aggregate specific use cases and identify recurring themes of StatsBot usage (e.g., on non-statistical interactions or specific methods). Overall, this study provides empirical evidence of real-world interactions with LLMs in an academic setting, offering detailed insights into both the statistical topics students seek assistance with and how they communicate with an AI chatbot. All data and analyses are openly shared with the scientific community.

Symbolic, neural, and neuro-symbolic AI for evaluating graphical test responses
Dr. Sonja Hahn | DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Sonja Hahn | DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education | Germany
Dr. Fabian Zehner | DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education | Germany
Longwei Cong | DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education
Prof. Ulf Kroehne | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany

While AI approaches have been frequently applied to evaluate text responses from assessments, corresponding approaches from computer vision for evaluating graphical responses like free hand drawings are less researched . Within the field of AI, several paradigms have evolved, including so-called symbolic or explicit approaches (i.e., transparent to humans, mimicking expert decisions or yielding interpretable coefficients) and – as an alternative approach – deep neural networks (e.g., using transformer architectures). Currently, neuro-symbolic approaches have emerged with the objective of combining the advantages of deep neural architectures with those of explicitly designed systems.

The present contribution compares three exemplary procedures based on data from an applied assessment (hand-drawn fraction bars, two items with n=95 / n=91 student responses). Each drawing provides information on several learner concepts, captured by a distinct classification task, respectively.

The different approaches yield

- for a rule-based symbolic approach: adequate and consistent results (F1=0.76–0.92 / F1=0.87–0.98; range on classification tasks for first/second item);
- for a pretrained neural network: mixed results (F1=0.02–0.96 / F1=0.23–0.94);
- for a hybrid approach (training neural network on data generated with a prespecified scheme): very effective behavior except for one classification task for the second item (F1=0.80–0.98 / F1=0.34–0.99).

We discuss shortcomings of these approaches (e.g., pretrained neural networks’ lack of counting capabilities), propose strategies for transfer to other items, and elaborate on possibilities for improvement based on observed misclassified responses. These follow the notion of the neuro-symbolic paradigm and illustrate how symbolic and neural approaches can be fused in different ways.

Faking Human? Detecting AI Agents in Online Survey Responses
Dr. Kristin Jankowsky | University of Kassel | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Kristin Jankowsky | University of Kassel | Germany
Dr. Leon Wendt
Prof. Johannes Zimmermann
Prof. Ulrich Schroeders

An increasing number of social scientists rely on online testing to obtain large, heterogeneous samples in a cost- and time-efficient manner. It is estimated that approximately half of all studies published in social and personality psychology now utilise online samples, with platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk and Prolific supporting hundreds of thousands of studies annually. However, recent studies have demonstrated that artificial agents that employ large language models (LLMs) can autonomously complete online surveys and produce coherent, consistent responses that mimic attentive human participants. This raises concerns that participants with fraudulent intentions may use such tools to receive financial gratification, thereby threatening the integrity of online research. In this study, we examined which detection techniques may be used to differentiate between human and LLM-generated data. Our sample comprised 500 responses from human participants recruited from Prolific and 500 responses generated by GPT-5 agents. We employed a variety of indicators, including traditional measures of careless or inconsistent responding, incidental data (e.g. response times and click counts), and novel tasks designed to detect LLM responses. Using a decision tree model that incorporated the most effective indicators for distinguishing between human and LLM-generated responses (i.e., mouse movements, performance in declarative knowledge and maze-solving tasks), we were able to classify respondents correctly into humans or agents with 98% accuracy. We provide researchers with recommendations for designing and implementing procedures that improve the detection of LLM-generated responses and thereby help safeguard the credibility of online survey data now and in the future.

Reasons for Effect Size Variability
Chair(s) Jens Fünderich (LMU München)
Maximilian Frank (LMU Munich)
Room: NL
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Variation in effect sizes - commonly referred to as heterogeneity - poses a central challenge for interpreting replication studies and for building cumulative psychological theory. When heterogeneity is substantial but poorly understood, apparent replication failures may reflect systematic contextual dependence rather than the absence of an effect. This symposium brings together methodological, empirical, and theoretical perspectives to examine when, why, and how effect sizes vary across studies, and what this implies for replicability and generalizability in the behavioral, social, and cognitive sciences. Across six contributions, the symposium investigates multiple sources and mechanisms of heterogeneity, including manipulation strength and scaling of effects, functional relationships between predictors and outcomes, cultural and contextual variation in decision processes, and the joint influence of person-level and study-level factors.
Several talks draw on data from a novel ManyClusters design, which uses clustering variables to construct a meta-analytic panel structure from a single large dataset. This approach enables resource-efficient exploration of heterogeneity patterns typically studied in multi-lab replications and meta-analyses. Complementing these empirical analyses, simulation-based modeling work examines how heterogeneity emerges under realistic data-generating processes, investigating relative contributions to heterogeneity, and evaluates performance and interpretation of commonly used heterogeneity estimators in meta-analytic workflows.
The symposium aims to advance both conceptual understanding and methodological practice by identifying conditions under which heterogeneity is expected, detectable, and informative, thereby improving the interpretation of replication evidence and supporting more robust cumulative science.

A data-generating model to understand heterogeneity
Maximilian Frank | LMU Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Maximilian Frank | LMU Munich | Germany
Moritz Heene | LMU Munich

Variation in effect sizes is a central challenge for psychological theory and for interpreting replication studies. When heterogeneity is substantial but poorly understood, replication estimates become hard to generalize, and apparent “failures to replicate” may reflect contextual dependence rather than the absence of an effect. In practice, replications often vary experimental features unsystematically, even though many factors can influence effect sizes (e.g., sampling, experimental setups, operationalisation). Meanwhile, commonly used heterogeneity statistics and standard two-stage meta-analytic workflows have methodological limitations. This combination can lead researchers to underestimate the uncertainty of meta-analytic conclusions. To clarify how heterogeneity arises and how it should be modeled, we present a data-generating model that jointly models person-level and study-level sources of variation. The model captures heterogeneity within studies (e.g. individual differences across respondents) and between studies (e.g., design differences across labs). Simulation parameters are calibrated to empirically plausible ranges using evidence from large-scale replication initiatives in psychology and the social sciences (e.g. ManyLabs, Registered Replication Reports). We analyze heterogeneity measures (e.g., tau, I2, coefficient of variation) based on these simulated datasets using conventional two-stage meta-analysis and location–scale models that allow heterogeneity to vary across subgroups and contexts. By systematically manipulating contextual and individual-level factors, we identify conditions under which heterogeneity is expected, detectable and which factors contribute to it. The results inform the interpretation of replication results and provide guidance for designing future replication studies by choosing analytic models that better support claims about replicability and generalizability in psychological research.

Untangling the Group Association: Exploring Meta-Analytic Heterogeneity through Clustering
Teresa Rupprecht | LMU Munich
Show details
Authors:
Teresa Rupprecht | LMU Munich
Jens H. Fünderich | LMU Munich | Germany
Frank Renkewitz | University of Erfurt

Large-scale collaborative projects such as the ManyLabs initiatives have substantially advanced psychological science by testing the robustness and generalizability of empirical effects across diverse samples and settings. However, ManyLabs studies typically collect only a limited number of person-related characteristics, constraining the extent to which individual differences can be examined as potential sources of variance in observed effects. The current ManyClusters project addresses this limitation by incorporating a broader range of person-related variables into a ManyLabs-style research design. These variables include demographic data such as age, gender, and place of residence, as well as personality characteristics and preferences.

Using these variables, we form empirically derived participant clusters and treat each cluster as an individual implementation of the same study. This approach allows us to examine whether effect sizes vary systematically across clusters, thereby assessing heterogeneity attributable to person-related differences rather than sampling variability alone. In the first ManyClusters study, we applied this approach to several well-established psychological phenomena, including the halo effect, the sunk cost effect, and the anchoring effect.

By examining the extent to which effect estimates differ across person-based clusters, we can evaluate whether person-related characteristics meaningfully structure variation in psychological effects. Evidence of systematic heterogeneity across clusters would suggest that such characteristics exert a stronger influence on psychological outcomes than is typically assumed. More broadly, these findings would underscore the importance of more routinely measuring and incorporating person-related variables in the design, analysis, and interpretation of psychological research, particularly in large-scale collaborative and replication-oriented studies.

Scaling Effects to Study Heterogeneity: When Does Variability Track Effect Size?
Frank Renkewitz | LMU Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Frank Renkewitz | LMU Munich | Germany
Teresa Rupprecht | LMU Munich | Germany
Jens H. Fünderich | LMU Munich | Germany

Meta-research synthesizing large numbers of psychological meta-analyses, along with re-analyses of multicenter replication projects across a wide range of phenomena, has repeatedly reported a substantial association between mean effect size and heterogeneity. In other words, variability across repeated tests of the same hypothesis appears to increase as the average effect increases.
If this pattern is general, it has far-reaching implications for both single-study interpretation and the quantification of heterogeneity. It implies, for example, that large effects observed in individual studies may be estimated with lower precision and may generalize less reliably than smaller effects. It also suggests that heterogeneity cannot be meaningfully compared across substantive domains without accounting for the corresponding effect magnitudes. At the same time, the mechanisms that generate this association remain unclear.
To better identify these mechanisms, we shift the focus from comparing different phenomena to comparing scalable effects within the same phenomena. In the ManyClusters study, we systematically varied manipulation strength for four established paradigms, thereby inducing graded variation in effect size within each paradigm. When pooling data across paradigms, we again observe a substantial positive association between effect size and heterogeneity. Within paradigms, however, the association varies markedly and is absent in some cases. This pattern suggests that heterogeneity across phenomena reflects not only differences in moderators but also differences in underlying causal processes. We discuss how distinct empirical patterns constrain candidate explanations of heterogeneity and outline implications for measuring and interpreting heterogeneity more broadly.

Functional Relationship Advice – Assessing the Association between Non-Linearity and Effect Heterogeneity in ManyClusters data
Jens H. Fünderich | LMU Munich
Show details
Authors:
Jens H. Fünderich | LMU Munich
Teresa Rupprecht | LMU Munich
Frank Renkewitz | LMU Munich

The functional relationship between the predictor and the outcome is rarely considered among the many potential explanations in the literature on effect heterogeneity in experimental designs. Often, the predictor is represented only by a simple comparison between conditions, severely restricting the analytical options to get any insight into the functional relationship. Manipulation checks and designs that vary the manipulation strength across experimental conditions have been proposed to overcome that limitation. In the ManyClusters approach, we implemented both to explore their informational value regarding the functional relationship and its relationship to meta-analytic effect heterogeneity. One of the challenges of investigating non-linearity in an experimental context is that many of the existing analyses and interpretations from observational data are not applicable. I present analytical solutions, for example via model-comparisons, on how to reject the assumption of a linear functional relationship with data from the ManyClusters pilot. The presentation also covers an exploration of the association between meta-analytic effect heterogeneity and the functional relationship, as well as simulations to evaluate sample size requirements for this type of design and analysis.

Culture as a Source of Heterogeneity in Models of Decision Making Processes
Rima-Maria Rahal | Vienna University of Economics and Business | Austria
Show details
Author:
Rima-Maria Rahal | Vienna University of Economics and Business | Austria

Much contemporary theorizing on how people make decisions follows the Lewinian principle that behavior is a function of person and situation. This framework treats both variables, and their interaction, as potential sources of heterogeneity. But where does the situation end and the culture begin? Treating culture as a mere component of situational context risks obscuring distinct, higher level factors that influence cognition and behavior. Concurrently, psychological theories of cultural influences on cognition and behavior have long stipulated that culture warrants consideration. Still, although situational heterogeneity is commonly recognized, most models of decision processes are mute on whether effects generalize across cultures. Empirical investigations also tend to omit testing variability between cultures as a source of potential heterogeneity.

Using an example of normative decision making, I assess processes that depend on theoretically postulated cultural differences in tightness-looseness across eight countries. I study sources of heterogeneity at the level of process data obtained via eye tracking, as well as at the level of choice data obtained in two incentivized games, assessing heterogeneity both in predicting underlying decision processes and observable decision outcomes. I model person-level differences in social norm espousal, situational differences in game type, and country-level differences. Data from 1110 participants demonstrate substantial heterogeneity across factors. I discuss the formal inclusion of culture, alongside person and situation, as a source of heterogeneity in psychological effects, both for modeling decision behavior and for modeling underlying cognitive processes.

Trust Across Digital Interactions: Explanations, Nudges, Transparency, and Trust Repair
Psychological Dynamics of Trust in the Digital Age
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Markus Langer (Universität Freiburg)
Room: FI
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

This symposium brings together research on the conditions, mechanisms, and challenges of trust in digital and AI‑related application contexts. At its core lies the question of how people evaluate digital and AI‑supported processes and which factors guide their trust development. The contributions of this symposium shed light on a) how different trust violations by an AI chatbot affect customer trust and customer behavior, b) how different AI explanations in recruiting shape perceptions of fairness and trust, c) how digital nudges in tourism can be designed to be effective and whether nudge effectiveness depends on trust in the nudge provider, d) how AI‑based transparency mechanisms can reduce misunderstandings in dynamic pricing and e) how trust violations in online consumer relationships emerge and can be repaired through attributional processes. This symposium closes with f) a theoretical contribution which tries to concretize the concept of “calibrated trust” and identifies points in the trust development process that can be calibrated in order to achieve better joint human-AI decision performance. Together, the contributions provide an integrated view of the psychological dynamics of trust in the digital age.

The Trust Calibration Points Framework - A Revised Theory for Trust Calibration in Automation and Artificial Intelligence
Nadine Frauke Schlicker | Philipps-Universität Marburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Markus Langer | Institut für Psychologie
Show details
Authors:
Nadine Frauke Schlicker | Philipps-Universität Marburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Markus Langer | Institut für Psychologie
Dr. Matouš Jelínek | University of Southern Denmark | Denmark
Prof. Dr. Ewart de Visser | George Mason University | United States

As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports human decision-making, addressing the challenge of opaque models and fostering trust in AI systems becomes critical. Trust in AI must be “calibrated” - enabling users to rely on accurate recommendations and reject incorrect ones. Calibrated trust is therefore considered an important factor for human-AI decision-making. However, definitions on "calibrated trust" are heterogeneous and research on “calibrated trust” often lacks conceptual clarity, which highlights the need for a unified model that integrates different approaches. We argue that this heterogeneity stems from the lack of a unified trust model. Building on the Trustworthiness Assessment Model and the Organizational Trust Model, we propose the Trust-Calibration Points (T-CaP) Framework as a solution. Within the T-CaP framework, we identify and elaborate on six calibration points within the trust development process that help a) to diagnose where a potential miscalibration might have occurred, and b) how to counteract these miscalibrations. These points include maximum joint performance benchmarking, trustworthiness assessment, alignment of individual standards, risk-benefit assessment, dispositions, and behavioral adaptation. By providing theoretical and terminological clarity, the T-CaP framework addresses conceptual challenges and offers actionable insights for researchers and practitioners to refine trust calibration and improve collaboration between humans and AI systems

Fairness or Efficiency? How AI Explanations and Individual Career Goals Influence Reactions to AI-Supported Recruitment
Prof. Dr. Julia Hiemer | Technical University of Applied Sciences Würzburg-Schweinfurt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Julia Hiemer | Technical University of Applied Sciences Würzburg-Schweinfurt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christine Hennighausen | Ingolstadt University of Applied Sciences | Germany

In today’s organizations, recruitment processes increasingly involve AI, yet its use can adversely affect candidates' perceptions of justice regarding the recruitment process and trust in the company. Providing explanations for why AI is implemented in the process may enhance candidates’ perceptions of justice and trust, but more research is needed to identify which explanations are specifically effective. Furthermore, the impact of candidates’ individual career goals (agentic vs. communal) on these perceptions remains underexplored. This study utilizes the model of agency and communion to examine the impacts of fairness versus efficiency explanations for the use of AI in the recruitment process. An online experiment with N = 210 participants assessed the effects of the explanation type on perceptions of justice, trust, organizational attractiveness, and application intention. Participants were randomly assigned to a recruiting scenario that either emphasized the use of AI to enhance fairness and to reduce bias or described the use of AI to enhance efficiency and speed. Moreover, participants indicated their career goals and their attitude towards AI. Results revealed that specifically participants with strong agentic goals perceived greater justice and organizational attractiveness and were more likely to apply for a job at the company when the use of AI was described as being for efficiency reasons. Additionally positive attitudes towards AI enhanced company perceptions on all dependent variables. The results shed light on the complex interplay between individual differences and perceptions of AI in a recruiting process.

The role of trust in the context of acceptance and effectiveness of digital behavior-oriented interventions
Malin Anna Wenzke | Lucerne School of Business | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Malin Anna Wenzke | Lucerne School of Business | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Jörn Basel | Lucerne School of Business | Switzerland

In tourism, around three-quarters of emissions stem from travel to and from destinations, making travellers' decisions about their means of transport key. Although nudging tourists – motivating them to behave in the desired manner through targeted incentives without restricting their freedom of choice – is considered a promising approach, there is a significant research gap in tourism mobility. This research, conducted with the Swiss destination Arosa, aims to motivate tourists to arrive by public transport through targeted digital nudges. Additionally, it explores whether their effectiveness depends on trust in the nudge provider, which has not been researched in this domain, although it could be central to the design of effective measures. To achieve the research objectives, various digital, cognitive nudges were designed and tested in an online pre-post experiment with a representative sample of urban Double-Income-No-Kids (DINKs) in Switzerland (N = 413). The design pursued three objectives: identifying factors influencing tourists' decision-making behaviour when choosing a means of transport, measuring the effectiveness of nudges, and evaluating the influence of trust in Arosa as a nudge provider on the effectiveness of nudges. The results show that hedonic motivation influences attitudes towards travelling by public transport, which in turn predicts intention, alongside habitual mobility behaviour. Nudges addressing social norms, hedonic motives, and provided identity-building information produced the strongest increases in the intention to travel to Arosa by public transport. However, trust did not moderate the effectiveness of the nudges.

AI-Enabled Transparency as a Trust-Building Mechanism in Dynamic Pricing: Insights from Mountain Railway Booking Platforms
Preveen Panakkal | Lucerne School of Business | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Preveen Panakkal | Lucerne School of Business | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Jörn Basel | Lucerne School of Business | Switzerland

Dynamic pricing (DP) has become increasingly widespread across industries , especially in tourism-related sectors. However, the underlying logic of DP often remains opaque. This lack of transparency risks lowering perceived price fairness and undermining customer trust. Increasing perceived transparency is therefore central to safeguarding trust in DP contexts, as emphasised by Tomlinson and Schnackenberg (2022). A promising approach to enhancing transparency is the use of an AI-chatbot capable of explaining price changes through personalised communication. Such an adaptive system can address individual concerns and prevalent myths surrounding DP, thereby counteracting misunderstandings that contribute to distrust. The present research examines whether interaction with an AI-based chatbot can strengthen customer trust in mountain railway booking platforms employing DP. In a first step, public reviews of mountain railway providers using DP will be qualitatively analysed. Through a systematically developed coding scheme, these reviews will be categorised to identify dominant customer myths and concerns related to DP. These insights will inform the design of an adaptive chatbot tailored to address these misconceptions and enhance perceived transparency. To evaluate the effectiveness of this intervention, an experimental online study with a between-subjects design will simulate a booking process with and without chatbot interaction. Potential mountain railway customers will be recruited via convenience sampling. As one of the first studies in this domain, the project explores the potential of AI as a facilitator of transparency and a driver of customer trust, contributing to greater acceptance of dynamic pricing.

Trust Violated, Trust Lost? How AI Chatbot Trust Violations Undermine Customer Trust and Purchase Intent, and Increase Negative Word-of-Mouth
Prof. Dr. Christine Hennighausen | Ingolstadt University of Applied Sciences | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Christine Hennighausen | Ingolstadt University of Applied Sciences | Germany
Vanessa Gabriela Yarza Navarro-Schär | Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. Eric Eller | Ingolstadt University of Applied Sciences | Germany
Marina Hofmann | Ingolstadt University of Applied Sciences | Germany

As AI chatbots increasingly mediate early customer–company interactions, understanding how trust can be disrupted in digital encounters becomes crucial. Drawing on trust literature, this study examines how the severity and type of AI chatbot trust violations (integrity-based vs. performance-based) affect trust in the chatbot, trust in the company using the chatbot, and subsequent customer behavior. In an online experiment (N = 469), participants were exposed to a depicted AI chatbot–customer interaction embedded in a vignette. Trust violations were manipulated by varying severity (low vs. high) and type (integrity-based vs. performance-based), alongside a no-violation control condition. Trust in the AI chatbot and in the company was measured after a neutral baseline interaction (T1) and again after a trust violation (T2). Purchase intention and negative word of mouth were assessed at T2. Results show that chatbot trust violations substantially reduced trust in the chatbot and, in turn, trust in the company compared to no violation. High-severity violations led to stronger trust erosion than low-severity violations, and integrity-based violations reduced trust more strongly than performance-based violations. Component-level analyses confirmed the specific nature of trust violations: integrity-based violations primarily undermined perceived integrity, whereas performance-based violations mainly reduced perceived competence. Serial mediation analyses further demonstrated that negative effects on customer behavior such as purchase intent and increase in negative word-of-mouth were transmitted through sequential reductions in trust in the chatbot and trust in the company.

One standard for me, another for you? Self-presentation and evaluation of AI use at work
Sophie Kerstan | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sophie Kerstan | Germany
Prof. Dr. Markus Langer | Uni Freiburg

AI is now widely used in office-based and knowledge-intensive work. However, experimental research suggests that such use can trigger negative evaluations of AI users (e.g., lower perceived competence). Beyond these experimental studies conducted primarily online, little is known about how presentation and evaluation of AI use emerge in organizational contexts. Understanding these processes is critical, as both concealed and openly disclosed AI use may entail adverse consequences (e.g., hidden AI-dependencies or employee evaluation penalties).
We report findings from 26 semi-structured interviews with employees across different occupations and industries examining how individuals talk about their own and evaluate others’ AI use, and which factors shape these processes.
Preliminary analyses using Grounded Theory reveal tensions between normative expectations regarding effort and competence and efficiency demands. These tensions structure both self-presentation and evaluations of AI use. Based on our data, we develop a typology of communication strategies (e.g., full disclosure, selective disclosure, concealment, active misrepresentation) employees use to navigate these tensions and their conditioning factors. Moreover, we find paradoxical evaluation patterns: factors invoked to legitimize one’s own AI use are not applied similarly when evaluating others’ use.
With this study, we extend existing research on impression management and attribution by linking communication strategies in the context of AI use to this literature. In addition, the findings provide starting points for designing work environments that foster open and effective AI use.
Future studies should validate the identified mechanisms using additional data sources (e.g., peer/supervisor ratings), as our analyses rely solely on interview data.

Health and Well-Being in Academia: Risks, Resources, and Responsibilities
Chair(s) Dr. Melanie Vilser (University of the Bundeswehr Munich)
Room: GR
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Health and well-being in academia have gained increasing attention in recent years, especially in the context of ongoing discussions about working conditions and the challenges faced by early career researchers. Following the strong interest generated by the symposium on this topic at the last DGPS Congress in Vienna, the topic is again addressed in a dedicated and structured symposium. The aim is to offer a compressive overview of mental health challenges along the academic trajectory.

The symposium brings together several contributions based on recent scientific studies covering different stages of the academic pathway. It begins with a focus on students, then moves to doctoral researchers, broadens the focus to power relations in academia, and finally considers the responsibilities and support structures of academic institutions. This structure makes it possible to illuminate individual, relational, and systematic factors influencing well-being in academia.

The key questions guiding the symposium are: a) How do effort-reward imbalance and fear of exams contribute to psychological strain in students? (Speaker: Jagla-Franke); b) How does boundary management influence early career researchers’ well-being (i.e., emotional exhaustion and work-nonwork balance)? (Speaker: Vilser); c) How can abusive behaviour within academic power structures be systematically captured? (Speaker: Vogel) and d) To what degree do German graduate institutions view the mental health of doctoral researchers as part of their responsibility, have sufficient resources at their disposal, and implement corresponding services? (Speaker: Bauer)

The goal is to provide insight into the latest scientific findings on the well-being of (doctoral) students and to stimulate discussion on how to foster a healthier and more supportive academic work environment.

Effort–Reward Imbalance, Test Anxiety, and Sleep Problems in College Students Across an Examination Period: A pilot study
Prof. Dr. Melanie Jagla-Franke | Hochschule Neubrandenburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Melanie Jagla-Franke | Hochschule Neubrandenburg | Germany
Michelle Röder | Hochschule Neubrandenburg | Germany
Jonas Hänsel | Hochschule Neubrandenburg | Germany
Theresa Wendt | Hochschule Neubrandenburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Gabriele Helga Franke | Hochschule Magdeburg-Stendal | Germany

Background: The present study aimed to examine temporal changes in effort-reward imbalance (ERI) and to identify student subgroups with distinct ERI profiles and associated risk patterns. Students experience increased stress and health problems during examination periods. While test anxiety and sleep disturbances are well documented, less is known about their interplay with effort–reward imbalance.

Method: Based on Siegrist’s ERI model, college students completed the ERI-Student version, the Insomnia Severity Index, and the Test Anxiety Inventory 4 weeks before (T1; n=79), during (T2; n=30), and 4 weeks after the exam period (T3; n=21) by using an online survey. Due to dropout, temporal changes were evaluated exploratively. A k-means cluster analysis (three-cluster solution) was conducted using ERI data at T1 to identify risk groups.

Results: No significant changes over time emerged across measures, likely due to reduced sample size. The cluster analysis revealed a low-risk group (n=36: low effort, high reward, low overcommitment), a moderate-risk group (n=24: moderate effort, reward, and overcommitment), and a high-risk group (n=19: high effort, low reward, high overcommitment). The high-risk cluster reported substantially higher test anxiety (η²=.33) and more sleep problems (η²=.21) compared with the other clusters. Similar patterns appeared at T2 and T3, with the high-risk cluster consistently showing elevated test anxiety.

Conclusion: Findings indicate that typical ERI profiles are present among college students and that a high-risk profile is consistently associated with pronounced test anxiety and sleep problems. The results underscore the need for targeted preventive measures within student health management.

Integrating the Effort-Reward Imbalance Model Into the Stressor-Detachment Model in Academia: Examining the Moderating Effect of Boundary Management
Dr. Melanie Vilser | University of the Bundeswehr Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Melanie Vilser | University of the Bundeswehr Munich | Germany
Hannah Jannott | Ludwig-Maximilians-University | Germany

Background: Early career researchers in Germany often face adverse working conditions, including high workload, time pressure, fixed-term contracts, and a lack of recognition from their supervisors/superiors. Thus, they may experience a subjective imbalance between high effort and low reward. The present study explores the relationship between effort-reward imbalance (ERI) and early career researchers’ well-being (i.e., emotional exhaustion and work-nonwork balance) by integrating the ERI model into the Stressor-Detachment Model. Therefore, the underlying mechanism of psychological detachment is tested. Furthermore, the use of boundary management tactics as a problem-focused coping strategy is examined.

Method: An online survey with 320 early career researchers from German universities/research institutes was conducted. A second measurement point was included six weeks later to gain a more comprehensive view.

Results: The results show that ERI (high effort/low reward) was positively associated with emotional exhaustion and negatively associated with work-nonwork balance. The mediating role of psychological detachment was only observed for work-nonwork balance as an outcome, while no mediating effect was found for emotional exhaustion. Contrary to the assumptions, the use of boundary management tactics did not moderate the relationship between ERI and psychological detachment and, thus, did not function as a coping strategy. Surprisingly, doctoral students and postdocs reported similar levels of emotional exhaustion and work-nonwork balance.

Discussion: The subjectively perceived imbalance between high effort and low reward can be considered a risk factor for early career researchers’ well-being, specifically for their emotional exhaustion and work-nonwork balance.

Development of a Measurement Instrument to Operationalize Power Abuse in Academia
Dr. Olga Vogel | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Olga Vogel | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jan Schilling | HSBI University of Applied Sciences and Arts Bielefeld | Germany
Prof. Dr. Annette Kluge | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany

Background: Abuse of power is receiving increasing attention within the academic landscape. Based on the recommendation of the DGPs Commission “Incentive Systems, Abuse of Power, and Scientific Misconduct” to conduct regular surveys at universities, the Self-Check Questionnaire on Abuse of Power in Academia was developed and initially validated in this study. It comprises three scales: personal boundary violations, task-related boundary violations, and affective reactions.

Method: N = 326 participants completed an online survey including the newly developed instrument, as well as measures of occupational and general self-efficacy, irritation, and intention to leave university and academia, along with demographic information.

Results: The findings indicate that experiences of power abuse are not isolated incidents and that task-related boundary violations occur more frequently than personal ones. Negative affective reactions to both task-related and personal boundary violations are associated with increased irritation and a stronger desire to leave university and academia. Contrary to expectations, all three scales showed positive correlations with aspects of self-efficacy related to managing professional challenges.

Discussion: The developed instrument can be applied in research, as an intervention tool within organizational development processes, and as part of psychological risk assessments in the workplace.

Supporting Doctoral Researchers’ Well-Being: Insights from a Nationwide Survey of German Graduate Institutions on Mental Health-Related Services
Dr. Jana F. Bauer | University of Cologne | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Jana F. Bauer | University of Cologne | Germany
Viola Gründemann | Leipzig University | Germany
Dr. Nicole Sachmerda-Schulz | iDiv | Germany
Dr. Anke Soellner | University of Mannheim | Germany

Background: Doctoral researchers have an increased risk of experiencing mental strain and mental health conditions. Graduate institutions often serve as a central point of orientation and support for doctoral researchers. They can thus offer low-threshold access to preventative mental health-related services. But to what extent do graduate institutions in Germany address this issue, view it as part of their responsibility to support the mental health of doctoral researchers, have sufficient resources at their disposal, and implement corresponding services?

Method: We conducted a nationwide online survey of German graduate institutions (N = 96) to investigate how they perceive their role and to get insights into their experiences, service offers, and necessary resources. The survey contained 30 questions, including open-ended, Likert-scaled, single-choice, and multiple-choice questions, and was pre-tested by members of the target group. The data was analyzed using descriptive statistics.

Results: Some graduate institutions perceive themselves as responsible and well-positioned to provide services and advice to doctoral researchers experiencing mental strain, while others do not see themselves in this role. They already offer a range of services and formats that explicitly or indirectly address mental health. However, there is significant variation in how well-equipped they feel to provide effective mental health-related advice, support, and services.

Discussion: While graduate institutions already play a crucial role in supporting the mental health of doctoral researchers, many require more resources to do so properly. In addition, there is a need for systemic changes to protect researchers' mental health in the long term.
