Notably, a scrambled-dot condition results in sustained PCEs, which may reflect preserved local motion trajectories. In the case of gaze primes, both upright and inverted versions generate similarly strong PCEs, with a decline observable only at longer SOAs. Motor activation triggered by gaze direction thus persists regardless of orientation. These findings indicate that inversion can influence motor activation during biological motion processing; however, this effect depends on the specific nature of the stimulus.

Show details
Author:
Friederike Schlaghecken

In 2-alternative interference tasks, congruency effects are typically smaller following an incongruent than following a congruent trial. According to high-level “conflict control” accounts, this congruency sequence effect (CSE) reflects active adaptation processes triggered by the mismatch between target and distractor information on incongruent trials. Conversely, low-level accounts explain CSEs as resulting from perceptual or learning confounds. Confound-minimized designs with two alternating sets of stimulus-response pairs (e.g., left/right vs up/down) provide mixed results, with CSEs found in some but not all paradigms. However, these studies typically average data across all trials, disregarding whether a given trial was preceded by one, two, or more (in-)congruent trials. Five experiments (total N > 700), using different interference paradigms, demonstrate that length of the preceding sequence is a crucial factor: CSEs never occurred following a single incongruent (vs a single congruent) trial. Only with sequences of at least two successive (in)congruent trials did CSEs emerge, driven by increasingly faster responses on congruency-repetition runs (i.e., congruent-preceded-by-congruent, incongruent-preceded-by-incongruent) of increasing length. These results contradict high-level “conflict control” interpretations and instead suggest that CSEs reflect expectancy-driven context adaptations.

Improving Conceptual Clarity in Psychological Science
Chair(s) Dr. Elisa Altgassen ( Universität Ulm)
Dr. Dirk U. Wulff (Max Planck Institute for Human Developmen)
Room: IE
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Imprecise constructs, inconsistent measurement, and ambiguous theories impede research robustness and replicability of psychological science. Therefore, in this symposium we address the need for enhanced conceptual and theoretical clarity and the application of methods to advance cumulative science. Building on recent theoretical critiques we acknowledge that psychological concepts are often inherently vague, lacking finite sets of necessary and sufficient criteria. Such poor theoretical specification undermines the value of empirical findings. Specifically, insights derived from Bayesian models highlight how ill-defined theories (including the concept they contain) prevent meaningful evidential evaluation and belief updating. Furthermore, moving beyond theoretical formalism, methodological rigor demands solutions to prevailing validity issues. One promising approach involves adopting cumulative item pools and item sampling strategies to standardize and improve measurement. Besides, also Large Language Models (LLMs) offer powerful tools, demonstrated by the development of the Synthetic Network for robustly estimating scale correlations. Finally, LLMs can also be utilized to systematically analyze and map the conceptual landscape of complex constructs like personality, bringing much-needed clarity to the foundational concepts that underpin the field.

On the Potential and the Limits of Conceptual Clarification in Psychology
Dr. Fabian Hutmacher | Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg
Show details
Author:
Dr. Fabian Hutmacher | Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg

Psychology is still grappling with the multilayered crisis stemming from the fact that the results of many studies cannot be replicated (replication crisis) and that many theories are ill-developed and underspecified (theory crisis). Sometimes, these crises diagnoses are considered to be tightly connected in the sense that one can only expect to find stable results when the applied theories and concepts have been clearly defined and operationalized. From this perspective, the vagueness of theoretical concepts is often considered a bug that needs to be fixed. The importance of conceptual clarification and theory specification notwithstanding, the talk will claim that conceptual vagueness in psychology is often not a bug, but a feature arising from the fact that the meanings and applications of psychological concepts shift as contexts, languages, and social practices shift. Hence, conceptual clarification is not about eliminating vagueness completely and permanently, but about making explicit the assumptions and boundaries relevant to a given theory or investigation in a particular setting and at a particular point in time. Keeping this perspective in mind can help psychologists better understand the potential and the limits of different attempts at conceptual clarification.

Extending Reproducibility to Theory: Theoretical Reproducibility and Precision as Foundations of Cumulative Science
Prof. Dr. Andreas Glöckner | Universität zu Köln
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Andreas Glöckner | Universität zu Köln

The demonstration that many published findings are not replicable has triggered intense methodological debates in psychology and related fields. While substantial efforts have been made to (re)establish methodological norms at the empirical level, comparatively little attention has been paid to reproducibility at the level of theory. This paper examines the interplay between theory and reproducibility and argues that cumulative knowledge development requires extending reproducibility concerns to the theoretical domain. To address the problem of theory ambiguity—situations in which theories are described so vaguely that different theoretical contents or predictions can be inferred—the concepts of theoretical reproducibility and theoretical precision are introduced. Theoretical reproducibility refers to the extent to which a theory is specified such that independent researchers would converge on the same theoretical content and predictions. Theoretical precision captures the degree to which a theory, even if perfectly specified, yields informative predictions. Both concepts are formally defined and their role in cumulative knowledge development is illustrated using a Bayesian framework. The difference between theoretical reproducibility and precision, on the one hand, and the background probability of a hypothesis, on the other hand, determines how much information can be gained from an empirical study. Assessing this difference is essential to ensure that empirical studies can meaningfully contribute to cumulative knowledge development. Finally, strategies for increasing theoretical reproducibility are discussed, highlighting how better-specified theories allow empirical research to be used more efficiently for cumulative science.

Cumulative Itempools to Overcome Jingle-Jangle Fallacies
Dr. Elisa Altgassen | Ulm University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Elisa Altgassen | Ulm University | Germany
Prof.Dr. Oliver Wilhelm | Ulm University

The development of psychological measures typically adheres to a cascading process. First, an Item Universe—the theoretically usually infinite set of indicators for a latent disposition—must be defined, which in practice is often both, neglected and tricky. Second, an initial item pool is extracted from this universe. Selecting this pool from the item universe often lacks systematic procedures, resulting in deficient representations of the disposition. Importantly, the selection likely contributes to jingle-jangle fallacies, i.e., measures supposedly capture a different disposition, but are identically labeled (jingle fallacy), or measures are labeled differently but assess the same disposition (jangle fallacy). We propose the approach of cumulative item pools as a step towards addressing and solving these problems. A cumulative item pool is created by aggregating existing items proposed in the literature for a specific disposition. Such cumulative pools serve as the best proxy for the complete Item Universe. Empirical examples will be used to illustrate how the combination of cumulative item pools and automated item selection strategies (e.g., advanced algorithms) improve the validity and conceptual clarity of our measurement tools.

Show details
Authors:
Dr. Björn Hommel | Leipzig University

Researchers have proposed over 30,000 allegedly distinct constructs, making it increasingly difficult to track redundancies and overlaps. Traditional approaches to identifying these redundancies require collecting participant responses, with costs that scale quadratically as measures multiply. Language models offer a data-efficient alternative. While earlier work used latent semantic analysis (LSA) to compare questionnaire text, LSA's reliance on word co-occurrences can produce misleading similarities and may even perpetuate the jingle-jangle fallacies it seeks to detect. Understanding the convergent and discriminant validity of psychological measures requires extensive empirical data collection that is often impractical. Here, I present a methodology that leverages task embeddings derived from large language models (LLMs) to predict the relationships between behavioral measures without requiring that all measures be administered to the same participants or using the same stimuli. The approach feeds task instructions and trial-level information into LLMs and trains a predictive model to predict human behavior, yielding importance-weighted embeddings that capture which task features are most diagnostic of performance. I validate this approach across three domains using large-scale datasets: psycholinguistic norms, risk-taking propensity, and exploration behavior. Across all domains, cosine similarity between task embeddings accurately predicts empirically observed correlations—even when measures were never administered to the same individuals or stimuli. These findings demonstrate that task embeddings offer a scalable approach to mapping the structure of psychological measures.

Measuring Learning in Highly Diverse Settings
Potentials and Challenges of Large-Scale Education Monitoring
Chair(s) Dr. Joanne Colling (University of Luxembourg)
Dr. Axel Grund (University of Luxembourg)
Room: CY
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Gaining insights into key competences that students have acquired at school and understanding their longitudinal development has been of considerable public interest since well before the so-called PISA shock. Therefore, at national and international level, considerable effort is being made to validly record process and outcome characteristics of schools in order to provide evidence-based recommendations to policymakers.

The symposium is introducing and discussing current potentials and challenges of such large-scale education monitoring, using the example of Luxembourg, whose education system is characterized by a linguistically diverse student population and consistent educational inequalities that are assumed to result at least partially out of high performance expectations in the country’s three national languages (i.e., Luxembourgish, German, and French). These numerous special features make Luxembourg a unique living laboratory for studying how large-scale education monitoring can capture learning and inequalities in highly diverse educational settings, with insights that are highly informative not only for but also beyond Luxembourg.

The symposium brings together four contributions from the primary and secondary school level, all of which are methodologically based and drawing on data from the well-established Luxembourg School Monitoring Programme, the “Épreuves Standardisées” (ÉpStan). They consist of standardized achievement tests in educational key areas (e.g., mathematics, German, and French) that are administered in autumn at the beginning of each new learning cycle to the full cohort of students in Luxembourg at five grade levels (Total N ≈ 30.000), allowing to monitor systematically whether the educational standards (as defined by the Ministry of Education, Children and Youth) have been achieved by all students in their respective grade. Besides these standardized achievement tests, the ÉpStan entails questionnaires to assess central features of students’ motivation and wellbeing.

All contributions of the present symposium discuss potentials and challenges related to such a large-scale education monitoring, demonstrating how evidence from Luxembourg’s highly diverse education system can inform educational research in general and school monitoring in complex systems more broadly. The first contribution by Krämer et al. addresses the question of how linguistic and mathematical competencies can be validly assessed in children at the lower level of the competence spectrum. The second contribution by Grund et al. presents the development and validation of a student self-report questionnaire designed to enable the generic assessment of learning environment characteristics (i.e., cognitive activation, student support, and classroom management) across school subjects and teachers. Third, Colling et al. report on the potential of large-school monitoring for evaluating two policy reforms that address the linguistic diversity of Luxembourg’s student population by presenting first results and discussing related methodological challenges (e.g., test comparability across language versions). In the final contribution, Botes et al. discuss methodological challenges in the longitudinal anchoring of performance tests across time and conceptually introduce the possibility of vertical scaling grounded in classifying test items according to shared cognitive characteristics. The symposium concludes with a discussion.

The conclusion will be dedicated to reflections on how to communicate our findings in the best way, or in other words, how assessment data could support students in their learning process.

Luxembourg’s student population is highly diverse with 68% having a non-Luxembourgish language background. Although this diversity is a great asset, the ÉpStan identified persistent inequalities indicating that non-Luxembourgish/German-speaking students are at a higher risk of struggling academically in an education system where literacy is acquired in German within the regular school system.

To counter the inequalities that are assumed to result at least partially from high language expectations, the government has flexibilised its language offer by introducing European Public Schools (EPS), allowing students to choose a main instruction language (German, French, English), and the literacy acquisition project ALPHA within the regular school system, giving 1st graders the option to start literacy acquisition in French instead of German.

Integrating EPS and ALPHA students into the ÉpStan provides full-cohort data collected annually across five grades, enabling a timely and encompassing evaluation of the two reforms. First results indicate that EPS students perform better in mathematics and languages than their peers following the Luxembourgish curriculum and both EPS and ALPHA students report higher motivation with parents feeling more able to support them academically. Results are particularly pronounced for students typically struggling in Luxembourg’s education system.

Despite the indication that this flexible language offer may reduce inequalities, evaluating policy reforms using large-scale monitoring poses considerable challenges, such as a limited comparability across students from different curricula taking tests in different languages, and the reliance on a limited set of standardized tests that are not designed to capture nuanced effects of specific reforms, highlighting the need to combine large-scale assessment results with more fine-grained measures.

Longitudinal data provides valuable insights into how students acquire and refine key school competencies across grade levels. For over a decade, the ÉpStan collected full-cohort data in mathematics and languages by testing students at five time points in their educational trajectory, thereby creating a unique longitudinal dataset.

To explore the full potential of a comprehensive longitudinal dataset, and to move beyond largely descriptive analyses, it is essential to place achievement test scores from multiple grades on a common measurement scale through vertical scaling. Conventional vertical scaling approaches typically rely on identical anchor items across administrations. In achievement testing, however, this comes with substantial methodological limitations, including risks of item overexposure and the possibility that identical tasks do not operate equivalently across age groups. Therefore, such traditional anchor items are not included in the ÉpStan, further underscoring the need for alternative scaling strategies.

This contribution explores an alternative approach grounded in cognitive theory. Instead of relying on literal item repetition across grades, mathematics items are classified according to shared cognitive characteristics (e.g., underlying mental processes, solution strategies, or sub‑skills) regardless of differences in surface features such as phrasing, layout, or context. This cognitive equivalence approach is particularly relevant in mathematics, where surface features naturally evolve with curricular progression, but core cognitive processes remain consistent across grades.
By systematically identifying these equivalences, existing ÉpStan data could be retrofitted onto a common measurement scale and capitalize on its unique potential for psychometrically valid analyses of the students’ longitudinal development in key school competences.

Room: LU
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Coupled symposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

This symposium focuses on the relationship between leadership and well-being. We will consider the impact of leadership on the well-being of followers, the role of leadership in critical contexts and with vulnerable groups, and the well-being of leaders themselves. Klug et al. demonstrate that a high leadership workload has a negative "trickle-down" effect, where leaders are less likely to improve working conditions for their followers. Schleu et al. utilize critical incident technique to examine the range of employees’ immediate responses that (different) leadership behaviors can evoke. Martinovic et al. aim to validate a measure of change-leadership roles and examine how these roles relate to employee exhaustion and subjective health in schools. Zill et al. approach a time-lagged mixed-methods design to study the role of leaders in social workers reaction to their clients’ aggression. Brzykcy et al. focus on the leaders’ response to their follower’s depression disclosure by analyzing videotaped real-time leader behavior from an experimental setting. Cook et al. use a time-lagged design to uncover the relation of leader social support and different conceptualizations of presenteeism for employees with chronic illnesses. Kirklies et al. present an approach to effectively, economically and comprehensively support individual leader health via behavioral prevention focusing on leaders’ self-care. Dennißen et al. examine whether empowering leadership constitutes a resource-gain or resource-loss process for leaders themselves over time. In her role as discussant, Birgit Schyns will critically reflect on the talks and the recent state of research on leadership and well-being.

There is considerable evidence about determinants of healthy work, such as a manageable workload, autonomy, and task variety. However, less is known about how more or less healthy work environments come about. Leaders play a key role in this context: Allocating tasks, or solving work organization problems, leaders frequently make decisions with repercussions for their employees’ work design. The aim of this study was to investigate leaders’ own working conditions, specifically workload and autonomy, as predictors of their work design decisions. Drawing on the JD-R Model and Broaden-and-Build Theory, we predicted that less favorable working conditions for leaders trickle down in terms of poorer decisions about their employees’ work design. Under conditions of low vs. high workload and low vs. high autonomy, N = 365 supervisors completed scenario tasks of work design decisions in terms of 1) enriching task allocation and 2) improving work design in response to organizational problems. Under high workload, respondents were less likely to improve employees’ work design in response to organizational problems, both directly and mediated via reduced engagement and positive affect. High autonomy attenuated the indirect effect of workload via positive affect, but had no effect on its own on leaders’ work design decisions. Enriching task allocation was not affected by workload or control. Taken together, the results suggest that leaders’ workload may impair employees’ work design. The findings contribute to research on the antecedents of work design and point to leaders as important targets for structural interventions to create healthy working conditions.

Leadership in organizational change processes is multidimensional, yet existing research remains inconclusive regarding which specific roles leaders should adopt across different phases of change to effectively support it. Most prior studies have focused on leadership styles such as transformational leadership, which conflate motivational, relational, and task-oriented aspects. This makes it difficult to identify the specific functions that are most critical for leaders when facilitating change. Investigating discrete leadership roles helps to clarify how leaders can foster change processes. Building on Cameron and Green’s (2008) five-role model of leadership, our study reports the development and validation of an innovative instrument assessing these five roles. In an online study, leaders (N= 400) responded to items developed based on the original items, and to related leadership constructs, change-related attitudes, and perceived change success and failure to specify the psychometric properties. The instrument has been applied in a BMBFSFJ-funded three-wave longitudinal multilevel panel involving approximately 150 schools undergoing organizational change. We report a selection of results regarding the link between change leadership and employee well-being. It is hypothesized that leadership roles differ substantially in their potential to foster well-being, with motivational and relational roles being more strongly associated with lower exhaustion and better subjective health than strategic or operational roles. By the time of the conference, first-wave results (Q1 2026) will be reported, offering insights into role-specific associations at both the individual and school level and laying the groundwork for subsequent analyses of leadership and well-being dynamics during organizational change.

Violent attacks by clients or relatives have increased significantly in Germany in recent years, with employees in social and nursing professions being among the most affected groups. Since employees and leaders only report a portion of the incidents, the current data represents a rather conservative estimate. Previous research shows that client aggression has a negative impact on employee health (e.g., burnout, posttraumatic stress, somatic symptoms). Because leaders are important in organizations and have a crucial impact on working conditions, prevention and intervention approaches should focus on leaders.
Our research aims to examine the role of leaders in the context of client aggression. This research provides us possible starting points, how leadership behavior is related to team behavior, the employee (e.g., voice behavior, aggression-related self-efficacy), and the extent of client aggression. We conducted an online study with two measurement points (2024 and 2025), which included quantitative and qualitative parts. Employees and leaders from various fields of social work in Germany participated in our study. First, our results show positive relationships between perceived leadership behavior and voice behavior and aggression-related self-efficacy of employees, and negative relationships to dysfunctional team behavior and employees' avoidance behavior towards clients, controlled for crucial job demands. Second, participants report several reasons for their silence behavior in relation to leaders (e.g., reporting achieves nothing, leader can do nothing, lack of leader support). Third, the perception and knowledge about reporting processes in organizations differ between employees and leaders. Implications are discussed.

Leaders often feel uncomfortable addressing mental health issues in one-on-one meetings with subordinates, yet timely conversations are critical for employee and organizational outcomes. Early interventions can prevent exhaustion from escalating into more severe mental health crises, and even small gestures can have substantial impact. For example, a simple recommendation by a direct supervisor significantly increases the likelihood that employees seek professional help.
At the same time, employees vary widely in whether and how they disclose mental health concerns when prompted. These variations likely shape interaction dynamics, yet little is known about how leaders respond to different disclosure styles.
We employed a randomized controlled experiment in which participants assigned to a leader role conducted a brief meeting with a professional actor portraying an employee using one of three depression disclosure styles: full disclosure, downplaying the condition, or downplaying it with humor. All 103 meetings were videorecorded. Participants were blinded to condition and completed surveys before and after the interaction.
Our study provides behavioral evidence on how leaders respond to depression disclosure and forms of non-disclosure. It further examines the potentially counterproductive role of humor by showing how humorous downplaying may delay effective responses to emerging mental health crises. By observing real-time leader behavior, this research extends existing work on workplace mental health beyond correlational and self-report approaches.

Benefits and costs of empowering leadership: A longitudinal study on leader well-being contingencies

Authors:

Although empowering leadership is associated with positive outcomes for followers, its implications for leaders remain largely unexplored. This is a critical oversight given the dual role of leaders as agents who empower others by sharing their own power base and as recipients within a dynamic process with consequences for leaders’ own well-being and subsequent leadership behavior.
Adopting an actor-centric and resource-based perspective, we investigate the dynamic relationship between empowering leadership behavior and leaders’ well-being. We further examine whether this relationship is contingent on organizational-, team-, and role-related boundary conditions, namely leaders’ felt accountability, perceived team capability, and role ambiguity. In addition, we explore whether leaders’ well-being states subsequently shape leadership behavior, with a particular focus on the emergence of laissez-faire leadership.
We employ a four-wave longitudinal design with one-month lags between measurement occasions. Data will be collected from approximately 750 leaders who participate at all four waves. Analyses will be conducted using RI-CLPM.
Overall, empowering leadership is expected to enhance leaders’ well-being under favorable conditions (i.e., high felt accountability, high perceived team capability, and low role ambiguity). Under unfavorable conditions (i.e., low felt accountability, low perceived team capability, and high role ambiguity), however, empowering leadership may deplete leaders’ well-being and increase the likelihood of laissez-faire leadership.
Our actor-centric and dynamic lens can advance our understanding of the consequences of empowering leadership for leaders themselves. This nuanced view contributes to a more sustainable understanding of how leaders react to and adapt their leadership behaviors in contemporary work contexts.

Interdisziplinäre Perspektiven auf die psychische Gesundheit und psychosoziale Versorgung von Schüler:innen in Deutschland

Room: PT
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Coupled symposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

Die psychische Gesundheit von Kindern und Jugendlichen hat sich in den vergangenen Jahren zu einer zentralen gesellschaftlichen Herausforderung entwickelt. Aktuelle Forschungsergebnisse zeigen, dass junge Menschen in Deutschland angesichts multipler gesellschaftlicher Krisen zunehmend psychisch belastet sind. Gleichzeitig bestehen erhebliche Lücken in der psychosozialen Versorgung sowie Barrieren im Zugang zu Unterstützungsangeboten. Dem Lebensraum Schule kommt hierbei eine besondere Bedeutung zu, da Kinder und Jugendliche hier einen Großteil ihrer Zeit verbringen und schulische Erfahrungen die psychische Gesundheit maßgeblich mitprägen. Trotz dieser Relevanz mangelt es bislang an umfassender epidemiologischer und versorgungsbezogener Forschung zur psychischen Gesundheit von Kindern und Jugendlichen innerhalb und außerhalb des schulischen Kontexts.
Das Symposium bietet einen interdisziplinären Überblick aus Klinischer und Pädagogischer Psychologie sowie Kommunikationswissenschaften über aktuelle Forschungsergebnisse zur psychischen Gesundheit und psychosozialen Versorgung von Schüler:innen in Deutschland, entlang zentraler Entwicklungsphasen, Belastungslagen und struktureller Rahmenbedingungen.
Vorgestellt werden unter anderem Ergebnisse einer bundesweiten Längsschnittstudie zur Entwicklung der psychischen Gesundheit von Kindern und Jugendlichen während und nach der COVID-19-Pandemie. Ergänzend werden Daten aus Screenings im Vorschulalter präsentiert, die das soziale Wohlbefinden im Übergang zur Schule untersuchen. Eine weitere längsschnittliche Schüler:innenbefragung liefert Einblicke in Zusammenhänge zwischen schulischem Wohlbefinden, Unterrichtsgestaltung und psychischer Gesundheit. Darüber hinaus beleuchten mehrere groß angelegte Befragungen aktueller Belastungsfaktoren wie Cyber-Mobbing sowie die psychischen Auswirkungen des Klimawandels auf junge Menschen, einschließlich deren Coping-Strategien.
Ein weiterer Schwerpunkt des Symposiums liegt auf psychosozialen Versorgungsstrukturen. Ergebnisse aus zwei Schulleitungsbefragungen geben Aufschluss über die Verfügbarkeit psychosozialer Infrastruktur an Schulen, wahrgenommene psychische Belastungen von Schüler:innen sowie den Bedarf an Präventions- und Interventionsmaßnahmen. Ergänzend liefern mehrjährige bundesweite Befragungen von Kinder- und Jugendlichenpsychotherapeut:innen Erkenntnisse zur Versorgungssituation sowie zu Zugangsbarrieren in der ambulanten psychotherapeutischen Behandlung. Darüber hinaus bietet eine kommunikationswissenschaftliche Perspektive basierend auf qualitativen Interviews mit Schüler:innen, Lehrkräften und Erziehungsberechtigten Einblick zu Stigmatisierungsphänomenen im Schulkontext als mögliche Barriere bei der Inanspruchnahme psychosozialer Hilfsangebote.

Hintergrund: Kinder und Jugendliche wachsen zunehmend in einem Umfeld multipler globaler Krisen auf. Klimawandel, Kriege, wirtschaftliche Unsicherheit und digitale Belastungen treffen auf fortbestehende psychosoziale Folgen der COVID-19-Pandemie. Studien zeigen, dass junge Menschen in Krisenzeiten häufiger Zukunftsängste, emotionale Belastungen und Verhaltensprobleme berichten. Die COPSY-Längsschnittstudie ermöglicht es, diese Entwicklungen über mehrere Jahre hinweg zu verfolgen.

Methoden: In acht Erhebungswellen der bevölkerungsbasierten COPSY-Studie (2020-2025; N = 1.500-1.700 pro Welle) wurden 7- bis 23-Jährige sowie ihre Eltern zu gesundheitsbezogener Lebensqualität (KIDSCREEN-10), psychischen Auffälligkeiten (SDQ), Ängsten (SCARED), depressiven Symptomen (CES-DC) und Einsamkeit (UCLA) befragt. Zusätzlich wurden krisenbezogene Sorgen, Zukunftsängste, Coping-Strategien sowie Aspekte der digitalen Medien- und KI-Nutzung erhoben.

Ergebnisse: Zu Beginn der Pandemie kam es zu deutlichen Verschlechterungen der psychischen Gesundheit. Zwar nahmen die Belastungen in den Folgejahren ab, doch im Herbst 2025 zeigte weiterhin etwa jedes fünfte Kind eine geminderte Lebensqualität und psychische Auffälligkeiten. Sorgen über Klima, Krieg und wirtschaftliche Instabilität waren weit verbreitet und mit höheren Belastungswerten verbunden. Familiäre Unterstützung und aktive Bewältigungsstrategien wirkten entlastend. Digitale Medien und KI spielten eine wichtige Rolle und gingen mit hohen Nutzungszeiten und belastenden Erfahrungen einher.

Schlussfolgerung: Kinder und Jugendliche sind weiterhin erheblichen psychosozialen Belastungen in einem von globalen Krisen geprägten Umfeld ausgesetzt. Neben den Folgen der Pandemie rücken Zukunftsängste stärker in den Vordergrund. Zur Förderung der psychischen Gesundheit sind niedrigschwellige, ressourcenorientierte Präventions- und Unterstützungsangebote erforderlich, die junge Menschen und ihre Familien wirksam begleiten.

Soziales Wohlbefinden im Übergang vom Kindergarten in die Grundschule: Überblick und vorläufige Ergebnisse des SWITCH Projekts
Prof. Dr. Lars Otto White | Universität Bremen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Lars Otto White | Universität Bremen | Germany
Dr. Pascal Vrticka | University of Essex | United Kingdom
Dr. Rebecca Böhme | Linköping University | Sweden
Dr. Marlon Göring | Universität Leipzig | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stefanie Höhl | Universität Wien | Austria
Prof. Dr. Dr. Tina Malti | Universität Leipzig/University of Toronto | Germany

Als einer der frühesten bedeutsamen Übergänge in der Kindheit bietet der Schuleintritt sowohl zahlreiche Chancen als auch Risiken für Wohlbefinden und psychische Gesundheit. Ein erfolgreicher Übergang in die Schule hängt dabei nicht allein von den individuellen kognitiven Fähigkeiten der Kinder ab, sondern ebenso von ihrem sozialen Wohlbefinden, das insbesondere familiäre Bindungen und soziale Netzwerke umfasst. Bislang fehlt jedoch ein breiter Konsens über zentrale Dimensionen sozialen Wohlbefindens. Entsprechend variieren die Praktiken des Schuleintritts in Europa erheblich, was die Notwendigkeit eines empirisch fundierten Zugangs zur sozio-emotionalen Entwicklung in dieser Phase unterstreicht.

Vor diesem Hintergrund rekrutiert die SWITCH-Studie derzeit fünf groß angelegte, repräsentative Stichproben im Vorschulalter in vier europäischen Ländern (Deutschland, Schweden, Vereinigtes Königreich, Österreich). Ziel ist es, den einzigartigen, kontextübergreifenden Beitrag des sozialen Wohlbefindens zu einem erfolgreichen Schuleintritt über andere Dimensionen des Wohlbefindens und der psychischen Gesundheit hinaus zu bestimmen. Dabei werden demografische und altersbezogene Effekte sowie Variationen in den Schuleintrittsbedingungen innerhalb und zwischen den beteiligten Ländern berücksichtigt (Welle 1).

Diese Datengrundlage ermöglicht in weiteren Erhebungswellen gezielte Substichproben, um biobehaviorale Mechanismen des sozialen Wohlbefindens im Zusammenspiel mit kognitiven Fähigkeiten sowie frühen Lese-, Schreib- und Rechenkompetenzen zu untersuchen. Zudem soll deren prognostische Bedeutung für psychische Gesundheit, Wohlbefinden sowie frühe schulische Kompetenzen am Ende der ersten Klasse analysiert werden. Der Beitrag stellt die Zielsetzungen von SWITCH vor und präsentiert erste vorläufige Datenanalysen der ersten Vorschul-Erhebungswelle.

Unterrichtsbezogene Determinanten schulischen Wohlbefindens in der Sekundarstufe I
Natalia Lüneburger | Universität Leipzig, Institut für Bildungswissenschaften
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Franziska Greiner-Döchert | Universität Leipzig, Institut für Bildungswissenschaften | Germany
Natalia Lüneburger | Universität Leipzig, Institut für Bildungswissenschaften
Prof. Dr. Henrik Saalbach | Universität Leipzig, Institut für Bildungswissenschaften | Germany

Das schulische Wohlbefinden (SWB) von Kindern und Jugendlichen ist Bildungsvoraussetzung und Bildungsziel zugleich. Während individuelle Determinanten SWB (z. B. akademisches Selbstkonzept) gut erforscht sind, mangelt es an Befunden zu unterrichtsbezogenen Einflussfaktoren. Untersucht wird daher der Zusammenhang zwischen SWB und Merkmalen der Unterrichtsqualität.

Analysiert wurden Daten von N = 1078 Schüler:innen der Sekundarstufe I. SWB wurde über positive (z. B. Freude, Optimismus) und negative Indikatoren (Sorgen, psychosomatische Beschwerden, soziale Probleme) erfasst (EPOCH-G-S; Hascher & Baillod, 2000). Klassenführung, kognitive Aktivierung sowie emotionale und kognitive Unterstützung wurden mit etablierten Skalen erhoben.

Hypothetisiert wird, dass die Unterrichtsmerkmale positiv mit positiven und negativ mit negativen SWB-Indikatoren zusammenhängen.
Geschätzt wurden Strukturgleichungsmodelle.

Emotionale Unterstützung erwies sich als robustester Prädiktor: Sie hing positiv mit den positiven SWB-Indikatoren (B = .47***) und negativ mit den negativen Indikatoren (B = −.52***) zusammen. Für kognitive Unterstützung zeigten sich keine signifikanten Zusammenhänge. Klassenführung war schwach positiv mit positiven (B = .09*) und negativ mit negativen Indikatoren des SWB assoziiert (B = −.12**). Entgegen der Hypothese wies kognitive Aktivierung geringe negative Zusammenhänge mit positiven (B = −.15**) sowie positive Zusammenhänge mit negativen Indikatoren des SWB auf (B = .27***).

Die Zusammenhänge blieben auch unter Berücksichtigung des akademischen Selbstkonzepts weitgehend stabil; einzig der negative Zusammenhang zwischen positiven SWB-Indikatoren und kognitiver Aktivierung war dann nicht mehr signifikant.

Unsere Befunde unterstreichen die Rolle emotionaler Unterstützung und Klassenführung für die Prävention negativer SWB-Indikatoren. Derzeit wird der Längsschnitt (N = 748) ausgewertet, sodass Veränderungen und Prädiktoren über die Zeit berichtet werden können.

Wenn Klassenzimmer und Schulhof keinen geschützten Raum (mehr) bieten: Mobbing und Cybermobbing unter Schüler:innen als Faktor psychischer Instabilität, geringem schulischem Wohlbefinden und sozialer Desintegration
Prof. Dr. Eva Baumann | Hochschule für Musik, Theater und Medien Hannover, Hanover Center for Health Communication [HC]² | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Eva Baumann | Hochschule für Musik, Theater und Medien Hannover, Hanover Center for Health Communication [HC]² | Germany

Werden Schüler:innen wiederholt und über längere Zeit im direkten Miteinander und/oder über digitale Medien bloßgestellt, beschimpft, ausgegrenzt, bedroht oder zum Ziel diffamierender Gerüchte, beeinträchtigt dies das Wohlbefinden, erhöht das Risiko psychischer Erkrankungen und belastet die Schule als Schutz- und Entwicklungsraum. (Cyber-)Mobbing kann Betroffene somit erheblich belasten und ein produktives Lernumfeld nachhaltig beeinträchtigen.

Eingebettet in die nationale und internationale Forschungslage präsentieren wir Befunde einer repräsentativen Online-Befragung von 1.232 Schüler:innen (11 bis 17 Jahre) sowie je eines Elternteils hinsichtlich Prävalenz und Erscheinungsformen von Mobbing und Cybermobbing unter Schüler:innen und deren psychosoziale Zusammenhänge sowie schulische Kontextaspekte.

30 % der Schüler:innen berichten von mind. monatlichen Mobbingerfahrungen im letzten Schuljahr, wobei 20 % regelmäßig unterschiedliche Erscheinungsformen erleben. Einzelnen Mobbinghandlungen sind 4 bis 10 % wöchentlich bis täglich ausgesetzt. Mobbing erfolgt meist im direkt-persönlichen Kontakt, wird jedoch häufig durch Cybermobbing flankiert. Es zeigt sich ein Peak im Alter von 14 Jahren, Geschlechterunterschiede fallen gering aus.

Mobbingerfahrungen sind deutlich mit reduziertem schulischem Wohlbefinden und Zugehörigkeitsgefühl, geringerer schulischer Leistung sowie erhöhter psychischer Auffälligkeit assoziiert. Unterschiede zwischen der Prävalenz eigener, aber ggf. nicht solche bezeichneter (Cyber-)Mobbingerfahrung und der Beobachtung explizit als Cybermobbing bezeichneter Handlungen gegen Mitschüler:innen sowie eigener Beteiligung hieran weisen auf Diskrepanzen der Selbst- und Fremdwahrnehmung sowie im Labeling sowie auf Sensibilisierungsbedarfe hin.

Deutlich wird die Notwendigkeit früh ansetzender, systematischer Prävention und Unterstützung an Schulen, die traditionelles Mobbing und Cybermobbing berücksichtigen und die Schule als sicheren Sozialraum stärken.

Sorgen um die Zukunft: Die Rolle klimabedingter Emotionen bei Kindern und Jugendlichen mit psychischen Störungen in stationärer Behandlung
Clara Sophie Beer | Ruhr Universität Bochum, LWL Universitätsklinikum Hamm | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Clara Sophie Beer | Ruhr Universität Bochum, LWL Universitätsklinikum Hamm | Germany
Prof. Dr. Julia Asbrand | Friedrich-Universität Jena, Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Prof. Dr. Dr. Martin Holtmann | Ruhr Universität Bochum, LWL Universitätsklinikum Hamm | Germany
Prof. Dr. Tanja Legenbauer | Ruhr Universität Bochum, LWL Universitätsklinikum Hamm | Germany

Ziel: Klimabezogene Emotionen (KBE) wie Angst, Traurigkeit und Wut werden zunehmend bei Kindern und Jugendlichen berichtet und können mit emotionalen Belastung einhergehen. Bislang ist unklar, inwieweit KBE auch mit einer psychischen Symptomatik assoziiert sind bzw. diese beeinflussen. Ziel der Studie ist es, in einer klinischen Stichprobe an Jugendlichen mit psychischen Störungen Auftretenshäufigkeit und Assoziation mit verschiedenen Symptomen unter Berücksichtigung des Alters zu prüfen.

Methoden: Tabletgestützte Befragung zu Klimawissen und klimabezogenen Emotionen von n=518 Patient:innen (Pat.) einer deutschen Kinder- und Jugendpsychiatrie (7–18 Jh.) im Rahmen der Routinediagnostik, zusätzlich Fragen zu allgemeiner Psychopathologie und spezifischen psychischen Symptomen. Prüfung der Hypothesen mit Korrelationsanalysen.

Ergebnisse: Über 80% der Pat. waren sich des Klimawandels bewusst und zeigten ein grundlegendes Verständnis des Phänomens. KBE einschließlich Angst, Wut und Traurigkeit, wurden im Allgemeinen mit geringer Intensität berichtet. Das Alter war signifikant mit der Intensität negativer KBE assoziiert. Allerdings berichteten jüngere Pat. höhere Level an Optimismus bezüglich des Klimawandels als ältere Pat. KBE waren signifikant mit der gesamten Psychopathologie sowie mit internalisierenden, externalisierenden und aufmerksamkeitsbezogenen Symptomen assoziiert.

Schlussfolgerung: KBE sind bei Jugendlichen mit psychischer Symptomatik vorhanden, werden aber im Allgemeinen mit geringer Intensität berichtet. Jugendliche zeigten stärkere negative KBE, jüngere Kinder waren aber optimistischer bzgl. des Klimawandels. Die beobachteten Zusammenhänge zwischen KBE und Psychopathologie unterstreichen die Relevanz der Berücksichtigung von KBE in der Behandlung von Kindern und Jugendlichen mit psychischen Störungen. Zukünftige Forschung sollte longitudinale Zusammenhänge untersuchen, um die Rolle von KBE für die psychische Gesundheit besser zu verstehen.

Klima im Kopf – Coping-Strategien junger Menschen im Umgang mit dem Klimawandel und Zusammenhänge mit psychischer Gesundheit und umweltfreundlichem Handeln
Nora Spirkl | Friedrich-Universität Jena, Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nora Spirkl | Friedrich-Universität Jena, Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Dr. Felix Peter | Landesschulamt Sachsen-Anhalt
Prof. Dr. Julia Asbrand | Friedrich-Universität Jena, Institut für Psychologie | Germany

Hintergrund: Der Klimawandel stellt für die Menschheit existentielle Bedrohung dar. Dies löst bei vielen jungen Menschen Emotionen wie Angst, Wut, und Traurigkeit aus, die einerseits psychisch belastend sein und anderseits klimafreundliches Handeln motivieren können. Die Auswirkungen sind davon abhängig, welche Coping-Strategien angewendet werden.

Fragestellung: Das primäre Ziel der vorliegenden Studie ist die Validierung eines neu entwickelten Fragebogens zu klimabezogenem Coping. Im Rahmen dieses Symposiums sollen die Ausprägungen der verschiedenen Coping-Strategien sowie Zusammenhänge mit Lebenszufriedenheit, psychischer Belastung, und umweltfreundlichem Handeln untersucht werden.

Methode: Zunächst wurde ein Fragebogen für klimabezogenes Coping basierend auf dem Brief COPE entwickelt und anhand von Daten aus einer ersten Pilotstudie gekürzt und finalisiert. Aktuell ist eine Validierung des Fragebogens in einer repräsentativen Stichprobe junger Menschen (N = 500, 15¬–25 Jahre) in Deutschland geplant. Zur Auswertung der obigen Fragestellung werden zusätzlich Fragebögen zur psychischen Belastung (DASS-21), zur Lebenszufriedenheit (SWLS) sowie zum umweltfreundlichen Handeln erhoben, um Zusammenhänge mit den Coping-Strategien analysieren zu können. Dazu werden multiple Regressionen mit den verschiedenen Coping-Strategien als Prädiktoren berechnet.

Ergebnis: Die Datenerhebung ist nach Erhebung einer ersten Pilotstudie aktuell in Vorbereitung. Bis zum Kongress werden die Ergebnisse planmäßig vorliegen.
Schlussfolgerung: Das Projekt soll zu einem besseren Verständnis von Copingstrategien beitragen, die bei jungen Menschen sowohl mit psychischem Wohlbefinden als auch umweltfreundlichem Verhalten zusammenhängen. So können diese gezielt durch das soziale Umfeld sowie psychotherapeutisch und auf gesellschaftlicher Ebene gefördert werden und dadurch junge Menschen in einem gesunden Umgang mit dem Klimawandel und anderen globalen Krisen zu unterstützen.

Psychosoziale Versorgungsstrukturen für Kinder und Jugendliche an Schulen in Deutschland. Ergebnisse aus dem Projekt Monitor und Bildung Psychische Gesundheit 2024 & 2026
Nina Tucholski | Universität Leipzig, Wilhelm-Wundt-Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nina Tucholski | Universität Leipzig, Wilhelm-Wundt-Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Prof. Dr. Julian Schmitz | Universität Leipzig, Wilhelm-Wundt-Institut für Psychologie | Germany

Kinder und Jugendliche sind häufig von psychischen Erkrankungen betroffen, die ihre Entwicklung beeinträchtigen können. Schulen verfügen mit Schulsozialarbeit (SSA), Beratungslehrkräften (BLK) und Schulpsychologie (SP) über zentrale Strukturen zur Prävention und Intervention. Trotz zunehmender psychischer Belastungen bei jungen Menschen deuten Befunde darauf hin, dass psychosoziale Unterstützungsangebote an Schulen nicht ausreichen. Die vorgestellte Studie untersucht Verfügbarkeit, Bedarf und Bedarfsdeckung psychosozialer Infrastrukturen an Schulen in Deutschland in den Schuljahren 2023/2024 und 2025/2026, sowie die Wahrnehmung psychischer Auffälligkeiten und Belastungsfaktoren von Schüler:innen.
Im Jahr 2024 wurde eine bundesweite Befragung von Schulleitungen in 13 Bundesländern mit 486 Teilnehmenden durchgeführt, gewichtet nach Schulform und Bundesland. Eine Folgeerhebung ist für April 2026 in 14 Bundesländern geplant.
Die Ergebnisse der ersten Erhebung zeigen, dass SSA an 75 % der Schulen verfügbar war, mit höheren Anteilen an Haupt-, Real- und Gesamtschulen. BLK waren an 38 % der Schulen vorhanden, häufiger an Gymnasien sowie an Haupt-, Real- und Gesamtschulen als an Grund- und Förderschulen. SP-Angebote bestanden an rund drei Viertel der Schulen, unabhängig von der Schulform. Über alle Strukturen hinweg berichteten die Schulleitungen, dass der Bedarf nicht gedeckt sei und im Vergleich zum Vorjahr zugenommen habe. Ressourcen für psychosoziale Unterstützung wurden überwiegend als unzureichend eingeschätzt. Gleichzeitig wurde ein Anstieg psychischer Auffälligkeiten wie Ängsten und Depressionen beobachtet, während Präventions- und Interventionsangebote nicht flächendeckend verfügbar waren. Im Vortrag werden zusätzlich die Ergebnisse der Erhebung aus dem Jahr 2026 vorgestellt.
Die Befunde verdeutlichen erhebliche Defizite in der psychosozialen Versorgung an Schulen und unterstreichen den Bedarf an bildungspolitischen Maßnahmen zur Stärkung entsprechender Strukturen.

Ambulante psychotherapeutische Versorgung von Kindern und Jugendlichen in Deutschland: Ergebnisse bundesweiter Befragungen 2024–2026
Kristin Rodney-Wolf | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Kristin Rodney-Wolf | Germany
Prof. Dr. Julian Schmitz | Universität Leipzig, Wilhelm-Wundt-Institut für Psychologie | Germany

Hintergrund: Psychische Gesundheit in Kindheit und Jugend bildet die Basis für eine gesunde Entwicklung, gesellschaftliche Teilhabe und psychisches Wohlbefinden über die gesamte Lebensspanne. Gleichzeitig erhalten nur bis zu 10 % psychisch erkrankter Kinder und Jugendlichen eine psychotherapeutische Behandlung, oft nach langen Wartezeiten. Die vorliegende Studie untersucht Einschätzungen niedergelassener Kinder- und Jugendlichenpsychotherapeut:innen zur ambulanten Versorgungslage.

Methode: Alle bundesweit an der vertragspsychotherapeutischen Versorgung teilnehmenden Kinder- und Jugendlichenpsychotherapeut:innen wurden 2024 und 2025 zu einer anonymen Online-Befragung eingeladen. Erhoben wurden u. a. Anfrageaufkommen, Wartezeiten, Behandlungsangebote, Belastungsfaktoren, Zugangsbarrieren, Versorgung marginalisierter Gruppen sowie Arbeitsbelastung.

Ergebnisse: In beiden Erhebungswellen zeigte sich, dass im Durchschnitt ein Drittel aller Anfragenden innerhalb von vier Wochen einen Termin für eine Sprechstunde in einer Praxis erhält. Die Hälfte der behandlungsbedürftigen Patient:innen bekommt anschließend einen Therapieplatz, im Mittel nach 28–30 Wochen Wartezeit. Als Hauptbelastungsfaktoren für Patient:innen werden familiäre Konflikte, schulischer Leistungsdruck und elterliche Überforderung benannt, während die geschätzte Belastung durch globale Konflikte und Krisen zunimmt. Marginalisierte Gruppen sind unter den Patient:innen anteilsmäßig unterrepräsentiert. Rund ein Viertel berichtet von starker beruflicher Belastung, vor allem durch Verwaltungsaufgaben und hohes Anfrageaufkommen. Weitere Ergebnisse einer dritten Erhebung 2026 werden zum Kongress vorliegen.

Schlussfolgerung: Die Ergebnisse zeigen eine deutliche Unterversorgung in der psychotherapeutischen Versorgung von Kindern und Jugendlichen. Lange Wartezeiten, nicht bedienbare Anfragen und eine hohe Belastung der Behandler:innen unterstreichen den Bedarf einer empirisch fundierten Reform der Bedarfsplanung.

Wahrnehmung von Stigmatisierung psychischer Belastungen, Erkrankungen und Hilfeinanspruchnahme aus Sicht von Schüler:innen, Eltern und Lehrkräften: Multiperspektivische Ergebnisse einer Interviewstudie zu Stigmatisierungsphänomenen im Schulkontext
Katarina Heitz | Hochschule für Musik, Theater und Medien Hannover, Hanover Center for Health Communication [HC]² | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Katarina Heitz | Hochschule für Musik, Theater und Medien Hannover, Hanover Center for Health Communication [HC]² | Germany
Prof. Dr. Eva Baumann | Hochschule für Musik, Theater und Medien Hannover, Hanover Center for Health Communication [HC]² | Germany
Friederike Gaitzsch | Leipzig University | Germany

Psychische Belastungen bei Kindern und Jugendlichen erfordern wirksame Zugänge zu psychosozialer Unterstützung. Schulen bieten hierfür einen zentralen Handlungsraum, zugleich wirken stigmatisierende Prozesse als erhebliche Barriere. Mit einem multiperspektivischen Ansatz sollen diese Mechanismen im Schulkontext exploriert werden. Die Studie stützt sich dabei theoretisch auf das Stigmatisierungskonzept von Link und Phelan (2001) und untersucht, welche Stigmatisierungsphänomene von Lehrkräften, Erziehungsberechtigten und Schüler:innen charakterisiert werden sowie welche Rolle der Schulkontext für das Entstehen und Fortbestehen dieser Prozesse spielt.
Im Jahr 2024 wurden 51 halbstrukturierte Leitfadeninterviews mit Schüler:innen, Erziehungsberechtigten und Lehrkräften geführt. Die computergestützte Auswertung erfolgte mittels typenbildender qualitativer Inhaltsanalyse in ATLAS.ti unter Anwendung einer deduktiv-induktiv kombinierten Kategorienbildung.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen mehrdimensionale, teils gruppenübergreifende Stigmatisierungsphänomene. Differenzierungen lassen sich insbesondere auf der Kontextebene (soziale Interaktion, individuelle Ebene, antizipierte Reaktionen) sowie auf der Perspektivebene identifizieren. Im schulischen Alltag findet beispielsweise ein Delegitimieren von psychischer Belastungen statt, es kommt zu Abwertung und sozialer Abgrenzung gegenüber betroffenen Schüler:innen, zu Ängsten vor negativen Konsequenzen einer Offenlegung sowie zu einer Tabuisierung von Gefühlen und Hilfebedarf.
Die Befunde erweitern das Verständnis schulspezifischer Stigmatisierungsprozesse im Kontext psychischer Gesundheit und liefern Ansatzpunkte für die Entwicklung entstigmatisierender Maßnahmen sowie zur Förderung der Hilfeinanspruchnahme im Schulkontext.

Individual Differences in Self-, Society-, and World-Related Beliefs: Where Do They Come From and How Do They Unfold?
Chair(s) Chiara Förster (Humbold-Universität zu Berlin)
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Patrick Mussel (Psychologische Hochschule Berlin)
Room: LT
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Beliefs play a key role in outcomes as central as health, life satisfaction, and social and political behavior. This symposium integrates insights into antecedents, dynamics, and consequences of beliefs across three levels: beliefs about the self (i.e., core beliefs), society (i.e., perceived anomie), and the world (i.e. primal world beliefs). We begin with research identifying psychosocial antecedents of interindividual differences in perceived anomie (the belief that society is broken) across 28 countries. The second talk focuses on associations and dynamic interactions between core beliefs (generalized beliefs about the self in social and cultural context), health, and life satisfaction, as well as their developmental trajectories. Zooming further into this dynamic perspective, the third talk sheds light on everyday dynamics of primal world beliefs (beliefs about the general character of the world as a whole), examining their bidirectional associations with both state and trait situation perception and well-being. The fourth talk examines how core beliefs, as mediators, can help explain associations between intellectual investment traits and life satisfaction. Finally, the fifth talk highlights how core beliefs, personality traits, and situational construals jointly shape intentional deceptive behavior. Taken together, these contributions integrate diverse methodological approaches, ranging from multinational surveys to longitudinal and experience sampling designs, thereby demonstrating both ways to and the potential of studying beliefs from an individual-differences perspective.

Perceptions of a Broken Society: Psychological Underpinnings of Anomie Across 28 Countries
Chiara Förster | Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Chiara Förster | Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Patrick Mussel | Psychologische Hochschule Berlin | Germany

Perceived anomie–the belief that the social fabric is deteriorating and leadership is ineffective or illegitimate–has been linked to pressing societal challenges, including polarization, extremism, and the spread of conspiracy theories. Yet prior research has primarily conceptualized anomie as a societal characteristic tied to country-level indicators of functioning, leaving unclear how much and why people within the same society differ in the extent to which they perceive society as broken. In this study, we examine psychological and contextual antecedents of interindividual differences in perceived anomie across multiple levels. Specifically, we test how perceived anomie is shaped by interindividual differences at the micro level (i.e., religiosity, perceptions of one’s personal economic situation), the meso level (i.e., perceived acceptance by society and isolation, self-perceived class and wealth), and the macro level (i.e, political orientation, dangerous world views, perceived inequality in society, and perceptions of the national economic situation). Using multinational data from 28 countries (N = 6,112) and hierarchical linear modeling, we disentangle within-country (i.e., individual-level) from between-country variance. By illuminating the interindividual differences that shape how people perceive the socio-political world, our findings advance a more person-centered understanding of anomie, underscore its relevance for personality psychology, and provide insights for interventions aimed at mitigating the downstream consequences of perceived societal breakdown.

Core Beliefs, Health and Life Satisfaction: Evidence for Relations and Developmental Trajectories
Prof. Dr. Patrick Mussel | Psychologische Hochschule Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Patrick Mussel | Psychologische Hochschule Berlin | Germany
Dr. Niklas Schulte | Freie Universität Berlin | Germany

Psychological and physiological health are central to individuals’ functioning and satisfaction across virtually all life domains. Investigating the dynamic interplay between health-related variables and individual differences in personality can clarify the antecedents and consequences of health, as well as identify potential starting points for intervention and prevention. In this research, we examine global indicators of health and life satisfaction in relation to core beliefs—defined as basic, generalized, and relatively stable cognitions reflecting how individuals perceive themselves within their social and cultural context. We propose that core beliefs may influence health-related variables (e.g., through life choices and lifestyle) and, conversely, that health-related variables may shape individuals’ fundamental assumptions about themselves (e.g., due to perceived capabilities in psychological functioning). In a large, diverse sample, we found substantial correlations between global health and life satisfaction indicators and core beliefs. A second study replicated these effects in a separate sample from a different country and revealed distinct patterns of correlation for more specific health indicators. A third, longitudinal study with three measurement points provided evidence of dynamic interactions between core beliefs and health-related variables, as well as their developmental trajectories. Notably, the size and direction of effects on these trajectories differed, suggesting distinct underlying mechanisms for psychological, compared to physiological health indicators. We discuss the theoretical and practical implications of these findings.

Theoretical work has hypothesized that fundamental assumptions about the nature of the world (e.g., “the world is safe”), referred to as primal world beliefs, function as highly stable cognitive schemas that shape how individuals perceive situations, with downstream consequences for emotional and behavioral responses. Despite this stability, emerging research suggests that under specific conditions primal world beliefs can adapt in response to current circumstances. However, underlying processes are still unclear. To better understand both the relevance of primal world beliefs for psychological functioning and their stability and change, the present project investigates these beliefs within a state–trait framework. Within a two-week experience sampling study with approximately 250 students using an interval-contingent design (up to five prompts per day), participants report at each prompt their current state world beliefs, well-being, and situation perception. Trait primal world beliefs, well-being, and situation perception are assessed immediately before and after the experience sampling period. Using multilevel structural equation modeling, we examine the unique and interactive contributions of state and trait primal world beliefs in predicting both state and trait situation perception and well-being. In addition, we explore to what extent changes in state and trait primal world beliefs predict changes in state and trait situation perception and well-being, and vice versa. Overall, this project aims to provide novel insights into the dynamics of primal world beliefs and their role in shaping everyday experiences and well-being.

Intellectual investment traits—personality traits which characterize individuals’ desire for thinking and learning—are established predictors for academic achievement but recent research also suggests a relevance to subjective well-being. However, the processes behind this association are not yet well understood. In this study, we examine associations of two investment traits, epistemic curiosity and intellect, with life satisfaction and self-related core beliefs. Using data from a German personality panel of up to 829 emerging adults, we found investment traits to correlate with life satisfaction as well as various core beliefs. Individuals with higher epistemic curiosity and intellect reported higher life satisfaction, more adaptive and fewer maladaptive beliefs regarding agency and self-esteem. Longitudinally, (mal)adaptive agency and self-esteem beliefs mediated the relationship between investment traits and life satisfaction. These results confirm previous findings of positive links between investment traits and well-being, offer potential explanations of the psychological processes at play, and provide support for calls to consider investment traits an important resource across different life domains.

Deceptive behaviour is common, yet little is known about the joint power of personality traits, core beliefs, and situational construals in predicting intentional deceptive behaviour (IDB). Findings highlight that IDB can be predicted from both stable dispositions and situation construals. The strong intersubjectivity demonstrates that vignettes reliably capture deceptive situational information.

Forensic Psychology in Family Law
Co-chair(s) Lara Schwarz (Basel University)
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Jelena Zumbach-Basu (Basel University)
Room: MT
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

This symposium brings together five complementary studies addressing central challenges in forensic psychology within family law, with a particular focus on child abuse risk assessment and judicial processes. Across ecological, psychometric, and procedural perspectives, the contributions highlight how parental risk and protective factors, dysfunctional parenting behavior and reliability of expert assessments shape child protection concerns and legal decision-making.
First, a meta-analytic review synthesizes four decades of research on intrafamilial CPM, identifying caregiver- and relationship-level factors as the most robust risks, while underscoring the scarcity of evidence on protective factors. Second, two empirical studies further advance the field by validating a novel self-report instrument for assessing CPM in forensic contexts and by examining stress as a mediating pathway between parents’ adverse childhood experiences and harmful parenting. Third, an experimental vignette study presents reliability assessment in expert risk assessments for family courts, pointing to the need for greater standardization. Finally, a systematic review examines how procedural justice is conceptualized and measured across legal settings, emphasizing its relevance for legitimacy and acceptance of court decisions. Together, these contributions inform evidence-based assessment, intervention, and judicial practice in child protection cases.

Prof. Dr. Jelena Zumbach-Basu | Switzerland
Show details

Katharina Zell | Switzerland
Asne Senberg | Germany
Anna-Luisa Sahlfeld | South Africa
Lara Schwarz | Switzerland
Dr. Annika Rademacher | Germany

Child psychological maltreatment (CPM) is the most prevalent yet least systematically examined form of child maltreatment, despite strong evidence linking it to adverse developmental and mental health outcomes. Despite growing interest in CPM, no comprehensive quantitative synthesis of its risk and protective factors has been available to date. This study aimed to systematically review and synthesize empirical evidence on risk and protective factors for intrafamilial CPM perpetrated by parents or primary caregivers. A systematic literature search identified 61 eligible studies published between 1984 and 2024, of which 30 provided sufficient statistical information for meta-analytic integration. Narrative synthesis was conducted across all studies, followed by meta-analyses of risk factors where possible. Risk factors were organized according to ecological and transactional frameworks. Results indicate that CPM is associated with a wide range of risk factors across multiple ecological levels, with the strongest and most consistent associations observed at the parent/caregiver and interpersonal (relationship) levels. In contrast, evidence for child-level risk factors was weak and inconsistent, and protective factors were rarely examined, precluding quantitative synthesis. Overall, the findings support ecological–transactional models of child maltreatment and underscore the conceptualization of CPM as a caregiving condition rooted primarily in caregiver behavior and relational context rather than child characteristics. The results underscore the need for improved risk and needs assessment instruments and for prevention and intervention strategies in child welfare that target modifiable risk factors.

Prof. Dr. Ute von Düring | Germany

Child psychological maltreatment (CPM) represents a significant global mental health concern. Broadly, CPM refers to acts of omission and commission that undermine a child’s basic needs and convey a sense of worthlessness. Despite diverse conceptual and definitional approaches, no clear consensus exists regarding how CPM should be defined or assessed. To address this gap, a parent self-report instrument was developed, guided by the framework of the American Professional Society on the Abuse of Children (APSAC). The instrument comprises 55 items assessing seven CPM subtypes, rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = does not apply to me to 5 = applies to me). The present study examines whether the proposed factor structure can be replicated and evaluates the instrument’s psychometric properties. The questionnaire was administered in a pilot study (N = 1,030 caregivers) and, after refinement, to a subsample of N = 491 caregivers (48.27% fathers) from Germany (67.82%) and Switzerland (31.36%) with a mean age of 44.81 years (SD = 8.57). To examine the factor structure, confirmatory factor analysis was conducted. To evaluate psychometric properties, measurement invariance testing as well as assessments of internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity were performed. This instrument provides a novel and reliable approach to assessing parenting behaviors within the spectrum of CPM, offering valuable applications in forensic contexts. It may also facilitate the evaluation of change following therapeutic and preventive interventions.

Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and elevated parental stress are well-established predictors of dysfunctional and potentially harmful parenting behavior. However, the mechanisms linking early adversity to later caregiving remain insufficiently understood. This study examines perceived parental stress as a key pathway connecting ACEs to harmful parenting practices in the general population. Data were collected in June 2025 via a 20-minute online survey from a population-based sample of n = 1,030 German and Swiss parents (52 % female, 48 % male) with children aged 0-18 years. Independent variables of this cross-sectional study were measured with the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (Bernstein et al., 2003) and the Perceived Stress Scale (Schneider et al., 2020). Outcome variables were measured with the Alabama Parenting Questionnaire (Reichle & Franiek, 2008), as well as the Screening Tool for Child Psychological Maltreatment (Schwarz & Zumbach-Basu, unpublished research version) in order to assess multiple domains of dysfunctional and potentially harmful parenting. We conducted analyses using structural equation modeling, controlling for parent`s gender. The results indicate whether higher levels of ACEs are associated with increased perceived stress and more dysfunctional parenting behaviors, and whether parental stress mediates these associations. By clarifying stress-related risk mechanisms linking early adversity to harmful parenting, the study contributes to a more differentiated understanding of child maltreatment risk mechanisms. The findings are expected to inform parenting capacity assessments and highlight stress-sensitive targets for prevention and intervention in child protection contexts.

Inter- and intrarater reliability of forensic experts in child maltreatment risk assessments – an explorative vignette study
Jonathan Foidl | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jonathan Foidl | Germany
Prof. Dr. Alexander Schmidt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jelena Zumbach-Basu | Switzerland

Expert recommendations provided for family courts in child protection proceedings can have far reaching consequences. Research on their inter- and intrarater reliability, however, is scarce. We sought to exploratively quantify the amount of inter- and intrarater agreement, as well as intrarater agreement under irrelevant context information. An experimental vignette study was conducted on mental health professionals with experience in conducting child maltreatment risk assessments for family courts in Germany. We examined the cross-sectional agreement between the experts (Nt1 = 32) and longitudinally within the same expert after three months (Nt2 = 16), as well as the effect of bias on intrarater agreement. Interrater reliability of the expert’s risk assessment was low (ICCs ≤ .26). Intrarater reliability was low to moderate (Cohen’s κs ≤ .35, ICCs ≤ .61). Reasons for low to moderate reliability are discussed and particularly explained by the lack of standardization in child maltreatment risk assessments in Germany. Building on these findings, a subsequent research project is currently underway to address the identified methodological limitations and to examine bias and structured approaches aimed at improving reliability. The presentation will also outline this ongoing project and its methodological advancements.

Perceptions of fairness in court and legal proceedings: A systematic review of procedural justice research
Lina Rustemeyer | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lina Rustemeyer | Germany
Antonia Schubert | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Jelena Zumbach-Basu | Switzerland

Procedural justice is a key determinant of perceived legitimacy and acceptance of judicial decisions. While distributive justice has traditionally received greater attention, psychological research increasingly emphasizes the importance of fair procedures, particularly in legal contexts characterized by high stakes, emotional involvement, and power asymmetries. Despite a strong theoretical foundation, important gaps remain regarding the measurement, contextual variability, and empirical investigation of procedural justice in judicial proceedings. This study presents a systematic review of empirical research on procedural justice in legal settings, conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a preregistered protocol. A comprehensive literature search in Web of Science, PsycInfo, and Scopus identified 90 eligible empirical studies. Most studies were conducted in the United States, with fewer originating from European and other international contexts. The majority focused on criminal proceedings, followed by civil legal contexts. Perceived procedural justice was most commonly assessed using self-report questionnaires (61 of 90 studies), followed by interview-based approaches (23 studies), whereas mixed and archival or case-based assessments were rare. Methodologically, most studies employed quantitative and cross-sectional designs, whereas longitudinal research remains comparatively scarce. The review addresses four central research questions concerning the measurement, conceptualization, perception, and determinants of procedural justice across legal settings. By synthesizing current empirical evidence, this review aims to clarify inconsistencies in measurement and conceptualization, identify key procedural components across legal contexts, and highlight directions for future research. The findings have implications for judicial training, courtroom practice, and the design of fair and transparent legal procedures.

Advancing Evidence, Measurement, and Practice in Youth Mentoring
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Tina Braun (Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule)
Room: SK
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Youth mentoring programmes, which aim to facilitate a supportive relationship between a young person and a non-parental figure, have become more popular in recent years. Although meta-analytic evidence indicates small to moderate positive effects, substantial theoretical and methodological questions remain open. The symposium integrates measurement innovation, longitudinal evidence, and multi-perspective analyses to refine theoretical models of mentoring effectiveness in European contexts. The first contribution by Esther N. Moszeik introduces and applies a newly developed pictorial version of the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI) in a German-speaking primary school sample. Addressing age-specific assessment challenges, the study compares 47 mentored children with 345 non-mentored peers and identifies differentiated socio-emotional skill patterns. In the second contribution, Adrian Fleckenstein develops a measure for empathic accuracy, particularly suited to measure empathy towards young mentees. Previous measures solely focus on adult targets, which is not consistent with a youth mentoring setting. The third contribution by Tina Braun investigates effects of long-term mentoring on mentees, extending the typically looked at timeframe of 12 to 18 months to a timespan of up to 14 years of mentoring. In the fourth contribution Timo von Oertzen investigates the effects of youth mentoring on three stakeholders: mentees, mentors, and parents. For each group of participants, he presents predictors of mentoring success and their respective factor structure. In the fifth and final contribution, Bernadine Brady investigates youth mentoring focusing on mental health service users. While youth mentoring can be a beneficial addition in these circumstances, she describes which factors need to be considered to ensure optimal effectiveness. Together, these contributions advance a more differentiated, mechanism-oriented, and context-sensitive understanding of youth mentoring.

Measuring Empathic Accuracy Toward Children: Evaluation of a Narrative-Based Assessment Paradigm
Adrian Fleckenstein | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Adrian Fleckenstein | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule | Germany
Prof. Dr. Tina Braun | Germany

Empathic accuracy—the ability to correctly infer another person’s emotional state—is a central component of adaptive social interaction. Although narrative-based empathic accuracy paradigms have been widely applied using adult targets, their applicability to child targets has received little systematic attention. This limitation is particularly relevant from a developmental perspective, as children’s emotional expressions and narratives differ qualitatively from those of adults.

The present work builds on an established narrative, video-based paradigm for assessing empathic accuracy with adult targets. In this standard procedure, observers watch short video clips in which targets describe emotionally meaningful experiences from their own lives. Targets subsequently rate their experienced emotions using a standardized affect measure, and observers rate the target’s emotions using the same scale. The correspondence between observer ratings and target self-ratings serves as an index of empathic accuracy.

In a first step, we examined whether this procedure can be directly transferred to child targets. Applying the paradigm to children revealed substantially lower agreement between observer ratings and self-ratings, as reflected in markedly reduced intraclass correlations, in some cases even yielding negative coefficients. Such reduced agreement may arise from different sources, including challenges related to children’s emotional expressiveness that affect observers’ ability to infer emotions, as well as developmental limitations in children’s ability to identify and verbally categorize their own emotions. The latter possibility may compromise the validity of self-reported emotion ratings in this age group. If children’s self-ratings do not accurately reflect their experienced emotions, observer–self correspondence may underestimate observers’ actual empathic accuracy.

To address this issue, we explore an alternative evaluation approach by incorporating expert reference ratings. Specifically, professionals with extensive experience in working with children’s emotions (ee.g. eachers) provide independent ratings of the target children’s emotional states, allowing comparison between self-based and expert-based benchmarks of empathic accuracy. Findings will be discussed with regard to possible future applications in the domain of youth mentoring.
