Prof. Dr. Elisabeth Kals | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany
Jun.-Prof. Dr. Christina Pfeuffer | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt | Germany

Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) wird zunehmend für Entscheidungen der Ressourcenallokation eingesetzt. Für die Wahrnehmung solcher Entscheidungen durch Nutzerinnen und Nutzer sind insbesondere distributive und prozedurale Fairness, Vertrauen, Akzeptanz, und Nutzungsbereitschaft zentral. Die vorliegende präregistrierte Studie untersuchte den Einfluss der Vorteilhaftigkeit des Ergebnisses und der Transparenz sowie des wahrgenommenen Aufgabentyps auf diese Bewertungen KI-basierter Entscheidungen. In einem annähernd für die deutsche Bevölkerung repräsentativen (Geschlecht, Bildung, Alter) onlinebasierten Vignettenexperiment bewerteten 929 Teilnehmende vier KI-gestützte Allokationsszenarien (Verteilung von Arbeitsaufgaben, Arbeitszeiten, Kindergartenplätzen, und Kleingartenparzellen). Das Design folgte einem 2 (Ergebnis: günstig vs. ungünstig; within) × 3 (Transparenz: niedrig vs. balanciert vs. hoch; between) Mixed-Design. Die Daten wurden mittels Bayes’scher linearer Mixed-Effects-Modelle ausgewertet.
Dabei zeigte sich die Vorteilhaftigkeit des Ergebnisses als mit Abstand stärkster Prädiktor für wahrgenommene Fairness, Vertrauen, Akzeptanz und die Bereitschaften, die KI zu nutzen. Auch der wahrgenommene Aufgabentyp beeinflusste die Bewertungen, denn je mechanischer (vs. menschlicher) eine Aufgabe wahrgenommen wurde, desto positiver fielen die Bewertungen von KI-Entscheidungen aus. Entgegen unserer Annahme zeigte sich allerdings unter anderem kein Haupteffekt von Transparenz, sondern nur eine Beteiligung des Prädiktors Transparenz an Interaktionen. Die Ergebnisse unterstreichen die zentrale Bedeutung von Ergebnisoptimierung für die Bewertung KI-basierter Entscheidungen. Der Einfluss von Transparenz scheint hingegen nuancierter und indirekter als bisher angenommen. Für die Gestaltung von KI-Systemen verdeutlicht dies, dass Nutzerakzeptanz maßgeblich durch die Fähigkeit des Systems zur vorteilhaften Problemlösung erzeugt wird.

Gestaltung organisationaler Gerechtigkeit in Algorithmifizierungs-Prozessen: Eine organisationskulturelle Perspektive

Während branchenübergreifend Unternehmen künstliche Intelligenz in ihre Geschäftsprozesse einführen, werden zwar ethische Fragen beachtet, aber weniger solche bzgl. organisationaler Gerechtigkeit dieser Maßnahmen und ihrer Gestaltung. Colquitt et al. (2023) kritisieren, dass Gerechtigkeit häufig als technisches Design-Element von KI angesehen, aber wenig als menschliches Erleben untersucht wird. Diese Forschungslücke schließen wir, indem wir erlebte Gerechtigkeit bei der Einführung von KI-Systemen im Kontext der organisationalen Kultur untersuchen. Hierzu wird das deutsche Organization Cultural Assessement Iventory ergänzt um die vier Dimensionen organ. Gerechtigkeit, spezifisch bezogen auf die Einführung von KI-Technologien. Eine Erhebung im Frühjahr 2026 ist geplant mit n≈300, die über deutsche Panels rekrutiert werden. Erste Ergebnisse zum Messinstrument werden präsentiert.
Mit den Erkenntnissen wird der CHAiO framework (Ontrup et al., in Begutachtung) zum Zusammenhang zwischen Organisationskultur und Algorithmifizierung um eine Perspektive organisationaler Gerechtigkeit erweitert. Es kann vermutet werden, dass nicht nur kulturspezifische Algorithmifizierungs-Strategien Fit von Menschen, Organisation und Technologie vorhersagen, sondern auch die Berücksichtigung bestimmter Gerechtigkeitsformen zu einer guten Passung führt. So wird unter anderem hypothetisiert, dass in Clan-Kulturen Organisationsmitglieder vor allem interaktionale Gerechtigkeit erwarten, während in Markt-Kulturen der Fokus auf distributiver Gerechtigkeit im Sinne fairer Aufteilung des zukünftigen Gewinnes liegt. Das daraus resultierende Modell kulturbasierter organisationaler Gerechtigkeit (CBOJ) kann einen Beitrag dazu leisten, die (Nicht-)Akzeptanz von Algorithmifizierung durch die Beschäftigten auf Basis der Befriedigung kulturspezifischer Gerechtigkeitserwartungen zu verstehen.

KI in der Hochschullehre aus gerechtigkeitspsychologischer Perspektive
Leoni Brand | Universität Salzburg | Austria
Franziska Kinskofer | Universität Salzburg | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Leoni Brand | Universität Salzburg | Austria
Franziska Kinskofer | Universität Salzburg | Austria
Prof. Dr. Eva Jonas | Universität Salzburg | Austria

Auf Basis der Studie „Von KI lernen, mit KI lehren: Die Zukunft der Hochschulbildung“ (Brandhofer et al., 2024) diskutieren wir, wie der Einsatz generativer KI in der Hochschullehre Bildungsgerechtigkeit beeinflusst. Ausgangspunkt sind Befunde, die sowohl Chancen als auch Herausforderungen aus Sicht von 1767 Lehrenden, 3165 Studierenden und 14 Rektoraten sichtbar machen. Zudem zeigen sich geschlechtsspezifische Unterschiede in den subjektiven Unterstützungsbedarfen: Während männliche Lehrende primär technische Unterstützung nachfragen, stehen für weibliche Lehrende didaktische Fragen im Vordergrund (Tulis et al., 2025). Diese Differenzen verweisen auf ungleiche Bedürfnisse im Umgang mit KI und haben damit potenzielle Implikationen für die wahrgenommene, insbesondere prozedurale und informationale Gerechtigkeit.
Aus sozialpsychologischer Perspektive interpretieren wir die rasante technologische Disruption als Katalysator sozialer Kategorisierungsprozesse: Die wahrgenommene „Schere“ zwischen KI-affinen und KI-distanzierten Hochschulangehörigen begünstigt Ingroup-Outgroup-Dynamiken („wir, die sich auskennen/die Progressiven“ oder „wir, die noch selbst denken/die guten Wissenschaftler*innen“ vs. „die anderen“). Dies kann die Akzeptanz und Kooperationsbereitschaft durch Bedürfniserfüllung vs. -diskrepanz in der Organisation Hochschule beeinflussen (interpersonale Gerechtigkeit). In weiterer Folge sind auch Auswirkungen auf die Distribution von Ressourcen denkbar, die potenziell ungleiche Ausgangsbedingungen schaffen und damit auch die wahrgenommene distributive Gerechtigkeit beeinflussen.
Der Beitrag diskutiert, unter welchen Bedingungen die Implementierung von KI in der Hochschule als gerecht erlebt wird und welche Gestaltungsprinzipien erforderlich sind, um soziale Polarisierung zu vermeiden und gerechtigkeitssensitive Strategien weiterzuentwickeln.

Trust in Pedagogical Agents: An Investigation on Reliability, Formality, and Cognitive Anchoring
Fransisca Hapsari | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Fransisca Hapsari | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stephanie Pieschl | Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany

Numerous factors affecting trust in automated agents have been found in the past decades, and fewer have been successfully replicated in different contexts. In the underrepresented context of trust in educational technology, trust in Pedagogical Agents (PAs) should be appropriately calibrated against PAs’ reliability. However, learners might adjust their trust against less relevant factors, such as language style or the presence of a cognitive anchor.
Using a task in which participants answer 10-item general knowledge tasks with low recall probability, we investigated whether trust in PA is affected by those factors.
In each of two online experiments (Experiment 1, n = 139; Experiment 2, n = 192) using a between-subjects design with 2 (reliability) x 2 (language formality or cognitive anchor bias) factors, we tested the effects of reliability and specific bias on trust. In the first experiment, bias in the form of language formality groups is manipulated as formal vs. informal language of a chatbot. In the second experiment, the bias of cognitive anchoring is manipulated as forced anchor vs. non-forced anchor groups. Subjective trust was measured using an 11-point Likert scale, and objective trust using compliance and agreement.
The preliminary results using ANOVA and regression showed that reliability affects trust consistently. Unlike previous studies, we did not replicate the findings that formality and anchoring affect trust in the PAs. This suggests the context-dependency of trust in PAs, and the effects of various biases on trust existing in HCI literature should be re-examined, especially in a learning context.

Michelle Habenicht | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Michelle Habenicht | Germany
Lea Schönfelder
Noel Hagen
Dr. Astrid Carolus

AI chatbots are frequently discussed as potential risks in the context of misinformation or disinformation due to hallucinations or sycophantic agreement with users. This study examines two interface-related factors that may promote caution toward chatbot-provided information: forewarnings in the chatbot interface indicating that the chatbot can make mistakes, and the quality of sources cited at the end of chatbot messages.
We conducted a 2 (forewarning included vs. not) × 3 (cited sources: none, good, bad) between-subjects experiment. Participants (N = 193), recruited via Prolific, completed a 10-question multiple-choice quiz. For each question, participants could use the chatbot for assistance. However, the AI chatbot consistently provided incorrect answers. Outcome measures included the adoption of these incorrect chatbot answers, perceived message credibility, perceived source credibility of the chatbot as an information source, and trust in the chatbot.
Results showed a high overall adoption of chatbot answers. Answer adoption was significantly influenced by the cited sources, perceived message credibility, and the risk/distrust dimension of trust. Lower adoption occurred when participants perceived chatbot messages as less credible and expressed greater distrust toward the chatbot. Higher perceived message credibility significantly increased both trust in the chatbot and perceived source credibility. Forewarnings did not significantly affect any of the measured variables.
Overall, the results indicate that chatbot responses are often accepted without verification. The effects of generic forewarnings appear limited, underscoring the need for further research on effective design strategies to promote critical and reflective chatbot use across different contexts.

Dr. Astrid Carolus | Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg | Germany

With the prevalence of AI chatbots in everyday use, various aspects of these interactions are becoming the focus of interdisciplinary research. Building on a classical study of Lee et al. (2000) following the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, this study analyses if the design of chatbot interfaces elicits gender-stereotypical reactions in both users' perceptions and behavior.

In a 1x3 between-subjects experiment (N=155), participants viewed screenshots of a chatbot assisting a user in navigating a social dilemma. The chatbot interactions were identical across all three conditions, differing only in interface colors which were pink and blue, as well as grey for the control group. After reading the interactions, the participants assessed the chatbot’s competence, trust (including the sub-scales integrity, benevolence, perceived risk and general trust) and the conformity with the chatbot’s recommendations as well as the perceived gender of the chatbot.

Results revealed that the chatbot with the pink interface was significantly more often attributed a female gender than the blue interface. In addition, male participants attributed significantly higher benevolence and integrity to the pink chatbot but followed the recommendations of the blue chatbot significantly more often. There were no significant differences among female participants.

The results illustrate that even simple visual design decisions such as the color scheme of an interface can elicit social attributions and affect information processing and judgement. Therefore, designing chatbots for social discourse requires a nuanced consideration of gender-related heuristics that may modulate user acceptance and trust.

Explanations, in particular, are thought to improve users’ understanding and support calibrated trust. In a preregistered between-subjects experiment (N = 728) with three transparency conditions (real explanation, placebic explanation, and trust seal) and two levels of processing time (limited and unlimited), participants interacted with an AI-based trading system. Individual differences in AI literacy and willingness to understand were included as moderators. The results showed that neither real nor placebic explanations improved factual or perceived understanding compared to trust seals, regardless of the time available for processing. Self-reported trust was also unaffected by transparency interventions. However, behavioural trust differed significantly; participants were more likely to follow the AI’s recommendation when provided with a real explanation compared to a trust seal. Overall, the findings challenge core assumptions of explainable AI. Transparency interventions may increase reliance without improving understanding, raising concerns about miscalibrated trust.

However, we argue that proactive robots which do display situational judgement are perceived as both effective and safe, leading to more positive attributions than less proactive robots or those without situational judgement. The results only partly support our hypotheses, as robots which display situational judgement are indeed consistently rated more positively than those that do not; however, the combination of situational judgement with a medium degree of proactivity, in which the robot identifies possible actions but asks the user for consent before pursuing them, emerges as the most positively rated option in both samples and across all outcomes. Situational judgement did buffer negative effects of high proactivity, but only for workers in manufacturing, and only regarding satisfaction and perceived support. We conclude that basic robot social skills such as situational judgement and communication (i.e., asking for confirmation) can help workers engage with increasingly autonomous and proactive robots.

Advancements in Psychological Network Analysis
Chair(s) Kai Jannik Nehler (Health and Medical University Erfurt and Goethe University Frankfurt)
Room: NL
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Network analysis has become an increasingly popular framework for modeling psychological concepts and processes, conceptualizing them as systems of interacting components rather than as manifestations of a single latent factor. In applied research, however, network models are still predominantly used in an exploratory manner and often rely on default methodological choices, such as convex regularization via the (graphical) lasso in regularized idiographic network estimation or the use of Pearson correlations in cross-sectional settings, even when ordered categorical data are investigated. Recent methodological work suggests that these defaults can substantially influence the resulting network structures and the conclusions drawn from them, and that confirmatory approaches may allow researchers to extract more information from network analyses.

Across its contributions, this symposium examines the impact of common methodological defaults, highlights alternative approaches, and introduces new methodological tools. The first contribution examines the consequences of analyzing ordered categorical data using Pearson correlations in network analysis, under the assumption that the observed categories arise from a discretized continuous latent variable via a threshold model. Another contribution reviews the types of hypotheses that are of interest in applied network research and evaluates the extent to which appropriate methods are used to test these hypotheses. A third contribution introduces methodological tools for testing underspecified hypotheses in cross-sectional network analysis. Finally, the symposium includes a contribution that introduces and evaluates network estimation methods for idiographic data based on nonconvex regularization.

Can Ordered-Categorical Data Ever Be Treated as Continuous? Impact on Sparsity and Edge Weight Estimation and Their Consequences for Network Analysis
Kai Jannik Nehler | Health and Medical University Erfurt and Goethe University Frankfurt
Show details
Authors:
Julien Patrick Irmer | University of Freiburg
Kai Jannik Nehler | Health and Medical University Erfurt and Goethe University Frankfurt
Martin Schultze | Goethe University Frankfurt

Psychological network analyses are mainly applied to questionnaire data measured on Likert-type, ordered-categorical scales. Substantively, such items are commonly conceptualized as discretized measurements of underlying continuous latent variables, which can be described via a threshold model. Within this framework, associations between variables are assumed to operate at the latent level and are not directly observable. In applied network research, ordinal responses are nevertheless often treated as continuous, and networks are estimated using Pearson correlations. In this talk, we discuss a fundamental consequence of this practice: the correlation structure of observed ordinal variables does not, in general, preserve the correlation structure of the underlying latent variables. Even when latent variables exhibit zero partial correlations, thresholding can induce nonzero associations at the observed level. As a result, zero edges are not preserved after categorization. Using analytical population-level results, we show that the bias induced by treating ordered-categorical data as continuous can be arbitrarily large and depends, for example, on threshold heterogeneity. This helps explain why many previous simulation studies have reported optimistic results: they implicitly focused on idealized settings, such as symmetric and equidistant thresholds. Outside such restrictive conditions, systematic bias in both edge weights and network sparsity is unavoidable and substantially larger than previously suggested. Our simulation results further show that these biases persist in finite samples and directly affect network estimation, including the recovery of zero edges.

Theory and Hypothesis Testing in Psychological Network Analysis: A Systematic Review of Current Practices
Tatiana Kvetnaya | Goethe University Frankfurt
Show details
Authors:
Tatiana Kvetnaya | Goethe University Frankfurt
Kai Jannik Nehler | Health and Medical University Erfurt and Goethe University Frankfurt
Martin Schultze | Goethe University Frankfurt

Modeling psychological constructs as networks allows researchers to represent conditional dependencies among variables of interest. This has facilitated a novel conceptualization of such constructs as dynamic systems, and has stimulated theory formation. However, theory development requires precise and testable hypotheses. In contrast, it has been critically observed that applied network research is largely exploratory and descriptive. While confirmatory methods became more accessible within the last years, recent work indicates they are used only in a small proportion of studies, such that information that could, in principle, have been gained from network analyses often remained unexploited (Blanchard et al., 2023; Schumacher et al., 2024).

To shed light on current developments in confirmatory network testing, we present a systematic literature review of psychological network analyses published over the last five years. We systematically investigate what kinds of hypotheses have been proposed in the literature, whether (and how exactly) they were tested in a formal confirmatory manner, and to what extent the data analyses were in line with verbal theory articulated in research articles. In particular, our goal is to assess the extent to which current practices already align with established guidelines for theory construction and testable model development (e.g., Borsboom et al., 2021; Smaldino, 2020), and to identify possible areas in which statistical methods to achieve this alignment are lacking. By highlighting such mismatches between commonly studied hypothesis scenarios and existing methodological tools, this work aims to inform future methodological development and provide recommendations for strengthening theory-guided psychological network analysis.

Testing Underspecified Hypotheses in Network Analysis
Martin Schultze | Goethe University Frankfurt
Show details
Authors:
Martin Schultze | Goethe University Frankfurt
Tatiana Kvetnaya | Goethe University Frankfurt

In light of what has been termed the theory crisis in psychology (e.g., Eronen & Bringmann, 2021), calls to improve theory building have grown louder in recent years. A wide array of frameworks providing formal foundations for theory development has been proposed across different areas of psychology (Glöckner & Fiedler, 2025). In clinical psychology in particular, the network approach has gained popularity as a way of conceptualizing the structure and development of psychopathology (Robinaugh et al., 2020). However, the development of complex theories is typically an iterative process in which proto-theories rarely allow reliable predictions about all possible connections between relevant symptoms, protective factors, and vulnerabilities. Consequently, early stages of theory development require testing hypotheses about subsets of edges within larger networks, for which theoretical predictions are underspecified. In empirical practice, this challenge is often addressed through exploratory statistical methods, testing edges separately, or comparing summative statistics to theoretical expectations. While this provides descriptive insights, it does not allow for confirmatory testing at the network level, or is associated with multiple testing and inflated error rates. Building on the work of Lin et al. (2025), we present a flexible approach for testing hypotheses concerning the presence or absence of arbitrary subsets of edges in cross-sectional networks. We further illustrate how different fit measures can be applied to different types of network hypotheses. The approach is demonstrated using an empirical example on Internet Gaming Disorder, complemented by a simulation study examining the conditions under which the method can be applied.

Nonconvex Regularization in Idiographic Network Analysis
Kai Jannik Nehler | Health and Medical University Erfurt and Goethe University Frankfurt
Show details
Author:
Kai Jannik Nehler | Health and Medical University Erfurt and Goethe University Frankfurt

Recent calls for person-centered approaches in psychological research emphasize the need for methods that support individualized modeling, particularly in contexts where between-person analyses may obscure theoretically relevant within-person dynamics. Idiographic network analysis addresses this need by modeling temporal and contemporaneous relationships among symptoms or other characteristics of psychological constructs (e.g., symptoms of a psychological disorder) within one individual, with estimation based on intensive longitudinal data from that person.

While several methods for estimating such networks exist, convex regularization approaches based on the (graphical) lasso remain particularly prominent. However, research in cross-sectional network analysis suggests that nonconvex regularization alternatives can outperform convex methods under certain conditions, for example by better preserving sparsity as the number of observations increases and by yielding less biased edge-weight estimates. Nevertheless, it remains unclear to what extent methodological findings from cross-sectional network analysis generalize to idiographic network settings with intensive longitudinal within-person data.

This talk presents a simulation study comparing convex and nonconvex regularization methods for idiographic network estimation under realistic psychological data-generating processes. Performance is examined across varying numbers of observations and degrees of sparsity in the population network. Evaluation focuses on edge recovery, assessed via sensitivity and specificity, as well as bias in estimated edge weights. All evaluation criteria are examined separately for the temporal and contemporaneous components of the network. Based on the simulation findings, practical guidelines are derived to inform the choice between convex and nonconvex regularization approaches in applied idiographic network analysis.

Vom Kindergarten bis zur Hochschule: Die Rolle von Mindsets entlang der Bildungslaufbahn
Chair(s) Vivien Rieder (Heidelberg University)
Room: FI
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Mindsets sind implizite Überzeugungen über die Veränderbarkeit und Bedeutung zentraler persönlicher Merkmale und Prozesse (Dweck & Leggett, 1988). Sie gelten als wichtige Determinanten von Lernen, Motivation und Selbstregulation (Lüftenegger & Chen, 2017). Relevant werden sie bereits im Vorschulalter, wenn Kinder selbstregulatorische Vorläuferfähigkeiten einüben, die später für das selbstregulierte Lernen zentral sind. Über den Verlauf der Schulzeit bis in den Hochschulkontext hängen Mindsets mit bildungsrelevanten Variablen wie Motivation und Lernerfolg zusammen (Yeager et al., 2019). Die Entwicklung individueller Mindsets findet dabei in Interaktion mit Bezugspersonen wie Eltern und Lehrkräften statt (Haimovitz & Dweck, 2016; Kroeper et al., 2022). Das vorliegende Symposium rückt Zusammenhänge zwischen Mindsets und Selbstregulation, Motivation sowie Einstellungen zu Inklusion in den Fokus. Die Beiträge untersuchen domänenübergreifende und domänenspezifische Mindsets in unterschiedlichen Altersgruppen und Bildungskontexten.
Ein erster Beitrag beleuchtet Zusammenhänge zwischen elterlichen und kindlichen Mindsets und der Selbstregulationsfähigkeit von Kindern im Übergang vom Kindergarten in die Schule. Darauf aufbauend berichten zwei Beiträge schulbezogene Befunde: Der zweite Beitrag zeigt, dass unterschiedliche intelligenzbezogene Mindsetdimensionen (Veränderbarkeit, Relevanz, Kompensierbarkeit) differenziell mit motivationalen Erwartungs-, Wert- und Kostenkomponenten bei Schüler:innen in der Mittelstufe verknüpft sind. In einem dritten Beitrag werden erstmals repräsentative Befunde zu Lehrkräfte-Mindsets in Deutschland sowie deren Zusammenhang mit Einstellungen zu Inklusion und Heterogenität vorgestellt. Den Abschluss bildet eine groß angelegte Interventionsstudie im Hochschulkontext, die zeigt, wie niedrigschwellige „wise interventions“ zu Mindsets bezüglich Interessen, Zugehörigkeit und Identitätsumdeutung insbesondere für vulnerable Studierendengruppen wirksam sein können.
Gemeinsam verdeutlichen die Beiträge die Relevanz von Mindsets unterschiedlicher Akteursgruppen entlang der Bildungslaufbahn sowie deren Potenzial für evidenzbasierte Interventionen.

Aus Fehlern lernen? Bedeutung elterlicher und kindlicher Mindsets für die kindliche Selbstregulation
Madita Sophia Weißmann
Show details
Authors:
Madita Sophia Weißmann
Vivien Rieder
Dr. Maren Stern
Leonie Köllbichler
Dr. Maya Adam
Dr. Torsten Wüstenberg
Prof. Dr. Yves Karlen
Prof. Dr. Silke Hertel

Die Fähigkeit zur Selbstregulation ist eine zentrale Voraussetzung für erfolgreiches Lernen und umfasst kognitive, behaviorale und emotionale Steuerungsprozesse (z.B. Blair & Razza, 2007). Forschungsergebnisse zeigen, dass das Selbstregulations-Mindset und Überzeugungen über die Bedeutung von Misserfolg mit der Selbstregulationsfähigkeit verknüpft sind (z.B. Hertel & Karlen, 2021). Frühere Studien weisen darauf hin, dass das elterliche Misserfolgs-Mindset die Wahrnehmung und Bewältigung von Herausforderungen bei Kindern prägt (Haimovitz & Dweck, 2016). Es ist anzunehmen, dass sowohl elterliche als auch kindliche Mindsets mit Indikatoren kindlicher Selbstregulation zusammenhängen.

Die vorliegende Studie untersuchte diese Zusammenhänge in einer Stichprobe von N=107 Kindern (MAlter= 6.66 Jahre; 42,9% weiblich), die sich im letzten Kindergartenjahr oder im ersten Schuljahr befanden. Das Selbstregulations- und Misserfolgs-Mindset der Kinder und Eltern wurde mittels Fragebogen erfasst. Die Eltern schätzten die kognitive und behaviorale Selbstregulationsfähigkeit der Kinder im Alltag in einem Fragebogen (BRIEF) ein. Zusätzlich wurde die Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulder-Task (HTKS) als verhaltensbasiertes Maß der Selbstregulation eingesetzt.

Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass ein lernförderliches Misserfolgs-Mindset der Eltern mit einer besseren Einschätzung der kognitiven Selbstregulation ihrer Kinder korrelierte (ß = -.30, p < .01), während keine signifikanten Korrelationen mit behavioralen BRIEF-Werten bestanden.
Darüber hinaus hing ein lernförderliches Misserfolgs-Mindset der Kinder mit einer besseren HTKS-Performanz zusammen (ß = .30, p < .01). Auch das elterliche Selbstregulations-Mindset zeigte einen positiven Zusammenhang mit der HTKS-Leistung (ß = .19, p < .05).

Die Ergebnisse verdeutlichen, dass elterliche und kindliche Mindsets mit verschiedenen Indikatoren der Selbstregulation verknüpft sind. Die Ergebnisse unterstreichen das Potenzial von Mindset-Interventionen, die selbstregulatorischen Fähigkeiten im Kindesalter zu unterstützen.

Mehr als Growth Mindset: Differenzielle Zusammenhänge intelligenzbezogener Mindsetdimensionen mit Motivation
Vivien Rieder
Show details
Authors:
Vivien Rieder
Dr. Lorena Fleischmann
Prof. Dr. Birgit Spinath

Intelligenzbezogene Mindsets beschreiben implizite Überzeugungen über die Veränderbarkeit von Intelligenz, ihre Relevanz für akademischen Erfolg sowie die Kompensierbarkeit geringerer Intelligenz durch Anstrengung (Spinath & Schöne, 2003). Sie stehen in Zusammenhang mit lern- und leistungsbezogenem Verhalten (Burnette et al., 2013). Frühere Studien zeigen, dass Growth Mindsets mit höherer Motivation im Sinne der situierten Erwartungs-Wert-Theorie (SEVT; Eccles & Wigfield, 2020) assoziiert sind, insbesondere mit höheren Wertüberzeugungen und indirekt mit Erfolgserwartungen (Chen & Pajares, 2010; Degol et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2023). Fixed Mindsets hingegen werden mit Testängstlichkeit in Verbindung gebracht, die einen Aspekt motivationaler Kosten darstellt (Lee et al., 2025). Während sich bisherige Befunde überwiegend auf die Veränderbarkeit von Intelligenz fokussieren, untersucht der vorliegende Beitrag alle drei Mindsetdimensionen im Kontext der SEVT-Komponenten (Erwartungen, Werte und Kosten).
Im Rahmen des Projekts ENR!CHMENT befragten wir 427 Schüler:innen (52 % männlich, 47 % weiblich, 1 % divers) der Klassen 7 und 8 an Gymnasien und Gemeinschaftsschulen. Die motivationalen Maße bezogen sich auf die Teilnahme an Angeboten zur Begabungsförderung. Mittels latenter Strukturgleichungsmodelle zweiter Ordnung analysierten wir Zusammenhänge zwischen den Mindsetdimensionen und motivationalen Komponenten.
Ein höheres Kompensierbarkeitsmindset ging mit höheren Erfolgserwartungen und Werten einher, während eine stärkere Zuschreibung von Relevanz an Intelligenz mit höheren psychologischen Kosten verbunden war. Für das Veränderbarkeitsmindset zeigten sich keine signifikanten Zusammenhänge.
Die Ergebnisse verdeutlichen, dass die Mindsetdimensionen differenziell mit Motivation assoziiert sind. Insbesondere die Annahme, Defizite durch Anstrengung ausgleichen zu können, scheint im Kontext der Begabungsförderung motivationsförderlich, während die Betonung der Bedeutung von Intelligenz mit erhöhten motivationalen Belastungen einhergehen kann.

Lehrkräfte-Mindsets in Deutschland: Erste repräsentative Befunde aus dem Deutschen Schulbarometer
Dr. Katharina Asbury
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Katharina Asbury
Prof. Dr. Uta Klusmann

Das Konzept der Mindsets beschreibt Überzeugungen über die Veränderbarkeit intellektueller Fähigkeiten. Während ein Growth Mindset davon ausgeht, dass Fähigkeiten durch Lernen und Anstrengung entwickelbar sind, betont ein Fixed Mindset deren Unveränderbarkeit. Internationale Studien zeigen Zusammenhänge zwischen Lehrkräfte-Mindsets, Unterrichtspraktiken und Schülerleistungen; für Deutschland fehlen bislang jedoch repräsentative Befunde.
Die vorliegende Studie untersucht (1) die Verbreitung von Growth und Fixed Mindsets unter Lehrkräften in Deutschland sowie (2) deren Zusammenhänge mit Einstellungen zu Inklusion und zum Umgang mit Heterogenität. Datengrundlage ist das Deutsche Schulbarometer 2025, eine repräsentative Onlinebefragung von N = 1.540 Lehrkräften und Schulleitungen an allgemein- und berufsbildenden Schulen. Mindsets wurden mit international etablierten Items zu impliziten Theorien der Intelligenz erfasst. Zusätzlich wurden Einstellungen zu Inklusion, Heterogenität und Fortbildungsinteressen erhoben. Die Analysen umfassen gewichtete deskriptive Auswertungen sowie multiple Regressionsmodelle unter Kontrolle von Geschlecht, Alter, Fachrichtung und Funktion. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass 13 % der Lehrkräfte ein ausgeprägtes Growth Mindset und 12 % ein ausgeprägtes Fixed Mindset aufweisen, während die Mehrheit zwischen diesen Polen liegt. Ein stärkeres Growth Mindset geht mit positiveren Einstellungen zur inklusiven Beschulung und einer höheren Bereitschaft zur Anpassung des Unterrichts an heterogene Lernstände einher. Fixed Mindsets stehen hingegen mit stärkeren Vorbehalten und höherem Belastungserleben im Umgang mit Heterogenität in Zusammenhang. Diese Effekte bleiben auch unter Kontrolle relevanter Kovariaten stabil. Der Beitrag zeigt, dass Lehrkräfte-Mindsets in Deutschland systematisch mit zentralen schulischen Herausforderungen verbunden sind und liefert damit eine empirische Grundlage für Diskussionen zu Lehrerbildung und inklusiver Schulentwicklung.

DIALOG – Eine groß angelegte, fundierte Interventionsstudie für Studienanfänger*innen
Luise Hönig
Show details
Authors:
Luise Hönig
Dr. Christina Bauer

Studienanfänger*innen stehen zu Beginn ihres Studiums vor vielfältigen Herausforderungen, darunter Zweifel an ihren Interessen, ihrer Zugehörigkeit sowie ihrer akademischen Identität. „Wise“-Interventionen – hoch skalierbare saying-is-believing-Übungen, die diese Herausforderungen adressieren – haben sich im US-amerikanischen und britischen Hochschulkontext als wirksam erwiesen, wurden bislang jedoch nicht im österreichischen Hochschulsystem (d. h. an öffentlichen, deutschsprachigen Universitäten) untersucht. Zur Schließung dieser Forschungslücke führten wir drei Interventionen mit einer großen Stichprobe von Studienanfänger*innen (N = 1.944) an einer österreichischen Universität durch: (i) eine Intervention zur Förderung von growth-interest, die die Überzeugung stärkt, dass Interessen veränderbar sind; (ii) eine Intervention zur Umdeutung der Identität, die Erstakademiker*innen (d. h. Studierende, deren Eltern oder Erziehungsberechtigte keinen Hochschulabschluss haben) dazu ermutigt, akademische Herausforderungen als Quellen von Stärke zu reinterpretieren; sowie (iii) eine Intervention zur Förderung von Zugehörigkeit, die das institutionelle Zugehörigkeitsgefühl von Erstakademiker*innen stärkt. Die Studie untersucht sowohl unmittelbare als auch langfristige Effekte der Interventionen. Erstens zeigte die Intervention zur Umdeutung der Identität deskriptive Verbesserungen im Zugehörigkeitsgefühl und in der Selbstwirksamkeit von Erstakademiker*innen. Zweitens erwies sich die growth-interest-Intervention insbesondere für Studierende mit vergleichsweise geringem intrinsischem Interesse an ihrem Studium als vorteilhaft. Insgesamt trägt die Studie zur evidenzbasierten institutionellen Integration niedrigschwelliger Interventionen bei, die Studienanfänger*innen den Übergang an die Universität erleichtern und ihren akademischen Erfolg fördert.

Early Adversity and Its Developmental Sequelae: Integrating Clinical, Biological, and Cognitive Perspectives
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Robert Kumsta (University of Luxembourg)
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Pascale Engel de Abreu
Room: GR
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Early adversity is one of the most robust predictors of later mental health problems, educational difficulties, and impaired socio-emotional development. Children growing up in contexts of neglect, maltreatment, or poverty are exposed to cumulative stressors that shape emotional regulation, learning processes, and biological stress systems. At the same time, outcomes are highly heterogeneous, pointing to the importance of integrative approaches that combine clinical, developmental, and biological perspectives. This symposium brings together longitudinal, network-analytic, and experimental research across four countries and two continents to advance our understanding of how early adversity influences mental health and cognitive development.
The first contribution stems from the Childhood and Mental Health Project project (CHAMP, University of Luxembourg) with children in out-of-home care in Luxembourg. The study examines the network structure of mental health problems in children growing up in institutional and foster care, identifying central symptom clusters and potential intervention targets.
Results from a large longitudinal study from the University of Basel that followed individuals with a history of out-of-home care into young adulthood in Switzerland will be presented in two talks. One presentation characterizes long-term clinical profiles and trajectories of psychopathology, while the other investigates links between early adversity and epigenetic aging.
A contribution from Ruhr University Bochum examines the impact of early adversity on extinction learning and probabilistic learning in children from Germany, highlighting cognitive mechanisms that may underlie vulnerability or resilience.
Finally, the « Poverty and the Mind” project, conducted by an international team of scientists from Bazil and Luxembourg, explores the impact of socioeconomic status on executive function in 355 Brazilian children aged 6-8 years across the full SES spectrum.
Together, these five talks integrate clinical, biological, and cognitive perspectives to deepen our understanding of pathways from early adversity to mental health and developmental outcomes.

Cyril Wealer | University of Luxemburg
Dr. Carolina Nikaedo | University of Luxemburg
Prof. Dr. Robert Kumsta | University of Luxemburg

Children in out-of-home care (OOHC) often report elevated rates of early adversity and trauma (EAT), and are at increased risk for developing mental health problems. Despite high rates of pre-placement adversity in both foster-based (FBC) and residential care (RC) settings, developmental outcomes show substantial heterogeneity, with meta-analytic evidence indicating more favorable mental health outcomes in FBC compared to RC. Network analysis offers a framework to examine mental health symptom structure, how specific adversities connect to mental health symptoms and whether these associations differ across care contexts.
Aims: To examine whether mental health networks differ between OOHC and non-placed children, to compare the structure and strength of adversity related-mental health networks between FBC and RC, and to identify adversity types that function as bridging nodes and compare their prominence across care settings.
Methods: Data were drawn from the CHAMP Project in Luxembourg, including FBC (n=115), RC (n=247), and primary school controls (n=1,768). Gaussian Graphical Models were estimated using EBICglasso. Networks included early adversity dimensions and mental health indicators (emotional and behavioral symptoms, executive functioning, attachment-related behaviors). Network Comparison Tests and bridge centrality analyses were conducted.
Preliminary Results: Analyses indicate differential connectivity patterns, with early adversity showing minimal direct associations with mental health in FBC, whereas these associations persist in RC. Full results will be presented at the conference.

Exploring links between type- and timing-specific characteristics of childhood maltreatment and epigenetic aging in formerly out-of-home placed young adults
Dr. Maria Meier | Universität Konstanz
Show details
Authors:

Dr. David Bürgin | University Basel
Prof. Dr. Marc Schmid | University Basel
Dr. Eva Unternährer | University Basel
Prof. Dr. Inga Schalinski | Universität der Bundeswehr
Prof. Dr. Vera Clemens | Universitätsklinikum Ulm

Background. Childhood maltreatment (CM) increases the risk for pathology and premature mortality, which may be mediated by epigenetic processes like DNA methylation (DNAm). While type and timing of CM are increasingly acknowledged when evaluating CM’s link to pathology, those factors have rarely been considered when evaluating methylation-based estimates of aging or mortality risk.
Objective. We explored how type- and timing-specific characteristics of CM – compared to global measures (e.g., severity, multiplicity, and duration) – relate to epigenetic aging, mortality risk and the pace of aging in formerly out-of-home placed young adults.
Methods. Overall, 117 adults (32% women, age mean = 26.3 years, SD = 3.6 years) completed the Maltreatment and Abuse Chronology of Exposure (MACE-X). We estimated DNAm from blood samples and calculated two epigenetic clocks (i.e., Hannum’s age, PhenoAge) and the pace of aging (i.e., DunedinPACE). As preregistered, we estimated the importance of CM type (abuse, neglect, peer victimization and sexual abuse), timing (ages 3-18) and global scores (severity, multiplicity, duration) on age acceleration and pace of aging using conditional random forest regressions.
Preliminary results. Sex-adjusted regressions showed that global CM severity predicted Hannum’s age acceleration, beta = -.60, p = .03. The results of the random forest regressions will be presented at the conference.
Discussion. In this high-risk sample of formerly institutionalized individuals, CM was linked to epigenetic age deceleration. While this finding replicates across different CM operationalizations in our sample, its generalizability should be tested in other high-risk populations to better understand which factors affect stress-related adaptations following CM.

Prof. Dr. Marc Schmid | University Basel

Background: Child maltreatment (CM) is a major transdiagnostic risk factor for psychopathology across the lifespan and is highly prevalent among youth placed in residential or out-of-home care. However, the specific roles of adversity type, timing, and accumulation in shaping the development and stability of psychopathology within this group remain insufficiently understood.

Objectives: This talk examines how CM contributes to the development and persistence of psychopathology adolescents and young adults in and after residential care, focusing on heterogeneity and developmental timing of maltreatment exposure.

Methods: Data stem from the Swiss JAEL study, a longitudinal investigation of young adults formerly placed in out-of-home care (N=231). Person-oriented latent profile and transition analyses identified subgroups with distinct symptom patterns and their changes over time. Conditional random forest regression was used to analyze effects of CM types and timing.

Results: Findings show high rates of exposure to multiple adversities. Greater severity and multiplicity of CA were linked to more persistent and complex psychopathology, particularly internalizing problems. Early abuse and late adolescent peer violence specifically predicted externalizing symptoms, highlighting both cumulative and timing-specific effects.

Conclusion: Young people placed out-of-home show enduring and multifaceted mental health difficulties associated with diverse CM exposures. Integrating person- and variable-centered analytic approaches fosters a more nuanced understanding of developmental risk and informs targeted and maltreatment-informed interventions for this vulnerable population.

Adverse experiences in early childhood and adolescence (Early Life Stress; ELS), have a substantial impact on the development of children and adolescents and increase the risk for psychopathology. Despite the prominent role that learning and memory processes play in the development of common psychopathological symptoms such as anxiety disorders, their potential role as a link between ELS and psychopathology is insufficiently understood. A thorough understanding of the interplay between ELS, cognitive mechanisms and later mental disorders is required to improve the prevention and treatment of mental disorders.
Accordingly, this study investigates the role of ELS for learning, psychopathology and positive mental health. Different types of learning, including extinction learning (studied via an eyeblink conditioning task) and probability learning (studied via a computerized probability learning task), are assessed in young children (3-5 years), primary school children (7-8 years), adolescents (12-17 years) and adults (25-40 years). ELS is assessed dimensionally via interviews with children, adolescents and adults as well as caregivers of young children, children and adolescents. Psychopathology is assessed via diagnostic interviews and questionnaires, also assessed in both, participants and caregivers.
The study design as well as some preliminary results will be presented. The preliminary results indicate that our dimensional, cross-age approach to assessing ELS appears promising. Together with initial analyses from the learning paradigms, our findings suggest good feasibility of the study procedures across age groups, thereby representing a promising approach for gaining a more sustainable and comprehensive understanding of ELS and its underlying mechanisms in relation to psychopathology.

Poverty as Early Adversity: Executive Function Development in Brazilian Children Across the Socioeconomic Spectrum
Prof. Dr. Pascale Engel de Abreu
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Pascale Engel de Abreu

Poverty is one of the most prevalent and preventable forms of early adversity worldwide. As a chronic and cumulative stressor, it shapes children’s developmental environments by limiting cognitive stimulation, linguistic input, and material resources, all factors known to influence brain development and long-term mental health. We examined executive function (EF) development in 355 Brazilian children aged 6–8 years growing up across the full socioeconomic spectrum, including children living in extreme poverty, in one of the most unequal countries globally, characterized by a persistently high Gini index.

Children completed a comprehensive battery assessing working memory, cognitive flexibility, selective attention, inhibitory suppression, and motor inhibition, alongside standardized vocabulary measures. Socioeconomic status (SES) was assessed multidimensionally, including household income, parental education, parental occupation, and household wealth. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a differentiated yet interrelated three-factor EF structure. SES and EF were strongly associated, sharing nearly 50% of their variance, which is substantially higher than estimates reported in samples from high-income countries and in line with bioecological models, which propose that environmental effects on cognition are more pronounced at lower SES levels. Notably, vocabulary fully mediated the association between SES and EF, suggesting that differences in linguistic and cognitive stimulation may constitute a central developmental pathway.

Because EF are foundational for emotion regulation, learning, and mental health, these findings identify a cognitive mechanism linking socioeconomic adversity to long-term vulnerability. Reducing socioeconomic inequality itself, alongside targeted cognitive interventions, may therefore represent a powerful lever for altering developmental trajectories shaped by early adversity.

What Keeps Newcomers Engaged? The Role of Perceived Organizational Support Level and Stability during Organizational Entry
Annabell Mitschelen | TU Braunschweig - Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Annabell Mitschelen | TU Braunschweig - Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Dr. Patrik Fröhlich | Bergische Universität Wuppertal
Dr. Hannes Schilling | TU Braunschweig - Institut für Psychologie
Prof. Dr. Stefan Diestel | Bergische Universität Wuppertal
Prof. Dr. Simone Kauffeld | TU Braunschweig - Institut für Psychologie

Perceived organizational support (POS) shapes employees’ early experiences during organizational entry. This study examines how newcomers’ POS develops during the early stages of employment and how this growth in POS relates to affective commitment, turnover intention, and innovative performance. Prior research has largely relied on static assessments, leaving open whether initial POS or changes in POS are more consequential for early retention, commitment, and innovative performance.
Grounded in Organizational Support Theory and Conservation of Resources Theory, POS is a dynamic resource for successful onboarding and retention. Using a four-wave longitudinal design with 231 newly hired employees in Germany at a public university, we applied latent growth modelling to analyze how intercept and slope of POS predict turnover intention, affective commitment, and innovative performance.
Results showed that turnover intention was related to both the intercept and slope of POS, affective commitment was related to the intercept only, and innovative performance was related to the slope. Overall, the results suggest that sustained increases in POS are particularly relevant for innovative performance and turnover intention, whereas initial POS appears more relevant for affective commitment. This pattern underscores that not only the amount but also the development of POS matters during organizational onboarding.
The findings highlight that maintaining organizational support throughout onboarding is associated with favourable attitudinal and behavioural outcomes. By introducing a temporal perspective on POS, this study advances research on organizational entry and offers practical guidance for designing support strategies that strengthen newcomers’ affective commitment, lower turnover intentions, and foster innovative performance.

Organizational objectification, need satisfaction, and deviance: The moderating role of person-organization fit
Dr. Katerina (Aikaterini Eleni) Tsantila | Justus Liebig University Giessen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Katerina (Aikaterini Eleni) Tsantila | Justus Liebig University Giessen | Germany
Dr. Bibi Zhang | Swansea University | United Kingdom
Prof. Frank Walter | Justus Liebig University Giessen | Germany

Experiencing organizational objectification (i.e., being treated as an instrument for organizational purposes) is a common phenomenon. Despite strong evidence that such experiences can have negative personal, interpersonal, and organizational consequences, some scholars view workplace objectification as inevitable and perhaps even beneficial. Combining propositions from Self-Determination Theory and the person-organization (PO) fit literature, we expect that when PO fit is low (i.e., when the organizational and personal values are less compatible), being treated as an instrument for organizational objectives may help to satisfy employees’ basic needs for competence and relatedness, because they feel useful and connected in pursuing collective goals. When PO fit is high, by contrast, organizational objectification may thwart employees’ needs for competence and relatedness, because employees may then find objectifying treatment to be more conflicting with their higher expectations toward the organization. As a result, those employees may be more inclined to retaliate through deviant behaviors. Using two-wave data from 129 employees in Germany, we indeed found that the associations between organizational objectification and competence/relatedness need satisfaction were positive when PO fit was low, but negative when PO fit was high. Furthermore, PO fit moderated the indirect relationship between organizational objectification and deviance through competence need satisfaction. This research adds to our understanding of the complex implications of organizational objectification and reveals boundary conditions and mechanisms through which such objectification affects employee deviance.

Paying for Cooperation: How Reward Systems Shape Relational Climates and Cooperative Behaviour in Organizations.
Michael Rauch | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Michael Rauch | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München | Germany
PD Dr. Katharina G. Kugler | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München | Germany

Organizational reward systems influence employees’ behaviours by providing incentives for desired forms of conduct. Thus, reward systems are key elements of organizational control to align individual employee actions with organizational objectives. Traditionally, research on reward systems has focused primarily on performance-based outcomes while paying less attention to a potential impact on employees’ social behaviour. Drawing on Relational Models Theory (RMT), Relationship Regulation Theory (RRT) and Relational Incentives Theory (RIT) which posit that relational incentives shape and modify fundamental forms of relationships, we proposed that organizational reward systems encompass relational incentive schemes that form predominant relationship patterns within the organization (i.e., ‘relational climates’). Further, we argued that employees’ perceptions of these relational climates influence employees’ motives for cooperative behaviour. To test these assumptions, we conducted a cross-sectional field study collecting data from 211 working individuals across various organizations. Our hypotheses were mainly supported: Different relational incentive schemes of the organizational reward system positively predicted employees’ perceptions of corresponding relational climates which in turn positively predicted employees’ corresponding motives for cooperative behaviour (mediation analysis). Overall, our findings emphasize how organizational structures, such as reward systems, affect employees’ relationships, thereby shaping (pro-)social behaviour within the organization.

Negative training transfer as a one-way-street? The role of affective responses and perceived organizational support in the context of dynamic training transfer
Charlotte Sophie Diekmann | MSB Medical School Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Charlotte Sophie Diekmann | MSB Medical School Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Alexander Pundt | MSB Medical School Berlin
Prof. Dr. Laura Venz | Leuphana Universität Lüneburg
Prof. Dr. Franziska Pundt | MSB Medical School Berlin

Objective: Adopting a dynamic perspective on training transfer, this study conceptualizes training transfer as an evolving process encompassing both positive and negative application attempts. Drawing on the Dynamic Transfer Model and attribution theory, it examines how organizations can support transfer following perceived failures in post-training knowledge application. Recognizing that transfer-related experiences influence different outcomes over the course of the dynamic process, we investigate whether the relationship between negative transfer experiences and changes in self-efficacy is mediated by negative affective reactions and moderated by perceived organizational support.

Methods: Self-report survey data were collected from a total of N = 285 training participants across two studies following the completion of job-related training programs (Study 1: 93 leaders assessed at two measurement points four weeks apart, Study 2: cross-sectional sample of 192 employees without leadership responsibility), capturing transfer experiences, emotional reactions, support, and self-efficacy.

Results: Moderated mediation analyses revealed a significant overall effect among employees without leadership responsibility, whereas no such effect was found for leaders. Among leaders, affective reactions were responsive to transfer experiences but did not account for changes in self-efficacy while perceived organizational support was relevant yet did not operate indirectly via emotional processes.

Conclusions: Overall, the findings underscore the importance of affective reactions and organizational support in the training transfer process and extend prior research by explicitly addressing the unexplored phenomenon of negative transfer experiences. By considering different target groups, the study highlights the context-dependent functioning of transfer mechanisms and advances a nuanced, more process-oriented understanding of training transfer.

Two Pathways to Remembering Intentions: A Bi-Factor Modeling Approach to Prospective Memory

Show details
Authors:

Dr. Kathrin Sadus

Event-based prospective memory (PM) is the ability to remember to execute an intended action in response to an external target. According to the Dynamic Multi-Process Theory, successful PM performance involves two cognitive processes interacting in a dynamic fashion: top-down preparatory processing and bottom-up spontaneous retrieval. Topic: Open Area

Successful aging is a multidimensional concept referring to a person's ability to maintain physical, psychological, and social well-being throughout later life. We leverage theory-based approaches and cutting-edge statistical tools to gain a deeper understanding of how successful aging is shaped by contextual factors such as daily events or intergenerational ties. ST describes the fear of conforming a negative stereotype about one’s group (Shapiro & Aronson, 2013) and leads to underachievement despite similar cognitive abilities (Appel et al., 2015). While ST is well researched in achievement situations, less is known about its impact on learning and affective-motivational characteristics constituting the multi-dimensional construct academic success. Therefore, we investigated the manifold ST impact as well as important personal and contextual moderators and mediators. Based on 106 university students with a self-assigned immigrant background (Mage=23.92, SD=3.98; 73.6% female, 1.9% diverse), we analyzed whether ST affects academic vocabulary learning, motivation (interest in learning new academic vocabulary, success expectations), and well-being (life satisfaction, positive/negative affect, anxiety). Sense of belonging and identification with country of origin/Germany were investigated as moderators, social identity threat as mediator. Reliabilities were satisfactory to good (α=.66–.89). ANCOVAs revealed significant ST effects on well-being (positive/negative affect, anxiety), F(8,190)=2.65, p < .01, Wilk`s Λ=0.81, η²p =.10. Sense of belonging moderated the relation between threat and vocabulary growth, F(2,91)=8.03, p < .001, η²p=.15. High belonging buffered negative effects, whereas explicit threat impaired performance among students with low belonging. Social identity threat served not as mediator. Results are discussed regarding content, methodological issues, and future research implications.

Findings support SDT’s framework, indicating that a calling enhances well-being primarily through autonomous work experiences that satisfy core psychological needs. Associations Between Self-Regulation, Intrinsic Goals, and (Anti)Social Goals
Chair(s) Dr. Ariadne Brandt (Universität Potsdam)
Room: PL
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Self-regulation (SR) refers to the capacity to modulate one’s cognitions, emotions, and actions, and includes a range of facets such as inhibition, cognitive flexibility, emotion regulation, and delay of gratification. SR facets play a significant role in pursuing future goals - both intrinsically motivated and socially motivated - that can benefit oneself (e.g., hedonic goals such as pleasure), benefit relationships (e.g., resolving conflict via adaptive interaction), benefit others (e.g., prosocial behavior such as helping) or, conversely, harm others (e.g., aggression and antisocial behavior). This symposium focuses on the relations between various SR facets and both intrinsic and social goals. All contributions make use of sophisticated modelling, including person-oriented or longitudinal methods while addressing developmental periods of middle childhood through adolescence and adulthood. The symposium’s first contribution highlights the daily interaction of SR with purely intrinsic processes, specifically hedonic experiences, and whether these increase the perceived success of SR in adults. The second contribution identifies latent profiles of adaptive versus maladaptive social information processing in adolescents and determines differences in SR abilities across these profiles. The third contribution investigates bidirectional associations between SR facets and prosocial behavior across four timepoints spanning childhood and adolescence. Complimenting this, the fourth contribution examines bidirectional effects of SR facets and aggressive and antisocial behavior across the same age groups and timepoints. Collectively, the symposium highlights multiple facets of SR and their relation to either intrinsic-, and/or social goal pursuit, suggesting that SR and its development is a key aspect for both personal and social well-being.

Participants (N ≈ 400) report on self-control conflicts, self-regulatory strategies, hedonic orientation and experience, affective well-being and self-control success up to five times per day over a period of seven days. We will use Multilevel Structural Equation Modelling to account for the nested data structure, latent variables, and an expected mediation effect whereby hedonic experience mediates the association between self-regulatory strategy use with hedonic orientation and self-control success/affective well-being. Results will be presented during the congress. Ultimately, this study aims to contribute to a more nuanced understanding of self-control by testing how exercising self-control can be a pleasant experience instead of the often proposed effortful one.

The avoidant SIP profile (18%) was shaped by high fear responsivity and a positive evaluation of passive social responses. Beyond Happiness: Rethinking Well-Being Across Contexts
Chair(s) Julian Scharbert
Chair(s) Jana Berkessel
Room: HR
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Increasing and maintaining well-being is a central human goal, yet well-being can manifest in different ways. Accordingly, the “good life” may not be limited to hedonic well-being—often emphasized in psychological research—but can also include meaning, psychological richness, and the fulfillment of personal goals and values.

This symposium brings together five projects that examine distinct perspectives on well-being across contexts (e.g., work, grandchild care, and life narratives) and methods (e.g., experiments, intensive longitudinal data, and text-based analyses), highlighting both convergence as well as trade-offs among different well-being facets.

The first talk investigates passion at work, showing that intense momentary passion, while rewarding in the moment, may be associated with lower perceived control and reduced performance. The second talk examines flow at work and its links to meaningful work and multiple well-being facets. The third talk explores daily role experiences (grandchild care, paid work, volunteering), revealing hedonic costs alongside increases in meaning in life across roles. The fourth talk considers obituary texts to demonstrate that psychological richness constitutes a distinct facet of well-being alongside happiness and meaning. Finally, the fifth talk introduces the Value Fulfillment Scale, a new measure designed to capture idiosyncratic conceptions of well-being—reflecting the diverse conceptions highlighted in the preceding talks.

Collectively, these contributions show that well-being is multi-faceted and person-sensitive: effects that appear beneficial on one facet may be neutral or even costly on another. The symposium underscores the value of expanding theory and measurement beyond happiness to better reflect how people define and pursue well-being.

Show details
Authors:
Kai Krautter

Passion for work is widely celebrated as a key driver of professional success, and prior research has established that passion positively predicts job performance. Yet, accounts of “too much passion” backfiring also populate the landscape, raising the question of whether more passion is always better. We reconcile these seemingly conflicting perspectives by developing a multilevel framework that differentiates the benefits of generally experiencing more passion (i.e., trait-level passion) from the costs of especially high momentary passion (i.e., state-level passion). We theorize that moments of intense passion reduce workers’ sense of control, leaving them myopically focused on prioritizing their experience over their performance, engaging in behaviors that prolong or increase their momentary passion (even when this undermines their performance). We also propose that workers who are generally more passionate are overwhelmed by “too much passion” more often, thereby dampening the overall extent to which passion enhances performance. In a daily diary field study of nurses (N = 792; k = 7,810) matched with supervisor-rated performance (N = 322; k = 3,610), we find a curvilinear relationship between state-level passion and performance alongside a positive but plateauing trait-level relationship. Two preregistered experiments (N = 655) and four supplemental studies (N = 1,144) identify the specific performance-impairing behaviors evoked by “too much passion,” provide evidence for reduced controllability as an underlying mechanism, and demonstrate discriminant validity from related constructs. We conclude with implications for how employees and leaders can effectively manage their passion at work to unlock its full potential.

Preliminary results from multilevel SEM models showed that on days when grandparents spent more time caregiving than usual, they reported greater fatigue, but also higher happiness and meaning in life. When grandparents worked or volunteered more than usual, they reported lower happiness and higher stress and fatigue, yet they also reported higher meaning in life. Hence, our preliminary results show mixed hedonic experiences for grandchild care, but highlight an eudaimonic gain, aligning with findings from parenthood research. Working was linked to eudaimonic gains (i.e., meaning in life), but only to hedonic costs. Our findings extend the limited research on the short-term effects of grandchild care, and for the first time, contrasted it with working as another typical role in young-old adulthood.

Show details
Authors:

Tobias Ebert

A good life is typically conceptualized as a happy or meaningful life. Recent studies have suggested a third facet: the psychologically rich life, characterized by a variety of interesting and perspective-changing experiences. In the current project, we introduce obituaries as a complementary and informative data source to (a) replicate happiness, meaning, and psychological richness as three robust and ubiquitous facets of a good life. We then (b) explore the role of life events, affect, and life domains in constituting a happy, meaningful, and psychologically rich life. To do so, we gather and analyze 333 newspaper obituaries (Study 1), and 1,200 obituaries from an online gravesite collection (Study 2). We further find (b) that life events primarily contribute to a psychologically rich life. We also find that positive affect is conducive to all three facets of a good life, while negative affect is only conducive to psychological richness. Regarding life domains, we find that work is positively related to meaning and psychological richness, while private life is negatively related to the two facets. Overall, our paper further establishes (a) psychological richness as a robust third facet of a good life and (b) life events, affect, and life domains as important contributing factors.

Show details
Authors:

The VFS entails an idiographic component by eliciting open-ended responses about individuals’ most important values in life, and a nomothetic component by utilizing Likert-scale questions to measure the degree of fulfillment and integration of these values. We present results regarding the scale development, factor structure, reliability, stability, and validity of the nomothetic part of the VFS based on data from >10,000 participants, along with insights based on a qualitative analysis of individuals’ idiographic, open-ended responses. We end by discussing how the VFS may be used to bridge idiographic and nomothetic approaches in well-being research.

Room: IT
Topic:
Form of presentation: Position Paper

Integrating Induction, Abduction, and Deduction: Toward a More Complete Epistemology for Psychological Science
Dr. Aaron Peikert | Max Planck Institute for Human Development | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Aaron Peikert | Max Planck Institute for Human Development | Germany
Jun.-Prof. Dr. Julia Möller | Leipzig University | Germany
Dr. Le Vy Phan | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany

Psychology’s dominant hypothetico-deductive epistemology construes scientific inquiry as a linear sequence of hypothesis formulation, prediction, and confirmation. This view artificially separates discovery from justification, privileges confirmatory reasoning, and obscures the indispensable roles of induction and abduction across the research process.

We argue that this simplification is both descriptively inaccurate and epistemologically detrimental: Real scientific practice requires a continuous interplay of inductive, abductive. and deductive processes. In particular, we highlight the central role of inductive inference as the primary mode of bottom-up generalization, and discuss how its systematic articulation is essential for developing a sound epistemological foundation. Treating deduction as the primary—or only—legitimate form of inference masks the actual role and mode of exploratory work, marginalizes theory development, and fosters inefficiencies such as the mislabeling of exploratory analyses, HARKing, and the underutilization of rigorous exploratory methods, including machine-learning approaches.

We propose a framework that maps the specific contributions and limitations of induction, abduction, and deduction onto each step of a prototypical research process. This integrative account clarifies how these inferential modes co-occur during hypothesis generation, data analysis, and interpretation, thereby increasing transparency, strengthening epistemological justification, and supporting methodological innovation in psychological science.

Open Science - Where do we stand? Where should we go?
Prof. Dr. Kai Sassenberg | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Kai Sassenberg | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany
Dr. André Bittermann | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) | Germany
Dr. Lena Hahn | Trier University
Prof. Dr. Mario Gollwitzer | Ludwigs-Maximilians Universität München | Germany

Fifteen years ago, Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn’s seminal “False Positive Psychology” paper kicked off the “credibility revolution” in psychology. Preregistrations, open data, open scripts, and adequately powered samples were promoted as standards to increase the reproducibility and replicability of research findings. The current talk will address the following questions based on metascience research: (a) To what extent have these standards been implemented? (b) If implemented, does the quality of the implementation meet the desired standards? (c) Did the implementation improve reproducibility and replicability? And finally, (d) what do these insights about the standards and their implementation imply for future research policies? To answer these questions, we will summarize research from our own and other labs. At the surface, the field shows continuous progress in applying the standards (e.g., increasing proportions of studies with power analyses, preregistrations, and open data). However, upon closer examination, for instance, of preregistrations, the consistency between preregistrations and publications, and the quality of the open data, implementations often fail to meet the desired standards. Given the limited quality of the implementation, it is not surprising that evidence regarding the effectiveness of the standards is mixed. Finally, we discuss how Open Science may become more effective based on changes in policies, workflows, and support measures (e.g., templates and research infrastructure), focusing on researchers' realities and motivation rather than on normative ideals and activism.

Position Paper: Motivated Reasoning / Morality
Room: IE
Topic:
Form of presentation: Position Paper

Understanding Motivated Reasoning: A Primer on the Current State of the Art
Dr. Fabian Hutmacher | University of Würzburg | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Fabian Hutmacher | University of Würzburg | Germany

Motivated reasoning denotes the phenomenon that individuals are more likely to arrive at conclusions that they want to arrive at. Over the past decades, motivated reasoning has attracted continued scholarly attention and has been demonstrated for a vast range of topics. Nevertheless, many unanswered questions remain. In this talk, I will discuss four key issues. First, it is still debated which preconditions give rise to motivated reasoning and whether research should rather focus on attitude roots (i.e., worldviews, identities) or surface attitudes (i.e., specific, concrete, and manifest attitudes). Second, it is unclear what (cognitive) processes lead to biased judgments, that is, whether motivated reasoning is primarily driven by changes in the quality or the quantity (i.e., the kind or the intensity) of information processing. Third, there is continued disagreement regarding the question under which conditions biased judgments can be unanimously interpreted as a sign of motivated reasoning. Fourth, there is an ongoing debate about whether more deliberation exacerbates motivated reasoning by allowing individuals to find sophisticated rationalizations for their preferred conclusions or whether it can be an antidote to biased reasoning. These four – and other, related – issues have long been identified but still stand. Therefore, research on motivated reasoning is not in need of new theoretical propositions: What is needed is a better understanding of the existing core concepts. The talk will outline how such an understanding can be achieved.

Aggressionen und Gewalt gegen Politiker*innen sowie deren Folgen haben in den letzten Jahren zunehmend Beachtung im gesellschaftlichen und wissenschaftlichen Diskurs gefunden, meist jedoch aus kriminologischer oder politikwissenschaftlicher Perspektive mit Fokus auf Konsequenzen für demokratische Prozesse. Mögliche Folgen auf individueller Ebene (z. B. für die psychische Gesundheit der Betroffenen) und mögliche vermittelnde Prozesse und Bewältigungsressourcen aus psychologischer Perspektive wurden bislang nur begrenzt untersucht. Aufbauend auf allgemeinen Bewältigungstheorien und vorhandener Forschung zu Kriminalitätsfurcht geht der vorliegende Beitrag daher den Fragen nach, ob tätigkeitsbezogene Viktimisierungen bei Politiker*innen mit Symptomen allgemeiner Angst und Depressionen einhergehen, ob diese Zusammenhänge durch tätigkeitsbezogene Furcht vor (Re-)Viktimisierung vermittelt werden und inwiefern in anderen Kontexten etablierte Bewältigungsressourcen (kognitive Bewältigungstendenzen, tätigkeitsbezogene Selbstwirksamkeit und soziale Unterstützung) diese Zusammenhänge moderieren. Basierend auf einer 2024 bis 2025 durchgeführten Online-Längsschnitt-Befragung unter deutschen Politiker*innen aller Ebenen (T1 2024: n = 1.997; T2 2025: n = 738) wurden regressionsbasierten Analysen (sowohl Querschnitts- als auch Längsschnittanalysen, einfache bivariate Korrelationen und komplexere SEM-Modelle) verwendet, um die vermuteten Zusammenhänge, Mediationen und Moderationen zu prüfen. Die Ergebnisse zeigen konsistente positive Zusammenhänge schwacher bis moderater Effektstärke zwischen tätigkeitsbezogener Viktimisierung, tätigkeitsbezogener Furcht vor (erneuter) Viktimisierung und Angst- und Depressionssymptomen. Hinweise auf eine mediierende Rolle der (Re -)Viktimisierungsfurcht fielen uneinheitlich aus, wohingegen moderierende Effekte (insbesondere von tätigkeitsbezogener Selbstwirksamkeit und sozialer Unterstützung) robuster nachweisbar waren. Insgesamt deuten die Befunde darauf hin, dass sowohl tatsächlich erlebte Viktimisierung als auch die Furcht vor erneuter Viktimisierung zur psychischen Belastung von Politiker*innen beitragen und dass individuelle sowie soziale Bewältigungsressourcen potenziell wirksame Ansatzpunkte für Prävention und Intervention darstellen können.

Zwischen Resilienz und Radikalisierung: Zusammenhänge zwischen Verschwörungsdenken, Wohlbefinden und individuellen Faktoren
Marvin Fendt | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Marvin Fendt | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München | Germany
Maximilian Ehle | Hochschule Fulda (Fulda University of Applied Sciences) | Germany

Hintergrund
Das komplexe Geflecht aus Verschwörungsdenken, mentaler Gesundheit, Mediennutzung und persönlichen Überzeugungen wird gesellschaftlich debattiert, bedarf jedoch weiterer Forschung (Douglas et al., 2019; Imhoff & Bertlich, 2024). Diese Studie untersucht deswegen die Zusammenhänge zwischen problematischer Mediennutzung, Schlafqualität, Angst, Wohlbefinden, Verschwörungsdenken und Populismus.

Methode
Es wurde eine quantitative Querschnittsbefragung (N=246; 70% weiblich; 83% hohe formale Bildung; MAlter=29.24, SDAlter=10.95) durchgeführt. In einem Strukturgleichungsmodell in lavaan für R wurden folgende latente Variablen verwendet: Populismus (Akkerman et al., 2014, ω=.82), Verschwörungsdenken (Uscinski & Olivella, 2017, ω=.77), Persuasionswissen (Fendt et al., 2025, ω=.89) sowie selbstentwickelte Skalen für problematische Mediennutzung (5 Items, ω=.77), Angst (7 Items, ω=.76), Wohlbefinden (5 Items, ω=85) und Schlafqualität (6 Items, ω=.78).

Ergebnisse
Das Strukturgleichungsmodell wies eine akzeptable Modellgüte auf (CFI=.914, TLI=.904, RMSEA=.047, SRMR=.067). Verschwörungsdenken war der stärkste Prädiktor für Populismus (β=.418, p=.001). Problematische Mediennutzung hatte keinen signifikanten direkten Effekt auf Populismus (p=.193), sagte jedoch erhöhte Angst (β=.35, p=.001) vorher. Persuasionswissen (p=.666) hatte keinen direkten Effekt auf Populismus, korrelierte jedoch mit Verschwörungsdenken (r=.54). Schlechte Schlafqualität war der stärkste Prädiktor für niedriges Wohlbefinden (β=.58, p=.001). Zudem zeigten sich negative Pfade von schlechterem Schlaf zu Angst (β=-.49, p=.001) und Mediennutzung zu niedrigerem Wohlbefinden (β=-.24, p=.001).

Diskussion
Die Ergebnisse stützen den Eindruck starker ideologische Zusammenhänge zwischen Verschwörungsdenken und Populismus, während ein direkter Effekt zwischen Mediennutzung auf Populismus ausblieb. Jedoch unterstützen die Ergebnisse die Annahme, dass ein Zusammenhang zwischen verstärkter Mediennutzung und schlechterer psychischer Gesundheit besteht. In der Präsentation diskutieren wir die Zusammenhänge zwischen Verschwörungsdenken und anderen individuellen Faktoren im Hinblick auf die Gestaltung zukünftiger Interventionen.
