Finally, results suggest that ideological ingroup

Studying Pro-Environmental Behavior in the Wild
Chair(s) Florian Lange
Anna Bosshard
Room: HU
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Changing consumption toward lower resource use and pollution is critical for staying within planetary boundaries. Understanding when and why individuals engage in environmentally relevant behaviors (like eating plant-based or reducing car travel) can support effective environmental mitigation. While controlled laboratory research may help reveal general behavior change principles, it often remains speculative how those principles apply to pro-environmental behaviors in the wild. This symposium showcases recent approaches for studying pro-environmental behaviors in the contexts where they naturally occur. Across different consumption domains, our contributions employ longitudinal and experimental field approaches as well as recent innovations in behavioral and impact measurement.

First, Neef examines whether and when environmental motivation predicts CO₂ emissions from travel behavior using high-resolution GPS tracking of everyday trips. The subsequent two talks showcase precise behavioral measurement in the clothing domain: Bosshard systematically reviews how observation and counting reports are used to study clothing acquisition and Carella assesses the effectiveness of a goal-setting intervention using such techniques, i.e., weekly reports of purchasing volumes across three months. Finally, two talks showcase field experiments and behavioral observation for studying sustainable diets: Gwozdz examines the potential of tailoring interventions to groups and contexts in promoting sustainable food choices across Europe, whereas Lange shows that prosocial incentives are effective for reducing plastic use as well as increasing plant-based food and drink choices.

Together, these contributions demonstrate the feasibility of studying pro-environmental behavior in the wild. They provide applied insights into the effectiveness of behavior change techniques and actionable knowledge for environmental policy design. The symposium will conclude with a 15-minute panel discussion.

Environmental Motivation’s Relevance for CO2 emissions
Nicolas Neef | Universität Hohenheim | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nicolas Neef | Universität Hohenheim | Germany
Ann-Kathrin Briem | Universität Hohenheim | Germany
Florian Kaiser | Otto-von-Guericke Universität | Germany

Recent research questions whether motivation is practically relevant: that is, whether people’s environmental motivation can be held accountable for their CO2 emissions. Using the highly emission-relevant mobility domain as our example case, we expound that environmental motivation is relevant for people’s emissions. Its relevance can, however, be overlooked easily for three reasons. (A) People differ—irrespective of their environmental motivation—in their travel performance (i.e., the overall distance they travel). (B) Environmental motivation controls people’s emissions exclusively indirectly by determining the likelihood of sustainable mode choices. (C) And environmental motivation’s emission efficacy will be attenuated by the typical majority of comparatively short trips. Accordingly, only when we account for people’s travel performance and only when people persistently choose sustainable modes of transportation for long-distance trips does the relevance of environmental motivations become more recognizable.
GPS mobility data tracked over the course of two weeks from 231 individuals were gathered, and, based on these data, people’s emissions were calculated. In total, 18,745 trips were recorded. A linear regression confirmed (A) that environmental motivation was, by and large, unrelated to people’s travel performance. A mixed-effect Bayesian logistic regression corroborated (B) that environmental motivation reliably influenced people's sustainable travel mode choices. Finally, mixed-effect Bayesian gamma and linear regression analyses confirmed (C) that environmental motivation’s emission-reducing efficacy strongly increased with increasing travel distance at the trip-level and overall travel performance. Essentially, we found environmental motivation to truly matter. This became recognizable when the emission-reduction potential is greatest: with long-distance trips and for people who travel more.

Global clothing production transgresses planetary boundaries, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and freshwater pollution. Behavior changes—especially among the richest 10%—are critical for environmental mitigation. Reducing acquisition has the highest mitigation potential, followed by shifts to second-hand clothes and eco-friendly (e.g., recycled) fabrics. Although clothing acquisition is widely studied in the social and behavioral sciences, most research relies on intentions, hypothetical choices, and retrospective self-reports of subjective frequencies. These approaches do not converge well with actual behavior, limiting their utility for understanding and changing acquisition and assessing the scaled mitigation potential of interventions. Here, we systematically review quantitative, empirical studies across psychology, marketing, sociology, and economics to (1) identify observational and precise self-reporting techniques for measuring clothing acquisition and (2) synthesize predictors of different acquisition types. Our search identified 67 peer-reviewed publications published between 2013 and 2025. Outcome measures included individual- and group-level acquisition in naturally occurring situations (by tracking purchases, sales, expenditure, or revenue) as well as arranged, consequential choices. Some studies estimated environmental impacts from purchase counts or expenditure. Preliminary results suggest that environmentalism is more consistently related to acquiring clothes from eco-friendly materials or second-hand than to general or conventional acquisition. In contrast, higher financial resources, advertising exposure, and material aspirations were consistently related to more conventional acquisition. Last, reduction goals and self-regulation were consistently related to less conventional acquisition. Overall, we hope to support theorizing on clothing acquisition and the development and assessment of behavioral interventions.

Within the EU-funded PLAN’EAT project, we examine how sustainable dietary behaviours can be promoted under real-world conditions using a multi-country living lab approach across seven EU countries. Interventions target heterogeneous populations, ranging from children to older adults, including socially disadvantaged groups.
Target behaviours were selected based on combined environmental and health impact as well as anticipated acceptability, resulting in context-specific dietary behaviours such as increasing legume or fruit and vegetable consumption. Behaviour selection was informed by expert interviews and structured expert ratings. Drawing on the COM-B model, behavioural barriers were assessed using theory-based questionnaires, enabling systematic identification of psychological capability, opportunity, and motivation constraints underlying dietary behaviour. Identified barriers informed the selection of intervention functions and behaviour change techniques following the Behaviour Change Wheel.
Intervention content was co-created with target groups to ensure contextual fit and feasibility. Examples include combining education, enablement, and environmental restructuring through repeated provision of legume-based food baskets, supported by recipe suggestions and digital prompts targeting habits, skills, and motivational processes.
Interventions are tested between October 2025 and February 2026 using designs ranging from quasi-experimental approaches and randomised controlled trials to micro-randomised trials enabling just-in-time adaptive interventions. Overall, the study demonstrates how systematic tailoring across who, what, and where can be achieved without compromising scientific rigour, advancing behavioural science by translating behavioural theory into empirically testable interventions in complex real-world food environments.

Compared to no-incentive control conditions, customers of a takeaway restaurant (N = 529) were observed to be less likely to take a plastic bag with their order if plastic-bag refusal led to charitable donations. Finally, customers of a coffee shop (N = 3807) were more likely to choose plant-based milk alternatives when doing so resulted in donations to a well-known human rights organization. Linking drink choices to donations to animal rights organizations or an unknown human rights organization was significantly less effective. In combination, these studies support the effectiveness of prosocial incentives for the promotion of pro-environmental behaviors. In addition, they illustrate how single-site field experiments involving randomization across multiple observation days can serve to evaluate behavior change techniques.

Advances in causal inference for theory building
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Steffi Pohl (Freie Universität Berlin)
Prof. Dr. Axel Mayer (University of Bielefeld)
Room: LT
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Psychology has often been criticized for relying on broad theories that are only loosely connected to statistical models and formal hypotheses. Causal inference can strengthen theory development by compelling researchers to translate general ideas into precise, testable claims about interventions, mechanisms, timing, and boundary conditions. In this symposium, we show how clearly defined causal estimands, rigorous study designs, and appropriate analytic strategies—combined with transparent and defensible identification assumptions—can transform theoretical concepts into more stringent empirical tests and, in turn, sharpen theory.
To enable more informative evaluations of models and hypotheses, Mayer shows how hypotheses on ordered treatment effects can be tested and evaluated in causal frameworks. Previous research has shown substantial variation in effects across replication studies, partly due to underspecified theories. Pohl, Twardawski, and Sengewald introduce a framework for identifying sources of effect heterogeneity also across quasiexperimental studies. Because theory building requires understanding how a treatment affects an outcome, Morelli, Faleh, and Brandt present an approach to causal mediation that relaxes the strong assumption that all mediator–outcome confounders are known and measured. Kiefer and Mayer clarify causal definitions and identification strategies for ratio-based effect measures. As treatments are often administered repeatedly and may vary over time, Münch and Koch propose a method for estimating the joint causal effect of an entire treatment regime using intensive longitudinal data, even in the presence of time-varying confounders. Völkle synthesizes the contributions, highlights central insights, and discusses implications for substantive research.

Informative hypothesis testing for average and conditional causal effects
Prof. Dr. Axel Mayer | University of Bielefeld | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Axel Mayer | University of Bielefeld | Germany

Classical null hypothesis significance testing often provides limited support for answering substantive research questions about causal effects, particularly when researchers have clear expectations about the ordering or direction of these effects. This contribution presents an integrated framework for informative hypothesis testing of average and conditional causal effects within the EffectLiteR approach. EffectLiteR directly targets quantities of interest such as average and conditional treatment effects and adjusted means in latent variable models. We extend the framework by incorporating informative hypotheses that encode theoretically grounded expectations (e.g., that a new treatment is more effective than an old treatment, which in turn outperforms a control condition). Methodologically, we demonstrate how informative hypotheses involving causal effects can be evaluated using the Fbar-test and generalized (non-linear) Wald statistics, allowing order restrictions to be incorporated into frequentist inference. Simulation studies show that informative hypothesis testing yields higher power than classical NHST, with power increasing as expected with sample size and effect magnitude. This highlights the increased sensitivity gained by aligning statistical tests with substantive expectations. In addition, we discuss the integration of model comparison approaches, including the generalized order restricted information criterion, and contrast p-value based decisions with informative model evaluation. Overall, informative hypothesis testing within the EffectLiteR framework provides a coherent and powerful alternative for evaluating average and conditional causal effects, narrowing the gap between research questions, theory, and statistical inference.

Identifying causes of effect-heterogeneity between quasi-experimental replication studies
Prof. Dr. Steffi Pohl | Freie Universität Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Steffi Pohl | Freie Universität Berlin | Germany
Dr. Mathias Twardawski | Ludwig-Maximilian-Universität München | Germany
Prof. Dr. Marie-Ann Sengewald | Friedrich-Alexander-University Erlangen-Nürnberg | Germany

When the same study is repeated, results are often not identical. Such differences are sometimes seen as flaws, but they can also arise for more natural reasons — for example, because participants differ, treatments are delivered in slightly different ways, or the studies take place in different settings. Understanding these differences is essential for developing stronger theories about how and why treatments work.
Ideally, researchers would compare studies that are identical except for one feature of interest. In practice, however, unintended differences are almost always present and can make it difficult to know what really caused the variation in results.
Previous work provided a causal framework for identifying causes of effect-heterogeneity between experimental studies. However, experimental studies are not applicable in all areas. When we want to investigate causes of effect-heterogeneity across quasi-experimental studies, confounding does not only occur between studies, but also within each single study – the original and the replication study. Adjustment must, thus, account for three different sources of confounding, which may partly overlap.
We provide an extension of the causal framework for effect heterogeneity between experimental studies that allows to investigate effect heterogeneity between quasi-experimental studies. We present formal definitions of the causal effects of interest, identification assumptions, and derive respective causal estimands as well as their estimation in real data. We show how the method can be applied and derive recommendation for conducting (replication) studies that may bring us closer to more informative theories.

For example, it is somewhat counter-intuitive in the context of ratio effects that an effect measure based on group averages does not necessarily resemble an average over individual effect measures, not even in randomized controlled trials. This phenomenon is known as (non-)collapsibility and has received quite a lot of attention in the biostatistics and epidemiology literature. In this talk, we use the stochastic theory of causal effects for defining different types of ratio effects and for clarifying the necessary assumptions for their identification. We briefly introduce the core aspects of the stochastic theory of causal effects before showing how to define ratio effects either as individual ratio effects or as average ratio effects. The different types of effects require different causality assumptions and have a different meaning, which only becomes clear when building on theories of causal effects.

Normativität ist das Grundproblem der Kriminalpsychologie (doch es ist lösbar!)
Dr. Marie Joséphine Hamatschek | Universität Hildesheim | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Marie Joséphine Hamatschek | Universität Hildesheim | Germany

Die Kriminalitätstheorie braucht die Psychologie. Dass Gesetze handlungswirksam sind, setzt innere Prozesse normbezogener Selbststeuerung voraus, die ohne psychologisches Wissen nicht zu verstehen sind. Gerade dieses Verständnis fehlt in der Kriminalitätstheorie. Die meisten Ansätze bieten vage oder gar zirkuläre Erklärungen, die ohne psychologisch verankerte Konstrukte auskommen. Die Hauptursache hierfür, so die Kernthese, liegt in der normativen Definition des Explanandums durch das Adjektiv 'kriminell'. Die Analyse ergibt, dass diese regelmäßig zu einer 'Kontamination' des gesamten nomologischen Netzes mit impliziten Werturteilen führt. Die dadurch entstehenden normativ aufgeladenen Konzepte, die als Ursachen betrachtet werden, werden allein durch die gleichgerichtete Bewertung als kohärent wahrgenommen ('normative Klammer'), obwohl sie auf Faktenebene heterogen und teils sogar widersprüchlich sind. Ein Beispiel hierfür ist das antisoziale Persönlichkeitsmuster. Gemeinsam erzeugen die normative Kontamination und die normative Klammer zirkuläre bis tautologische Erklärungsmodelle. Der vorgeschlagene Lösungsansatz besteht darin, die Normativität im Explanandum auf die psychologische Ebene zu übersetzen. Damit wird die Bewertung ausgelagert: Es wird nicht mehr modelliert, warum sich Menschen schlecht verhalten, sondern, warum Menschen (unter bestimmten Umständen) gegen eine internalisierte, motivational wirksame Rechtsnorm verstoßen - unabhängig davon, wie wir die Tat bewerten. Dieser Ansatz setzt ein handlungstheoretisches Verständnis von Kriminalität voraus. Zudem muss die psychologische Repräsentation des (Straf-)Gesetzes als innerer normativer Standard modelliert werden, einschließlich seines motivationalen Impetus. Erst wenn wir die normative Natur krimineller Handlungen ernst nehmen, können wir viele lange monierte Probleme beheben, so die mangelnde Integration von Personen- und Situationsvariablen, die fehlende Speisung aus Grundlagenforschung und das generelle Theoriedefizit.

Authors:

Dr. Diana Fischer-Preßler | Frankfurt University of Applied Sciences | Germany

Social media platforms are widely criticized for enabling misinformation and surveillance—societal challenges tied to centralized governance. As social media have become infrastruturalized—i.e., widely used and an essential aspect in the economy, government, and everyday life—such challenges must be addressed. Decentralized social media (DSM) platforms such as Mastodon (federated) and Steemit (blockchain-based) aim to address these issues by redistributing power and promoting user autonomy. This position paper examines whether decentralization offers effective solutions to misinformation and privacy concerns.
The paper reviews current research on social media platforms and the societal challenges they cause or exacerbate through their governance models. In doing so, this position paper employs a governance framework based on decision rights, accountability, and incentives to compare centralized and decentralized social media models and how these governance dimensions are linked to societal challenges. Based on our investigation, we argue that technical and governmental decentralization is difficult to achieve fully. Moreover, while DSM reduce corporate dominance, they introduce new vulnerabilities, such as fragmented moderation and misaligned incentives. We extract a triangular model of belief systems that shapes the various approaches to social media: (1) social media as-a-service, (2) as-a-public good, and (3) as-a-financialized asset. Each belief system reflects different assumptions about user agency and platform purpose, but none fully resolves the pressing challenges of content quality or user privacy. The position paper highlights that decentralization is not a universal fix; effective social media governance requires deliberate, value-aligned design.

Show details

Ellen Dapperger | University of the Bundeswehr Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. Karl-Heinz Renner

Most research on gaslighting focuses on victims, leaving the person behind perpetration largely unknown. Prior work has mainly emphasized dysfunctional personality traits and a narrow set of negative tactics (e.g., love bombing, isolation) among perpetrators. In contrast, this mixed-methods study investigates a broader range of both negative and positive perpetrator traits and behaviors, as the combination might explain why victims maintain a relationship.
We conducted semi-structured interviews with N = 100 self-identified gaslighting victims. After transcript-based verification that the reported experience met criteria for gaslighting (i.e., a valid perception of reality was undermined), N = 75 interviews were included in a qualitative content analysis to derive categories of perpetrator traits and behaviors.
Following the interview, participants completed an online questionnaire providing victim-rated assessments of perpetrator-related constructs (Big Five, Dark Triad, NARQ, and USM-motives scales) and the frequency of experience of 22 specific gaslighting behaviors (GBEQ).
Preliminary qualitative results suggest that victims often describe perpetrators in ways consistent with Dark Triad traits, while also attributing positive traits (e.g., loving, funny) and behaviors (e.g., emotional care, financial support). Quantitative analyses showed marked differences with high effect sizes, for example, lower scores on the BFI-2 dimension Conscientiousness (d = -1.99) and higher scores on the NARQ facet Devaluation as well as the USM motive Power (d > 1.9 for both).
Overall, the data point toward a perpetrator profile characterized by a combination of socially appealing and socially harmful traits and behaviors, which may be central to sustaining gaslighting dynamics.

Die Rolle persönlicher Wertorientierungen im Victim–Offender-Overlap bei Partnerschaftsgewalt
Dr. Laura Bartz | Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony | Germany
Show details

Prof. Dr. Stephan Thomsen | Leibniz University Hannover


Die Victim-Offender-Overlap-Theorie geht davon aus, dass Viktimisierungserfahrungen mit eigener Delinquenz in Zusammenhang stehen. Zahlreiche empirische Studien belegen einen positiven Zusammenhang zwischen Opfer- und Tätererfahrungen in unterschiedlichen Gewaltkontexten. Bislang ist jedoch wenig darüber bekannt, ob und wie persönliche Wertorientierungen diesen Zusammenhang beeinflussen. Die vorliegende Studie untersucht daher, inwiefern persönliche Werte den Zusammenhang zwischen Viktimisierung und Täterschaft bei partnerschaftlicher Gewalt moderieren.
Die Datengrundlage bildet eine Befragung mit zwei Messzeitpunkten im Rahmen eines Evaluationsprojekts zur Prävention von Partnerschaftsgewalt über soziale Medien (Nt1 = 1.973; Nt2 = 772). Analysiert wurden Zusammenhänge zwischen Viktimisierungserfahrungen, Täterschaft sowie ausgewählten Wertorientierungen aus den Bereichen Selbsterhöhung (Macht und Hedonismus) und Bewahrung des Bestehenden (Sicherheit und Konformität).
Die Ergebnisse zeigen einen positiven Zusammenhang zwischen Viktimisierung und Täterschaft. Querschnittliche Analysen zum ersten Messzeitpunkt deuten darauf hin, dass einzelne Wertorientierungen diesen Zusammenhang moderieren: Hohe Ausprägungen von Macht und Konformität verstärken den Zusammenhang zwischen Viktimisierung und Täterschaft, während Sicherheit eine abschwächende Wirkung zeigt. Diese Moderationseffekte lassen sich jedoch längsschnittlich nicht replizieren.
Insgesamt deuten die Ergebnisse darauf hin, dass persönliche Wertorientierungen den Zusammenhang zwischen Viktimisierung und Täterschaft unter bestimmten Bedingungen beeinflussen können. Diese Moderationseffekte sind jedoch nicht stabil, sondern möglicherweise kontext- oder stichprobenabhängig. Die Studie erweitert bestehende Ansätze zum Victim-Offender-Overlap, indem sie persönliche Wertorientierungen als individuelle Kontextfaktoren untersucht.

Häufig werden Intimizide als Eskalation vorheriger Beziehungsgewalt verstanden. Allerdings geht nicht allen Intimiziden eine Gewaltvorgeschichte voraus und nicht längst alle Gewaltvorfälle enden tödlich. Etablierte Risikoanalyseinstrumente wie das Danger Assessment (DA) und das Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment basieren trotzdem vornehmlich auf Kriterien, die frühere Partnerschaftsgewalt abbilden. Das neu entwickelte Risikoanalyseinstrument für Intimizide GaTe-RAI berücksichtigt hingegen andere tatrelevante Merkmale, wie Leaking (Ankündigungen einer potentiellen Tat), weitere Warnsignale und potentielle Trigger, die unabhängig vom Vorkommen vorheriger Gewalt sind. Das Instrumente zeigte bislang eine vielversprechende prädiktive Validität, aber es ist unklar, ob es einen Mehrwert zu bisherigen Risikoanalyseinstrumenten bietet. In der vorliegenden Stichprobe aus 79 versuchten und vollendeten Intimiziden in Deutschland sowie einer Kontrollgruppe aus 139 Fällen, in denen eine Tat angekündigt, jedoch nicht ausgeführt wurde, wurden alle drei Instrumente angewendet. Das DA erzielte in dieser Stichprobe eine Vorhersagegüte knapp über Zufallsniveau mit einem AUC von .55, GaTe-RAI von .83 und ODARA von .44. Eine Kombination aller Kriterien aus DA und GaTe-RAI und DA resultierte in einem finalen Model, das 2 Kriterien aus dem DA und 12 aus GaTe-RAI umfasste und die Vorhersagegenauigkeit gegenüber GaTe-RAI allein nicht erhöhte (AUC=.83). Die Ergebnisse bestätigen ähnliche Befunde einer unabhängigen deutschen Stichprobe und verdeutlichen, dass Intimizide nicht notwendigerweise eine Eskalation vorheriger Gewalt darstellen. Somit sollten Leaking, andere Warnsignale und potentielle Trigger in der Risikoanalyse mit berücksichtigt werden.

Insbesondere unbegleitete Vollzugslockerungen werden jedoch oft mit einem erhöhten Risiko für die Allgemeinheit in Verbindung gebracht, da sie den Patient*innen mehr Gelegenheiten für neue Straftaten eröffnen. Entsprechend wird die Entscheidung über die erstmalige Gewährung unbegleiteter Vollzugslockerungen in der Regel durch eine umfassende Risikoeinschätzung begleitet. Das optimale Vorgehen bei dieser spezifischen Form der Risikoeinschätzung ist bislang jedoch weitgehend ungeklärt. Häufig wird dabei auf sogenannte „Lockerungshindernisse“ zurückgegriffen, die überwiegend fixiert-dynamische Risikofaktoren umfassen. Deren prädiktive Validität ist bislang jedoch nicht empirisch überprüft worden. Vor diesem Hintergrund wurden am Kriminologischen Forschungsinstitut Niedersachsen Vollzugsakten von 219 Patient*innen aus zehn verschiedenen Einrichtungen des Maßregelvollzugs (§§ 63 und 64 StGB) ausgewertet. Auf Grundlage der Akten wurden mehrere etablierte Risikoprognoseinstrumente (VRAG-R, ORGS 3, Static-99r, SVG-5) sowie die Liste der Lockerungshindernisse codiert. Mittels ROC-Analysen wurde anschließend untersucht, inwiefern die Lockerungshindernisse, sowohl isoliert als auch in Kombination mit etablierten prognostischen Instrumenten, zur Vorhersage von Lockerungsmissbräuchen im Jahr nach der Gewährung der ersten unbegleiteten Vollzugslockerung beitragen. Erste Ergebnisse legen nahe, dass die Anzahl der Lockerungshindernisse keinen nachweisbaren Zusammenhang mit dem Risiko für Lockerungsmissbräuche aufweist. Weitere Befunde zu den Lockerungshindernissen sowie deren praktische Implikationen werden im Rahmen des Vortrags diskutiert.

Among laypeople and law-enforcement personnel alike, inconsistencies across repeated statements are commonly taken as indicators of fabrication. However, inconsistencies also occur in reports of events that have actually been experienced. This is taken into account by the concept of differential mnemonic consistency which implies that, within an experience-based statement, certain elements of an event (e.g., core activities) should be reported more consistently across interviews than others (e.g., peripheral activities). Given the widespread notion that consistency signals truthfulness, fabricated statements should largely lack this natural difference in consistency. We tested this expectation experimentally by conducting two successive interviews with participants who either reported an experienced physical examination or fabricated a statement in which they pretended to have undergone the examination. Two different measures of mnemonic consistency were examined, retention and repetition consistency. Both measures helped to differentiate between experience-based and fabricated statements, thereby providing strong empirical support for the potential of differential mnemonic consistency as a supplementary criterion in credibility assessment. Further, we report marked differences in patterns of omissions, additions and contradictions between experience-based and fabricated reports. These findings highlight the need to distinguish not only between core and peripheral elements, but also between different types of inconsistencies.

Human Augmentation Technologies: Interdisciplinary Psycho-Social perspectives
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Bertolt Meyer (TU Chemnitz)
Room: AT
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Human Augmentation Technologies (HATs)—from bionic prostheses and wearable brain–computer interfaces to occupational exoskeletons—are rapidly moving from niche applications into everyday and organizational contexts. Yet their societal impact hinges not only on technical performance, but on how augmentation is morally evaluated, psychologically experienced, and socially negotiated. This symposium brings together organizational and social psychology, human–computer interaction, and design research to advance an integrative psycho-social perspective on human augmentation.

Across four contributions, we examine key mechanisms and leverage complementary methods to capture both anticipated and lived consequences of HAT use. Paper 1 demonstrates, in large-scale vignette experiments on wearable BCIs, that moral appraisals systematically mediate how device characteristics (type, purpose) and user characteristics (disability status) translate into personal and societal adoption intentions. Paper 2 extends the focus from acceptance to social perception and the user’s perspective, combining experiments on stereotype-relevant judgments (e.g., competence, sociability, morality) with qualitative interviews on self-perceptions and meta-perceptions among expert users of bionic arm prostheses. Paper 3 introduces TechnoSapiens, an augmented-reality simulation platform enabling realistic experimentation with currently infeasible prosthetic concepts to study design-driven changes in perception and interaction in single- and multi-user settings. Paper 4 translates qualitative insights from industrial contexts into upstream design requirements for exoskeleton development, highlighting tensions around strain normalization, work identity, stigma, and resource-building.

Together, the symposium aims to move beyond “acceptance” as an end-point and toward psychologically informed, ethically grounded, and design-sensitive pathways for responsible human augmentation.

Besides their technical capabilities, these technologies prompt significant psychological and social questions, such as how users are perceived by others and how prolonged use affects users’ self-perceptions and meta-perceptions. To complement these quantitative results, a qualitative interview study with expert users of bionic arm prostheses further explored self-perceptions and meta-perceptions. Participants reported enhanced self-efficacy, confidence, and perceived competence after adopting advanced prostheses, along with observable changes in how others interacted with them.
Overall, these findings indicate that HATs affect both interpersonal perceptions and users’ self-concepts. Although these technologies offer significant potential, they may also lead to unintended social consequences, underscoring the need for psychologically informed, interdisciplinary approaches to human augmentation.

Occupational exoskeletons are commonly framed as ergonomic tools; however, they also constitute intimate forms of human augmentation that reshape posture, effort, proprioceptive feedback, and perceived bodily boundaries. Their organizational effectiveness, therefore, hinges not only on biomechanical performance but also on how augmentation is experienced, interpreted, and socially negotiated. We argue that these psychological dynamics should be treated as upstream design requirements throughout development, rather than downstream “acceptance” issues.
Drawing on our design practice and qualitative evidence from semi-structured interviews with employees in automobile assembly and warehouse logistics, we identify recurring tensions and opportunities in human–exoskeleton augmentation. (1) Augmentation under high demands: in contexts where strain is normalized, bodily signals may be muted, and workers can lack both opportunities and language to articulate early warning signs. This complicates requirement elicitation, risk communication, and the interpretation of “tolerance” as usability. (2) Augmentation and work identity: exoskeletons can cue stigma (“needing help”) or technomorphic readings (“Robocop”), shaping self-perception, peer interaction, and psychological safety—especially when managerial narratives foreground productivity. (3) Augmentation as a resource: beyond output gains, eyond output gains, can foster body awareness, health-related self-efficacy, and reflective work practices, strengthening resources rather than intensifying demands.
We conclude by translating these psychological considerations into corresponding design and implementation recommendations. These can help steer human augmentation toward positive, health-supportive experiences. We also outline how organizational psychology concepts can inform future development.

Humor spielt in beruflichen und gesellschaftlichen Kontexten eine wichtige, aber ambivalente Rolle. Da Humor unvermeidbar ist, beleuchten die hier vorgestellten Studien systematisch, wie Humor und Lachen in der Politik, in Führungspositionen und im Pflegebereich wirken bzw. gefördert werden können.
Scheel und Bachmann untersuchen alle Lachereignisse aus über 70 Jahren im Deutschen Bundestag und analysieren dabei sowohl Eigenschaften der Redner:innen als auch zeitliche Dynamiken und Ansteckungseffekte. Mikelopoulos und Gockel erforschen experimentell, wie gescheiterter Humor bei Führungskräften wahrgenommen wird und welche Rolle das Geschlecht dabei spielt. Korock und Scheel evaluieren ein siebenmonatiges, multimodulares Humortraining in Pflegeeinrichtungen hinsichtlich Zielerreichung und nachhaltigem Transfer. Soucek zeigt, dass eine webbasierte Humorintervention selbstaufwertenden Humor steigern und aggressiven Humor reduzieren kann.
Übergreifend differenzieren die Studien zwischen funktionalen und dysfunktionalen Humorformen und demonstrieren, dass Humor gezielt trainierbar ist. Methodisch kombiniert das Symposium Feldanalysen historischer Daten, experimentelle Szenarien und Interventionsstudien mit unterschiedlichen Zielgruppen.
Das mittlerweile zehnte Humorsymposium trägt dazu bei, Humor und Lachen als Kommunikationsmittel besser zu verstehen, sodass Humor zukünftig in der Organisationsentwicklung, Gesundheitsförderung und im politischen Kontext besser verständlich und einsetzbar wird. Humor und Lachen werden für Überzeugung oder Wettbewerb, verbindend oder trennend, legitimierend oder subversiv in der politischen Kommunikation eingesetzt. Es gibt v.a. experimentelle Befunde, aber kaum größere Feldstudien oder Analysen zeitlicher Dynamiken. Wir untersuchen Verteilung und Ansteckungsgrad von Lachereignissen in Jahrzehnten von Plenarsitzungen im Deutschen Bundestag, unter Berücksichtigung der Konnotation des Lachens sowie der Parteizugehörigkeit und Statusmerkmale der Redner:innen.
Datenbasis sind stenographische Protokolle der (~900k) Wortbeiträge (v.a. Reden) im Deutschen Bundestag (1949-2022) mit ca. 37k protokollierten Lachereignissen. Als Statusmerkmale werden Regierung (vs. Opposition), Seniorität, Geschlecht, sowie Ost-/Westdeutsch berücksichtigt. Neben Verteilungen zwischen Personen werden die Dynamiken von Lachereignissen von einem Wortbeitrag auf den nächsten, und über einen ganzen Sitzungstag hinweg, analysiert (Hawkes Prozess/ Event Clustering in Time). Deskriptiv zeigen sich durchschnittlich ein Lachereignis pro Wortbeitrag, sowie deutlich mehr feindselige (~23k) als affiliative Lachereignisse (~14k). (Die Analysen sind bis zum Kongress abgeschlossen.)
Limitierend ist, dass Lachen als Proxy, aber Humorproduktion nicht direkt erfasst wurde, und der thematische Kontext nicht berücksichtigt ist. Zukünftig sollte die Art des Humors analysiert werden. Die Studie liefert Hinweise auf moderierende Faktoren für die Wirkung spezifischer Humorarten, die bspw. Fraktionen für gezieltes Training nutzen können. Dies ist die erste Studie, die Ansteckung von Lachen im politischen Kontext über die Zeit untersucht sowie den Einfluss verschiedener Statusmerkmale auf Vorkommen und Art von Lachereignissen systematisch analysiert. Dies ist nicht zuletzt wichtig, um die Mechanismen in den Verhandlungen politischer Themen zu verstehen.

Geschlechtsspezifische Wahrnehmung von gescheitertem Humor bei Führungskräften: Eine experimentelle Szenario-Studie
Prof. Dr. Christine Gockel
Show details
Authors:
Alisea Mikelopoulos
Prof. Dr. Christine Gockel
Claudia Franz

Humor ist auch im Führungskontext ein verbreitetes Kommunikationsmittel, wird jedoch nicht in jeder Situation wie intendiert wahrgenommen. Gescheiterter Humor kann unterschiedliche Interpretationen hervorrufen und dadurch die Wahrnehmung von Führungskräften beeinflussen. Hierbei können geschlechtsbezogene Erwartungen die Bewertung von humorvoll-intendierten Bemerkungen beeinflussen. Aktuelle Studien deuten darauf hin, dass Frauen und Männer im Führungskontext unterschiedlich beurteilt werden, insbesondere wenn kommunikatives Verhalten von etablierten Rollenerwartungen abweicht. Wir untersuchen, ob gescheiterter Humor bei Führungskräften abhängig vom Geschlecht der handelnden Person unterschiedlich wahrgenommen wird.
Die Studie folgt einem experimentellen 2×2-Design mit zwei unabhängigen Variablen: Geschlecht der Führungskraft (weiblich vs. männlich) und Humorausgang (gelungen vs. gescheitert). In einer szenario-basierten Online-Erhebung bewerteten 105 Studierende eine Führungskraft nach einer kurzen humorbezogenen Situation im Arbeitskontext. Als abhängige Variablen wurden die LXM-Facetten Zuneigung und fachlicher Respekt erfasst. Als Kontrollvariablen wurden die Humorstile berücksichtigt.
Erste Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass gescheiterter Humor die Zuneigung zur Führungskraft vermindert, nicht aber den fachlichen Respekt ihr gegenüber beeinflusst. Das Geschlecht der Führungskraft hatte keinen Einfluss auf diese Einschätzungen.
Die Untersuchung basiert auf hypothetischen Szenarien und einmaligen Bewertungen. Dynamische Interaktionen sowie langfristige Effekte lassen sich daher nur eingeschränkt abbilden.
Unsere Studie verbindet Humorforschung mit Führungs- und Geschlechterforschung und geht der Frage nach, welche Rolle geschlechtsbezogene Erwartungen bei der Bewertung gescheiterten Humors spielen. Sie trägt dazu bei, humorvolle Kommunikation in Führungsrollen differenzierter zu betrachten.

Bleibt der Humor? Evaluation und Transfer eines multimodularen Humortrainings in der Langzeitpflege
Laura Korock
Show details
Authors:
Laura Korock
Prof. Dr. Tabea Scheel

Hohe körperliche und emotionale Arbeitsanforderungen sowie der Personalmangel in der Langzeitpflege erhöhen das Risiko für Erschöpfung, Burnout und Fluktuation. Wirksame Bewältigungsstrategien und ein positives Teamklima sind daher zentral. Obwohl Humortrainings das Wohlbefinden fördern, fehlen bislang Untersuchungen zur Nachhaltigkeit. Diese Studie evaluiert ein siebenmonatiges, multimodulares Humortraining in Pflegeeinrichtungen mit Fokus auf Transfer sowie individuelle und organisationale Effekte.
In einer vierjährigen Studie (2022-2026) im Interventions-Kontrollgruppendesign nahmen Mitarbeitende aus drei Pflegeeinrichtungen an drei Runden eines siebenmonatigen Humortrainings (vier Tagesseminare + Mentoring) teil. Eine vierte Einrichtung sowie Nichtteilnehmende aus den Interventionseinrichtungen dienten als Kontrollgruppen. Daten wurden zu Beginn (T0), bei jedem Seminar (S1–S4) sowie drei Monate post-training (T1) zu Zielerreichung, Trainingstransfer, humorbezogenen Variablen, individuellen Ressourcen, Wohlbefinden, Teamklima und organisationalen Outcomes erhoben. Vorläufige Analysen umfassen Daten der ersten beiden Durchläufe (nIG = 56, nCG = 39).
Vorläufig zeigt sich, dass Teilnehmende drei Monate nach der Schulung von einer moderaten Zielerreichung, einer hohen Zufriedenheit mit der Zielerreichung und einem hohen Grad an Anwendbarkeit in der Praxis berichten; außerdem gaben sie einen Rückgang des Glaubenssatzes „Humor sei nicht erlernbar“, einen gesteigerten Humoreinsatz, höhere Resilienz und niedrigere Kündigungsabsichten an.
Zu den Limitationen gehören Selbsteinschätzung, eine geringe Stichprobengröße sowie evtl. Verzerrungen durch Kontexteinflüsse.
Bestätigt sich das Potenzial, könnten Humortrainings im Pflegekontext breiter etabliert werden, um Bewältigungsmechanismen auf individueller und Zusammenarbeit auf organisationaler Ebene zu fördern.
Die Studie bietet Evidenz zu Wirksamkeit und Transfer von Humortrainings am Arbeitsplatz.

Evaluation einer webbasierten Intervention zur differenzierten Förderung verschiedener Humorstile
Prof. Dr. Roman Soucek
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Roman Soucek

Humor im Arbeitskontext hilft, schwierigen Situationen mit einer gewissen Leichtigkeit zu begegnen und trägt damit zu deren Bewältigung bei, was sich wiederum positiv auf das psychische Wohlbefinden auswirkt. In der Literatur werden jedoch verschiedene Humorstile unterschieden, die nicht nur eine positive Wirkung haben wie beispielsweise aggressiver Humor. Humorinterventionen sollten deswegen zwischen positiven und negativen Humorstilen unterscheiden und diese gezielt ansprechen. Bislang existieren kaum Studien, welche die Wirksamkeit von Interventionen hinsichtlich einzelner Humorstile untersuchten und keine Studie berichtete eine Senkung negativer Humorstile. In der vorliegenden Studie wird deswegen eine Intervention zur differenzierten Förderung verschiedener Humorstile vorgestellt.
Die Wirksamkeit der webbasierten Intervention wurde mit einem längsschnittlichen Untersuchungsdesign mit vier Messzeitpunkten überprüft; an der Intervention nahmen bislang 26 Personen teil. Die Intervention bestand aus zwei Kursen, die Humor in Bezug auf sich Selbst und auf Andere thematisierten. In beiden Kursen wurden positive wie auch negative Humorstile erläutert und verschiedene Übungen angeboten. Die Abfolge der beiden Kurse erfolgte randomisiert. Insgesamt umfasste die Intervention acht inhaltliche Sitzungen sowie vier Sitzungen mit Fragebögen zur Evaluation der Intervention.
Die Evaluation bezog sich auf die spezifische Wirkung der beiden Kurse und kontrollierte statistisch den allgemeinen Sinn für Humor. Die Ergebnisse belegten eine Erhöhung des selbst-aufwertenden Humorstils sowie eine Senkung des aggressiven Humorstils. Darüber hinaus zeigten sich Zusammenhänge einzelner Humorstile mit Indikatoren des psychischen Wohlbefindens wie etwa dem Abschalten von der Arbeit und emotionaler Erschöpfung. Insgesamt verdeutlichen die Ergebnisse, dass sich positive wie auch negative Humorstile gezielt verändern lassen und legen deren Relevanz für das psychische Wohlbefinden dar.

Social Dynamics and Well-Being: Advancing Methods Across Time Scales and Levels
Co-chair(s) Eva Bleckmann (Universität Hamburg)
Lara Kroencke (Universität Münster)
Room: BE
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Social interactions and relationships are fundamental to people’s well-being. While social needs are universal, their strength varies greatly across people, social contexts, and over time. Consequently, determining for whom, how, and when social factors impact well-being remains a complex challenge. This symposium features six talks that examine social dynamics—how they are measured, what predicts them, and how they are linked to well-being—across different temporal and analytical levels. The first four talks focus on daily life processes using experience sampling methods (ESM) and daily diaries: Palme et al. combine idiographic modeling and bottom-up clustering to uncover groups of people with similar within-person social dynamics, while Kroencke et al. explore between-person differences in different social interaction processes and their links to interpersonal traits and well-being. Bleckmann et al. investigate how momentary social features and stable relationship resources jointly shape self-esteem dynamics in daily life, and Kraemer et al. combine ESM and smartphone sensing to examine associations of social desire and positive affect with social contact across communication modes, time, and analytical levels. The final two talks broaden the temporal scope: Haehner et al. examine how different risk factors generate interpersonal stressors across hours, days, and weeks, and Schellenberg et al. present a meta-analysis on how daily social events link to well-being across within- and between-person levels. Collectively, this symposium offers a comprehensive overview of innovative methods that advance our understanding of social dynamics, their predictors, and their consequences for well-being across different timescales and analytical levels.

From Individuals’ Social Dynamics to Group Patterns: Combining Idiographic and Bottom-Up Integration
Elisa Palme | Universität Osnabrück
Show details
Authors:
Elisa Palme | Universität Osnabrück
Mitja Back | Universität Münster
Simon Breil | Universität Münster
Lara Kroencke | Universität Münster
Niclas Kuper | Universität Münster

Traditionally, research on personality and social relationships has been dominated by nomothetic approaches, which focus on static between-person differences. While these approaches offer valuable insights, they fail to capture individual-specific within-person processes underlying social personality. Over the past decade, research on such within-person processes has increased. However, analyses often focus on average patterns (e.g., average within-person effects), which neglect the heterogeneity of social processes across individuals. In addition, previous research has rarely simultaneously examined multiple social dynamics and individuals’ patterning of these. To close these gaps, we propose to first use idiographic modelling to estimate key person-specific state dynamics in social contexts (i.e., state mean-levels, social reactivities, state-state associations, and residual variabilities). Then, individual profiles of these dynamics are clustered to uncover groups of individuals with similar patterns of social dynamics. This bottom-up approach preserves individual-specificity while potentially uncovering patterns at the group-level that could be overlooked in more traditional nomothetic and population-based work. Overall, we thus connect within-person social processes with between-person differences which can reveal insights into both individual-level and general patterns of social personality. An illustration of the proposed approach is provided using experience sampling method (ESM) data.

An Interpersonal Approach to Emotional Dynamics in Everyday Life: Examining Individual Differences in Affective Expectations, Reactivities, and Calibrations
Lara Kroencke | Universität Münster
Show details
Authors:
Lara Kroencke | Universität Münster
Niclas Kuper | Universität Münster
Simon Breil | Universität Münster
Mitja Back | Universität Münster

Modern, dynamic theories of personality emphasize the importance of affective processes underlying interpersonal traits. Previous research has mostly focused on single processes in isolation rather than considering multiple processes together. To address this gap, this project jointly examines individual differences in three key social interaction processes: (a) affective expectations, which refer to individuals' anticipated affective responses to aspects of social interactions, (b) affective reactivities, which capture individuals' actual affective responses to these interactions, and (c) affective calibration, defined as the degree of matching between affective expectations and reactivities, reflecting whether individuals have accurate expectations about their reactivities. Individual differences in these processes will be examined based on a daily diary study, in which 431 participants first completed a baseline trait survey, including measures of interpersonal traits, well-being, and affective expectations. Subsequently, they reported their daily social behaviors and affect every night for 28 days. We will use multilevel modelling and Response Surface Analyses to answer three questions: First, we will quantify the amount of reliable individual differences in affective expectations, reactivities, and calibrations. Second, we will investigate the relationships of individual differences in affective expectations, reactivities, and calibrations with interpersonal traits (e.g., extraversion, agreeableness). Third, we will explore the effects of such differences on well-being. Overall, this research aims to advance modern process-based theories of interpersonal traits. Additionally, it could inform the development of evidence-based personalized interventions to enhance well-being.

Fleeting Moments, Stable Bonds? Social Determinants of Self-Esteem Dynamics in Adolescence
Eva Bleckmann | Universität Hamburg
Show details
Authors:
Eva Bleckmann | Universität Hamburg
Dr. Larissa L. Wieczorek | Universität Hamburg
Dennis Warnholtz | Universität Hamburg
Jenny Wagner | Universität Hamburg

Self-esteem is a key predictor of mental health from early adolescence onwards, yet it fluctuates considerably within and across days. While decades of research highlight the importance of social relationships and interactions in shaping self-esteem, we still know surprisingly little about which social features are meaningful for within- and between-person differences in self-esteem in the daily lives of adolescents. Addressing this gap, this study examines how social factors at two levels—momentary features (e.g., communicating face-to-face vs. digitally, type of interaction partner) and stable resources (e.g., relationship satisfaction with parents and peers, family-friends interdependence)—independently and jointly predict adolescent’ momentary self-esteem levels and variability. Using mixed-effects location scale models, we analyze data from >400 adolescents (ages 14–18) who participated in an experience sampling study across 10 days (>11,000 ESM entries). Findings of this preregistered study will illuminate how resource and risk factors at different social context levels shape self-esteem dynamics during the critical developmental period of adolescence, providing valuable insights for research and guiding targeted interventions.

Dynamic Networks of Social Contact, Social Desire, and Affect Across Time Scales
Dr. Michael Krämer | University of Zürich
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Michael Krämer | University of Zürich
Bernd Schaefer | Universität Bochum
Yannick Roos | Universität Heidelberg
David Richter | Freie Universität Berlin, Germany
Cornelia Wrzus | Universität Heidelberg

Social relationships are central to well-being because they fulfill social affiliation needs. To explain how social needs are regulated, theories describe daily-life processes among social desire, social contact, and affect. Still, these processes remain empirically underexplored because of their complexity. In this study, we estimated multivariate associations of social desire and affect with social contact across different modalities (in-person, digital), time scales (hourly, daily), and levels of analysis (between-person, contemporaneous, temporally lagged). Participants from two age-heterogeneous samples answered experience sampling questions and contributed data through unobtrusive smartphone sensing, with roughly hourly assessments across 2 days (N = 303) and daily assessments across 14 days (N = 377). Multi-level vector autoregressive network models revealed associations between social contact, social desire, and affect across levels of analysis. Results were highly specific to the examined time scale. When measured at an hourly timescale, people desired more social contact than usual when they engaged in more in-person contact, and higher social desire predicted more future social contact in both experience sampling and smartphone sensing. In contrast, at a daily timescale, social desire did not predict future contact. Bidirectional linkages of affect and social contact were also much denser hourly (vs. daily). Compared to in-person contact, calls and communication app usage generally showed distinct associations with affect. We discuss theoretical implications for the dynamic regulation of social needs, especially regarding homeostatic temporal processes and the role of positive affect in predicting social contact. Finally, we delineate future directions of multi-method research into daily-life social dynamics.

Interpersonal Stress Generation Across Hours, Days, and Weeks
Dr. Peter Haehner | University of Zürich
Show details
Authors:

Michael Krämer | Universität Zürich
Amanda Wright | Universität Zürich
Wiebke Bleidorn | Universität Zürich
Christopher Hopwood | Universität Zürich

Humans are social beings, but social relationships do not always run smoothly. Interpersonal hassles (e.g., conflicts with friends, romantic partners, or co-workers) and major interpersonal stressors (e.g., relationship breakups) can disrupt relationships and trigger health problems and reduced well-being. Interpersonal stress generation describes that people contribute to the occurrence of such interpersonal stressors. Although there is robust evidence for the general phenomenon of interpersonal stress generation, little is known about how stress generation processes unfold across different timescales—a topic of critical importance to advance stress generation theories, design empirical studies, and develop effective interventions. With the present study, we aimed to provide a better understanding of the temporal unfolding of interpersonal stress generation processes. To do so, we used data from a study (N = 403) that combined hourly (i.e., experience sampling), daily (i.e., daily diary), and weekly data (i.e., long-term longitudinal assessments). Across all three timescales, we examined whether established risk factors of stress generation—depression rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism—predict the occurrence of interpersonal stressors. We found that between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism were robustly linked to the occurrence of interpersonal stressors across all three timescales. Furthermore, within-person increases in neuroticism and rumination prospectively predicted the occurrence of interpersonal hassles at the next experience sampling assessment, providing insights into the mechanisms of stress generation at a micro-level. Overall, the present study contributes to a better understand of the temporal unfolding of interpersonal stress generation.

The Well-Being Consequences of Daily Events: A Meta-Analysis of Intensive Longitudinal Studies
Lukas Schellenberg | University of Zürich

Authors:

Lina Hungerbuehler | Universität Zürich
Max Lustenberger | Universität Bern
Wiebke Bleidorn | Universität Zürich
Peter Haehner | Universität Zürich

Theoretical accounts and a growing body of research indicate that daily events–frequently occurring, time-discrete experiences that can disrupt everyday life–can elicit changes in people’s momentary well-being. Yet, the strength and significance of these associations differ across studies, samples, assessment methods, and well-being dimensions. To advance our understanding of how such events relate to well-being, the present preregistered meta-analysis synthesizes within- and between-person associations between well-being and daily events across social as well as achievement-related and health-related domains, based on intensive longitudinal studies. A systematic literature search retrieved 2,804 studies. During the ongoing coding, we extract information on study, sample, and measurement characteristics as well as reported correlations. Multi-level meta-analyses will be used to aggregate correlations between daily events and well-being across studies and samples. Moderator analyses will test differences across studies, samples, measurement approaches, methodological features, and event domains. Findings are expected to provide clarity on the robustness and strength of the link between daily events and well-being, facilitate comparisons with other determinants of well-being, and highlight key moderators that determine when the consequences of daily events are most pronounced, helping to refine and advance theoretical accounts.

Happy Relationships Need Autonomy: Multiplicative Effects of Implicit and Explicit Autonomy Motives on Marital and Relationship Satisfaction
Dr. Marziyeh Rezaee | Ferdowsi University of Mashhad, Iran | Iran, Islamic Republic of
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Marziyeh Rezaee | Ferdowsi University of Mashhad, Iran | Iran, Islamic Republic of
Prof. Dr. Nicola Baumann | University of Trier, Germany | Germany

Experiencing satisfying relationships may be shaped by an individual’s own needs and motives, for example, the need for being close with others (affiliation motive) and the need for self-integration and self-boundaries (autonomy motive). Whereas research has already established important links between affiliation motives and relationship satisfaction, the autonomy motive has only recently been added as a fourth basic motive to the Big Three (affiliation, achievement, power). Thus, we are among the first to investigate how implicit and explicit autonomy motives relate to relationship satisfaction. In two studies, we measured the implicit autonomy motive with picture story exercises in the Operant Motive Test (OMT) and the explicit autonomy motive and relationship satisfaction by questionnaire. Consistent with our hypothesis, implicit and explicit autonomy motives had multiplicative effects on relationship satisfaction across two cultures (Iran and Germany) and across two types of relationships (marital and general). In Study 1 (N = 162 Persian-speaking married participants, 90 female, mean age = 34.46 years), individuals experienced highest marital satisfaction when both implicit and explicit autonomy motives were high. In Study 2 (N = 509 German-speaking participants, 281 female, mean age = 38.97 years), individuals experienced high relationship satisfaction when implicit and/or explicit autonomy motives were high and not both low. Our findings suggest that happy relationships need autonomy - and happy marriages even more. Supporting individuals in self-directed strivings while maintaining closeness to their partner may therefore be a promising focus for counseling.

Who Leaves and Why? Understanding Study Dropout in a Sample of Socioeconomically Underprivileged Families in Germany
Dr. Emilija Meier-Faust | DIW Berlin (Deutsches Institut für Wirtschaftsforschung) | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Dr. Annika Wienke | University of Bremen
Dr. Thorsten Macha | University of Bremen
Prof. Birgit Mathes | University of Bremen


Longitudinal intervention studies with socioeconomically underprivileged families are essential for understanding developmental processes and evaluating early support programs. However, engaging these families in longitudinal studies poses challenges to researchers since families with lower education, lower income, and greater life stress have been found to be more likely to leave investigations. Dropout rates can be particularly high when families face multiple risk factors. Attrition threatens statistical power, external validity, and the accurate estimation of intervention effects. The present study investigated predictors of study dropout in the Bremen Initiative to Foster Early Childhood Development (BRISE), a longitudinal, multimodal intervention project in the German city Bremen following underprivileged families from birth until school enrollment. Using data from 493 families who met at least one socioeconomic risk criterion (low parental education, migration background, or precarious employment), we examined whether sociodemographic characteristics, study-related factors, and psychosocial stressors predicted study dropout. Multiple logistic regression models with multiple imputation for missing data were estimated. Results showed that precarious parental employment, recruitment prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, and younger maternal age were associated with a higher likelihood of dropout. In contrast, low parental education, migration background, and family psychosocial stressors did not significantly predict attrition. Importantly, there was no evidence of systematic dropout among the most socioeconomically underprivileged families. The results indicate that dropout from BRISE was nevertheless related to time and resource constraints. This highlights the importance of flexible, relationship-based recruitment and retention strategies for minimizing selective dropout in longitudinal research with hard-to-reach populations.

Empathy in the Context of Sibling Relationships: A Meta-Analysis and Systematic Review
Annika Klugmann | Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Annika Klugmann | Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Tina Kretschmer | Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg

Sibling interactions offer countless opportunities to practice empathic behavior and learn about emotional expression of others. In line, various studies have examined links between sibling relationships and empathy. Aiming to provide a systematic overview of this field of research, this meta-analysis synthesizes studies, evaluates their quality, provides overall estimates of the strength of associations between empathy and sibling status, quality of the relationship, and presence of a sibling with a disability, and explores sources of heterogeneity in effect sizes. We conducted a systematic search of four databases and found 1180 records, of which 37 studies published between 1987 and 2025 were included. That resulted in 118 effect sizes from 26 samples reporting on n = 6665 participants (age range: 10 months to 81 years) to be included in the quantitative analysis. Additionally, findings of nine qualitative studies with a total of 101 participants were summarized. We detected no overall differences in empathy between only children and siblings, but did find a significant positive association between sibling relationship quality and empathy (r = .25), and significantly higher levels of empathy in people that have a sibling with a disability or chronic illness (r = .10). Generally, the field would benefit from a greater methodological variety, like longitudinal and qualitative studies. Taking a more integrated approach that acknowledges the complexity of early social development, would also be beneficial.

Mütter und Väter nach der Elternzeit: Beeinflussen Auszeitlänge und ein familienunterstützendes Organisationsumfeld die (Re)Integration?
Lara-Sophie Sondern | RWTH Aachen University - Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lara-Sophie Sondern | RWTH Aachen University - Institut für Psychologie | Germany
Dr. Anna M. Stertz | RWTH Aachen University - Institut für Psychologie
Dr. Kai Tak Poon | The Educational University of Hong Kong | Hong Kong, China
Prof. Dr. Bettina S. Wiese | RWTH Aachen University - Institut für Psychologie | Germany

Die Möglichkeit zur Elternzeit soll Erwerbstätigen erlauben, sich ohne Angst vor Verlust der Arbeitsstelle ihren Kindern zu widmen. Allerdings ist wenig darüber bekannt, welche sozialen Folgen Elternzeit im Arbeitskontext hat. Diese werden dann sichtbar, wenn die Eltern an den Arbeitsplatz zurückkehren. Die zeitweise Abwesenheit hat ggf. zu einer höheren Arbeitsbelastung in der Kollegenschaft geführt (Stressperspektive). Auch könnte Elternzeit von den Kolleg*innen als ungerechtes Privileg, von dem nur eine kleine Zahl von Beschäftigten profitiert, betrachtet werden (Gerechtigkeitsperspektive). Beides könnte die kollegiale Beziehung beeinträchtigen, insbesondere nach einer längeren Elternzeit und in einem wenig familienunterstützenden Organisationsumfeld. Daher nahmen wir an, dass die Dauer der Elternzeit die soziale (Re-)Integration nach der Rückkehr zum Arbeitsplatz beeinträchtigt, während ein als familienunterstützend wahrgenommenes Organisationsumfeld sie erleichtert. Die Analysen basieren auf Fragebogendaten von N = 389 in Deutschland ansässigen Ersteltern (52 % männlich; Alter: M = 32.2 Jahre, SD = 4.5). In Übereinstimmung mit nationalen Statistiken nahmen die Mütter längere Elternzeiten (M = 12.7 Monate, SD = 5.3) als die Väter (M = 1.6 Monate, SD = 1.7). Während sich bei Müttern die Dauer der Elternzeit hypothesenkonform negativ auf die soziale Integration auswirkte, war dies bei den Vätern nicht der Fall. Eine Erklärung könnte sein, dass die Elternzeiten der Väter derartig kurz waren, dass sie die soziale Integration von vornherein nicht gefährdet hatten. Nichtsdestotrotz fand sich eine positive Auswirkung eines als familienunterstützend wahrgenommenen Organisationsumfeldes auf die soziale Integration sowohl für Mütter als auch für Väter. Dies unterstreicht die Relevanz dieses organisationsspezifischen Merkmals für Erwerbstätige in der frühen Familienphase.

Elterliches Gatekeeping: Eine Längsschnittstudie mit Paaren

Authors:
Elias Czarnojan | RWTH Aachen | Germany
Dr. Anna M. Stertz | RWTH Aachen
Prof. Dr. Bettina Wiese | RWTH Aachen

Wenn aus Paaren Eltern werden, entstehen durch den Umgang mit dem Kind neue Herausforderungen auch für das Miteinander in der Partnerschaft. Wird versucht, Einfluss zu nehmen auf den Umgang mit dem Kind, spricht man von elterlichem Gatekeeping, wobei zwischen „Gate-Opening“ (= bestärkende/ermutigende Verhaltensweisen) und „Gate-Closing“ (= kritisierende/ausgrenzende Verhaltensweisen) unterschieden wird.
Wir sind der Frage nachgegangen, wie sich die Häufigkeit von elterlichem Gatekeeping in den ersten Monaten nach der Geburt des Kindes entwickelt und ob es Unterschiede gibt, in dem, was Mütter und Väter berichten. Schließlich wurde überprüft, ob Niveau und Veränderung dieser Verhaltensweisen innerhalb von Paaren in Beziehung stehen.
Die Daten stammen aus einer Längsschnittstudie mit 267 Ersteltern-Paaren. An vier Messzeitpunkten (3, 6, 12, und 18 Monate nach der Geburt des Kindes) wurden Mutter und Vater zur Häufigkeit des Gatekeeping-Verhaltens des Partners bzw. der Partnerin befragt (z.B., „Er sagt ihnen, dass Sie eine gute Mutter sind.“, „Sie schaut verärgert und rollt mit ihren Augen.“). Die Auswertung erfolgte mittels Dyadic Latent Growth Curve Modelling.
Es zeigte sich, dass sowohl Mütter als auch Väter initial häufiger „Gate-Opening“-Verhalten als „Gate-Closing“-Verhalten erlebten. Zugleich nahm das Gate-Opening über die Zeit linear ab, während das Gate-Closing linear anstieg. Dabei nahmen Frauen eine noch stärkere Abnahme ermutigender Verhaltensweisen wahr als Männer. Hier wird die zukünftige Forschung zeigen müssen, inwiefern dies auch zu unterschiedlichen Verläufen in der Partnerschaftszufriedenheit beiträgt. Es zeigten sich außerdem auf der Paarebene positive Zusammenhänge zwischen der initialen Häufigkeit, in der die Partner ermutigendes bzw. kritisierendes Verhalten erlebten, was den Wert eines dyadischen Forschungsansatzes unterstreicht.

The Complex Interplay Between Online Platforms and Political Behaviour, and How the Social Sciences Can Co-Shape It (Keynote Philipp Lorenz-Spreen)
Room: Room C
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Keynote
Duration: 60 Minutes

Over the past two decades, digital platforms have reorganized public discourse: their design and algorithms now curate what billions of people see, attention has become a scarce and fiercely contested resource, and generative AI has made content easier to produce than ever before. This talk asks what computational social science actually knows about the complex relationship between these technological shifts and changes in political behavior and attitudes. We will discuss how the attention economy amplifies psychological tendencies and how visibility and engagement are skewed towards divisive rhetoric and in favor for populist actors. Drawing on a systematic review of hundreds of studies on digital media and political outcomes, I will show that digital media’s effects are heterogenous and context dependent: Some patterns, like rising political participation, look promising in emerging democracies, while others, like declining trust and growing polarization, are more troubling in established ones. I will then turn to what can be done: behavioral interventions such as boosting comptences against manipulation, self-nudging tools that help people regulate their own smartphone use, and platform design choices that could better support autonomous, informed decision-making. The talk closes by mapping the challenges and the opportunities of how psychology can help co-shape the digital transformation toward outcomes that strengthen rather than erode democratic life.
