Response Time Modeling in Performance Assessment
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Florian Schmitz (Universität Duisburg-Essen, Institut für Psychologie)
Room: FI
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

With the density of information to-be-processed ever increasing in the digital age, the response time (RT) to cognitive tasks gains even more importance, and thus its modeling. In computerized testing, RTs may complement performance scores that are based on accuracy alone. However, RTs may reflect both the efficiency of processing (mental speed) or the time invested into solving a task (time-on-task; ToT). Formal models have been proposed to dissociate some of these interwoven processes. This symposium will provide an overview of recent developments in RT modeling, considering effects of the test requirements as well as differences between and within persons. The first contributions address the ToT effect in ability measures. Naumann et al. show that its mean direction depends on processing requirements in different language comprehension tests. Troche et al. identify a ToT effect in a reasoning test, which is positively related to achievement motivation. Weber et al. model the time it takes to switch between task sets as a predictor of performance in reasoning tests that either require rule transitions or not. The next contributions use continuous sampling models that jointly use the information in responses and response times. T. Schäfer et al. apply IRT race models to PISA mathematics ability data. Schubert and B. Schaefer test the psychometric utility of a novel diffusion model specifically designed for conflict tasks. Von Krause presents findings on individual differences in the within-person variability of cognitive parameters. Together, these contributions offer an overview and discussion of RT modeling in the digital age.

Time on Task Effects in A Low and High Complexity Language Comprehension Task in Written and Auditory Mode
Prof. Dr. Johannes Naumann | University of Wuppertal | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Johannes Naumann | University of Wuppertal | Germany
Patrick Dahdah | University of Wuppertal | Germany
Dr. Julia Schindler | Germany
Dr. Maj-Britt Haffmanns | University of Kassel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Tobias Richter | University of Würzburg | Germany

Language comprehension, both auditory and written, relies on a mixture of automatic and controlled cognitive processes. Drawing theoretically on the Simple View of Reading, the Verbal Efficiency Theory and the Cumulative Cognitive Complexity approach to the processing of local coherence relations, we contrasted time-on-task (ToT) effects for tasks tapping into a basic and easily automatized reading and listing process, phonological analysis (listening) and phonological recoding (reading), and a more complex and a cognitively demanding process, the processing of local coherence relations, in each in both modalities. For each process in each modality we estimated ToT effects in primary school children, grades 1-4, 612 < N < 1307. In accordance with theoretical assumptions, negative fixed ToT effects occurred for both listening tasks, and for the written phonological recoding task, while a positive fixed ToT effect occurred for the most demanding written local coherence task. For all tasks, person intercepts and slopes were negatively correlated, meaning that there were less positive (local coherence), and more negative (phonological analysis and recoding) person-specific ToT effects. Item-specific ToT effects were negative for phonological analysis and recoding, mixed for local coherence (auditory), and positive for local coherence (written). Together these results indicate that while processing phonology at the word level is largely automatic both in reading and listening (supporting the Verbal Efficiency Theory), children have to invest cognitive resources into building local coherence when reading, but less so when listening (in accordance with the Simple View of Reading and the Cumulative Cognitive Complexity Approach).

The Time-on-Task Effect in Reasoning Tests and Achievement Motivation
Prof. Dr. Stefan J. Troche | University of Bern | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Stefan J. Troche | University of Bern | Switzerland
Adrian Büchli | University of Bern | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Karl Schweizer | Goethe University Frankfurt | Germany
Dr. Natalie Borter | University of Bern | Switzerland

Measurement models of reasoning tests enable the consideration of item-position and difficulty factors as method effects. Previously, these method effects have also been identified in the latencies to reasoning test items. This prior investigation revealed that reasoning ability and reasoning speed are independent, while method effects on response accuracies and latencies were positively correlated. Accordingly, time-on-task (ToT) effects, i.e., longer response latencies associated with better performance, were especially pronounced in more difficult items and items presented later in the test. In the present study, we examined whether these ToT effects are functionally related to achievement motivation (hope of success, HoS, and fear of failure, FoF). For this purpose, an achievement motivation scale and a figural analogies test were administered to 227 participants (age: 18-78 years; 129 women). Reasoning items were presented without time limitation and in pseudorandom difficulty order. Difficulty factors were identified in the accuracy data and response latencies; the item-position factor only in latencies. When combining these two measurement models, reasoning ability and speed were found to be unrelated; however, the two difficulty factors correlated positively, indicating that better performance on difficult items was accompanied by longer latencies. HoS was not associated with reasoning ability and speed, but positively with the two difficulty factors. No systematic relationships were obtained for FoF. These results indicate that, in unspeeded reasoning tasks, individuals who spend more time on difficult items achieve better performance (ToT effect), and that this effect is especially pronounced in more motivated individuals, as defined by HoS.

Rethinking Rule Diversity in Figural Matrices: A Log File Analysis on the Role of Task Switching and Implications from a Validation Study
Dominik Weber | Saarland University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dominik Weber | Saarland University | Germany
Stella Jelen | Saarland University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Frank M. Spinath | Saarland University | Germany
Dr. Florian Krieger | TU Dortmund University | Germany
Dr. Marco Koch | Saarland University | Germany

Figural matrices typically consist of multiple distinct logical rules, requiring test-takers to disengage from one rule before applying the next one. Prior correlational studies suggest a moderate association between matrix performance and the time it takes to switch between task sets. The present two-study article aimed to (a) determine, on a theoretical level, whether task-switching ability is functionally involved in matrix processing, and (b) assess, from a diagnostic perspective, whether relaxing the constraint of distinct rules within a single matrix threatens psychometric validity. To this end, we manipulated matrices to include both distinct-rule and identical-rule transitions, enabling experimental within-subject comparisons of matrix processing in both conditions based on response time analyses. In study 1 (N = 209), the time to switch between task-sets was found to exert a functional influence only during distinct-rule transitions. However, the correlation between task-switching and matrix performance remained comparably strong even during identical-rule transitions, supporting the idea of a shared cognitive resource underlying both task-switching paradigms and matrix tests. In study 2 (N = 258), we evaluated the convergent validity of the newly designed mixed-rule format against the traditional distinct-rule format. Test scores were highly correlated (r = .87), and test characteristics (e.g., reliability, IRT and TIF parameters) and external validity were very similar. Taken together, these findings suggest that although task-switching demands can vary depending on matrix design, relaxing rule constraints does not compromise psychometric validity. This flexibility in item development may be useful in large-scale assessments or student selection tests.

Fast and Smart? An IRT Race Model for Student Mathematics Ability using PISA Response Time Data
Tobias Schäfer | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Tobias Schäfer | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Raimund Krämer | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Dr. Philipp Sterner | Technical University Munich | Germany
Prof. Dr. Florian Schmitz | University of Duisburg-Essen | Germany

The introduction of computerized testing in large scale educational assessment allows the use of process data to inspect student achievement. While response times in particular are frequently investigated, their use is mostly limited to the identification of latent classes of test-takers (Han et al., 2023; Hoş & Saraç, 2025), specifically those associated with low test-taking motivation (Michaelidis et al, 2020; Kuang & Sahin, 2023). Recent studies, however, suggest that IRT process models jointly fitted to response accuracies and response times are incrementally informative (Reis et al., 2021; Xie & Liu, 2025). In this line, the present study uses data of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018 to evaluate IRT race models fitted country-wise to responses and response times from all 12 item forms featuring two computer-based mathematics clusters. Subsequently, the relationship between the resulting ability estimates and conventional mathematics scores is investigated. Heterogeneity of the estimates across and within countries is evaluated by means of multi-level meta-analyses. Finally, validity is tested analogously in terms of correlations with performance in the science and reading domains, as well as questionnaire data.

Toward a Reliable Measurement of Attentional Control: Modeling Common Processes Across Flanker Tasks
Prof. Dr. Anna-Lena Schubert | Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Anna-Lena Schubert | Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz | Germany
Simon B. Schaefer | Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz | Germany

Traditional behavioral measures of attentional control derived from conflict tasks suffer from poor reliability and limited construct validity, undermining their utility in individual differences research. Computational models such as the Diffusion Model for Conflict Tasks (DMC; Ulrich et al., 2015) offer a promising alternative by decomposing performance into theoretically distinct components. However, whether model parameters reflecting attentional control generalize across task variants remains untested. This study investigates common latent factors underlying conflict-related parameters (e.g., Amplitude, Peak Latency) and non-attentional parameters (e.g., Boundary Separation, Drift Rate) across Arrow, Letter, and Number flanker tasks. We estimated individual model parameters using Amortized Bayesian Inference in a large sample (N = 290) and examined latent factor structures and associations with general cognitive ability using structural equation modeling. The findings show consistent factors across both conflict-related and non-attentional parameters. Although the associations of attentional parameters with fluid intelligence were modest, they exceed those obtained with traditional difference-score measures. These results support computational modeling as a viable path toward more reliable and valid measurement of attentional control in individual differences research (Rey-Mermet et al., 2025).

Within-Person Dynamics as a Source of Individual Differences in Cognition
Dr. Mischa von Krause | Heidelberg University | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Mischa von Krause | Heidelberg University | Germany

Psychological research on individual differences often focuses on average levels of cognitive performance. However, variability and temporal dynamics within individuals may carry important information about cognitive functioning that is not captured by mean measures alone. While this insight is well established in other domains, such as physiology, within-person variability in parameters derived from cognitive process models has received comparatively little attention. In this work, I investigate individual differences in the variability and dynamics of decision-making processes as described by the diffusion decision model (DDM). A key challenge in this area is that the number of trials typically available in individual differences research makes reliable estimation of variability parameters difficult. To address this, I combine hierarchical Bayesian modeling with recent advances in machine-learning–based inference, allowing stable parameter estimation even under lower trial counts. In addition, I apply a superstatistical framework to explicitly model trial-by-trial fluctuations and their temporal structure. Using several existing datasets, I examine whether individual differences in the dynamics of core DDM parameters—such as drift rate, non-decision time, and boundary separation—are systematically related to individual differences in cognitive abilities. The results reveal a nuanced pattern: measures of variability and dynamic structure provide information that goes beyond what is captured by average parameter estimates alone. Taken together, these findings suggest that incorporating within-person variability and temporal dynamics into cognitive process models can enrich our understanding of individual differences in cognition, and they highlight the value of modern Bayesian approaches for addressing longstanding measurement challenges in psychological research.

Anschließend an kurze Statements aus der DGPs-Kommission Psychologie in Lehramtsstudiengängen und von Vertreterinnen und Vertretern unterschiedlicher psychologischer Teildisziplinen wollen wir gemeinsam diskutieren, welche Forschungsinhalte und -ergebnisse für die Lehrkräftebildung relevant sind und wie sie Eingang in Studium und Weiterbildung von Lehrkräften finden können. For a long time, we have taken scientific freedom for granted. However, the US administration has restricted scientific freedom, affecting American colleagues and, less visibly, colleagues around the world. For example, recently, authors and publishers have begun removing DEI-related terms from publications. In addition, US libraries have asked publishers to remove DEI topics from advertising materials because they would otherwise be unable to order from them. In other words, Trump's politics are beginning to influence academic publishing worldwide. With the rise of populist parties around the world, scientific freedom might become restricted in other countries. At this podium, we will report anecdotal evidence and the results of a recent survey (N = 447) on the risks to academic freedom. Afterward, the current situation and measures to protect scientific freedom will be discussed with different stakeholders (e.g., junior and senior researchers, a scientific society, and a publisher).

Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Panel discussion
Duration: 60 Minutes

Der Berufsverband Deutscher Psychologinnen und Psychologen (BDP) und die Deutsche Gesellschaft für Psychologie (DGPs) fordern seit langem ein Gesetz zur Regelung der Berufsbezeichnung Psychologin und Psychologe. Der BDP hat einen ersten Gesetzesentwurf erarbeitet, beschlossen und im Mai 2024 in die Vorstandssitzung der Föderation Deutscher Psychologenvereinigungen (DGPs und BDP) eingebracht. Dieser Gesetzesentwurf des BDP wurde u.a. auf dem letzten DGPs-Kongress 2024 in Wien vorgestellt und diskutiert. Eine Föderations-Arbeitsgruppe zum Psychologen-Gesetz (PsyG) erarbeitete dann unter Einbezug zahlreicher Rückmeldungen von DGPs-Mitgliedern, Instituten und Fachgruppen einen gemeinsamen Entwurf, der nach breiter Abstimmung in zunächst beiden Verbänden (DGPs, BDP) und dann von der Föderation im Mai 2025 beschlossen und Ende Dezember 2025 an die Bundesministerin der Justiz und für Verbraucherschutz Dr. Stefanie Hubig gesandt wurde.
Ziel des Gesetzesentwurfs ist es, den Verbraucherschutz zu stärken, indem gesetzlich festlegt wird, welche beruflichen Standards Psychologinnen oder Psychologen erfüllen müssen und wer die Berufsbezeichnung als Psychologin oder Psychologe führen darf. Das angestrebte Gesetz soll damit den Beruf „Psychologin“ oder „Psychologe“, seine Voraussetzungen und Studieninhalte regeln sowie das Verhältnis der Berufe Psychologin/Psychologe und Psychotherapeutin/Psychotherapeut klären. Insbesondere die im Entwurf beschriebenen Regelungen zum Studium (u.a. Umfang, Tiefe, Breite), aber auch der beruflichen Standards berühren Fragen des Studiums und die Anforderungen an die Studierenden sowie Absolventinnen und Absolventen der Psychologie-Studiengänge und damit zentrale Interessen der DGPs, des Fakultätentags Psychologie und ihrer Mitglieder. Der aktuelle Stand dieser Gesetzesinitiative und das weitere Vorgehen, das von der Föderations-Arbeitsgruppe koordiniert wird, soll in der Paneldiskussion vorgestellt und mit den Teilnehmenden diskutiert werden, um das bestehende Mandat der Föderation fachlich zu stützen und die nächsten Schritte zu begleiten. Dabei wollen wir den 2024 in der DGPs begonnenen breiten Diskussionsprozess zu der Gesetzesinitiative fortführen, informieren, offene Fragen beantworten und Pros und Cons diskutieren.

Podiumsdiskussion: Echte Teilzeit im Wissenschaftssystem - (Wie) kann das gehen?
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Carolin Strobl (University of Zurich)
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Alexandra Bendixen (Chemnitz University of Technology)
Roland Imhoff (Johannes Gutenberg Universität Mainz)
Prof. Dr. Jens Lange (HMU Health and Medical University Erfurt)
Prof. Dr. Marie-Ann Sengewald (Friedrich-Alexander-University Erlangen-Nürnberg)
Dr. Maria-Therese Friehs (FernUniversität in Hagen)
Dr. Dorothea Klinck (Bundesagentur für Arbeit (BA))
Alexander Strobel (TU Dresden)
Prof. Johannes Zimmermann (University of Kassel)
Moderator(s) Prof. Dr. Sabine J. Schlittmeier (RWTH Aachen University)
Room: Workshop +1
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Panel discussion
Duration: 60 Minutes

Die Umsetzung echter Teilzeit in der Wissenschaft wurde als ein zentraler Wunsch zur Verbesserung der Vereinbarkeit von beruflichen und familiären Anforderungen in einer Bestandsaufnahme von knapp 1.000 Wissenschaftler:innen in der psychologischen Forschung identifiziert (Sengewald et al., 2024). Damit ist gemeint, dass von einer Person auf einer Teilzeitstelle (d.h. einem Beschäftigungsumfang von weniger als 100%) tatsächlich die vereinbarte, geringere Arbeitszeit erbracht wird. Auch wenn dies für Personen ausserhalb der Wissenschaft selbstverständlich klingt, sieht die Realität im Wissenschaftssystem anders aus (siehe auch Rentzsch et al., 2017). Ziel der Podiumsdiskussion ist eine kritische Analyse der aktuellen und zukünftigen Umsetzbarkeit echter Teilzeit im Wissenschaftssystem. Damit soll nicht impliziert werden, dass Teilzeitstellen für alle Wissenschaftler:innen mit Familienaufgaben das richtige Modell wären. Aber es soll diskutiert werden, ob und wie einer Person, die sich im Wissenschaftssystem für die Reduktion der eigenen Arbeitszeit entscheidet, dies in echter Teilzeit und ohne unangemessene Nachteile für die eigene Zukunft sowie für die Arbeitsgruppe ermöglicht werden kann. Dies würde neben Änderungen der strukturellen Rahmenbedingungen auch einiges an Umdenken im aktuellen Wissenschaftssystem erfordern. Vor diesem Hintergrund soll die Podiumsdiskussion erörtern, welche wissenschaftsspezifischen Herausforderungen im Zusammenhang mit Teilzeitarbeit bestehen und welche individuellen sowie strukturellen Handlungsempfehlungen daraus abgeleitet werden können. Anschließend sollen die vorgestellten Anregungen auf dem Podium und mit dem Publikum diskutiert werden. Hierzu sind Wissenschaftler:innen aller Karrierephasen herzlich eingeladen.

Meet the editors: In-Mind Magazin
Chair(s) Jan Crusius (Universität Greifswald)
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Laura König (University of Vienna)
Oliver Genschow (Leuphana University Lüneburg)
Room: DE
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 60 Minutes

Die Vermittlung wissenschaftlicher Methoden und Ergebnisse an die Öffentlichkeit ist ein zunehmend wichtiger Teil der Aufgaben wissenschaftlich tätiger Psycholog:innen. Gleichzeitig gibt es hohe Hürden für eine effektive Wissenschaftskommunikation. In-Mind ist ein internationales, ehrenamtliches Projekt innerhalb der wissenschaftlichen Gemeinschaft der Psychologie, das darauf abzielt, diese Barrieren abzubauen. Unser Ziel ist es, Psycholog:innen dabei zu unterstützen, ihre Arbeit einem breiten interessierten Publikum auf wissenschaftlich fundierte, verständliche und unterhaltsame Weise zugänglich zu machen. In-Mind bietet Publikationskanäle in mehreren Sprachen an, die ein großes Publikum erreichen, engagiert sich in den sozialen Medien und führt Kommunikationsworkshops für Wissenschaftler:innen durch. Die eigene Online-Publikation (https://de.in-mind.org) veröffentlicht längere Magazinartikel und kürzere Blogartikel aus allen Bereichen der Psychologie. Diese Artikel werden zur Unterstützung der Autor:innen einem Peer-Review-Verfahren unterzogen, um wissenschaftliche Korrektheit und Lesbarkeit zu gewährleisten. Auf diese Weise dient In-Mind auch als Plattform für psychologische Fragen, die in anderen Medien wenig Beachtung finden. Die Veranstaltung bietet die Gelegenheit, mit Jan Crusius, Laura M. König, Oliver Genschow und Melanie Sauerland, Herausgeber:innen der deutschsprachigen In-Mind-Version, in ungezwungener Atmosphäre zu sprechen. Wir freuen uns darauf, alle Fragen darüber zu beantworten, was und wie man bei In-Mind veröffentlichen kann, wie man zur Mission des Projekts beitragen kann und wie (und wie nicht) In-Mind eine Antwort auf Herausforderungen und eine Chance für die Wissenschaftskommunikation in der Psychologie sein kann.

A Critical Examination of the Therapeutic Alliance: Measurement & Theoretical Issues
Ronja Timm | Germany
Show details
Author:
Ronja Timm | Germany

The therapeutic alliance, as measured by the Working Alliance Inventory (WAI), constitutes one of the most researched and powerful predictors of therapy outcome within psychotherapy research. While the WAI has existed since 1989, several methodological issues with the instrument exist until this day. Similarly, discussion about the alliance concept, its facets, precursors, and connections to other psychological theories, is scarce within academia. However, without a solid theoretical foundation, the development of new instruments is unlikely to be particularly constructive or insightful.

The position talk aims to first outline current methodological issues of the Working Alliance Inventory. In particular, issues with response format, instruction, translation, comparability between rater versions as well as psychometric deficits of the WAI’s therapist version will be addressed. Regarding alliance theory, difficulties of disentangling therapeutic techniques and the alliance as well as the general factor structure of the alliance shall be discussed. Taking into account potential adjustments that could be made to alliance theory, propositions for future instruments and empirical research will be made afterwards. The following discussion invites participants to share their own critical perspectives on alliance theory and measurement.

152. Sozialmedizinische Behandlungen in der ambulanten Psychotherapie bei Patienten mit und ohne Arbeitsfähigkeitsproblemen
Prof. Dr. Beate Muschalla | Technische Universität Braunschweig | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Beate Muschalla | Technische Universität Braunschweig | Germany

Hintergrund: Die Behandlung (chronischer) psychischer Erkrankungen zielt sowohl auf die Symptomreduktion als auch auf die Verbesserung der sozialen und beruflichen Teilhabe durch sozialmedizinische Behandlungen und Beratung ab. Ziel der vorliegenden Studie war es, arbeitsfähige und arbeitsunfähige Psychotherapiepatienten im Hinblick auf Gemeinsamkeiten und Unterschiede des Patientenstatus und der Behandlungssituation zu vergleichen.
Methode: 73 kognitive Verhaltenstherapeuten und 58 psychodynamische Psychotherapeuten wurden zu 188 bzw. 134 aktuellen Patientenbehandlungen befragt. Die Fallberichte bezogen sich auf Patienten, die im Durchschnitt 42 Jahre alt waren (65 % Frauen).
Ergebnisse: Es gab keine Unterschiede zwischen Patienten ohne oder mit kurzer Krankschreibung (bis zu 6 Wochen, n=156) und Patienten mit längerer Krankschreibung (7 Wochen oder mehr, n=140) in Bezug auf grundlegende Merkmale der Behandlung (Nebenwirkungen, therapeutische Allianz). Patienten mit längerer Krankheitsdauer hatten schwerere Beeinträchtigungen der Leistungsfähigkeit und Teilhabe. Sie erhielten spezifischere, auf die Teilhabe am Arbeitsleben ausgerichtete Behandlungen, während allgemeine salutotherapeutische Aktivitäten (Sportverein, Beratung, Familienunterstützung) bei Patienten mit kürzerer oder längerer Krankheitsdauer in gleicher Weise durchgeführt wurden.
Diskussion: Die Therapeuten wählten die Behandlungsoptionen indikationsbezogen aus: Bei Patienten mit Problemen der Teilhabe am Arbeitsleben wurden mehr arbeitsbezogene Behandlungen durchgeführt, während Behandlungen zur Verbesserung der allgemeinen psychischen Gesundheit unabhängig von spezifischen Problemen der Teilhabe am Arbeitsleben eingesetzt wurden.

153. Implementation and Prospective Evaluation of the First Flexible Assertive Community Treatment (FACT) Service in Luxembourg
Maryse Georges | ZithaUnit asbl | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Maryse Georges | ZithaUnit asbl | Luxembourg
Jean-Paul Steinmetz | ZithaUnit asbl | Luxembourg

In October 2025, Luxembourg launched its first Flexible Assertive Community Treatment (FACT) service as a pilot initiative serving the northern region of the country, a predominantly rural area. This implementation, one core action of Luxembourg’s National Mental Health Plan 2024-2028, represents a significant development in the national mental health system, aiming to strengthen continuity of care, reduce reliance on inpatient services, and promote recovery-oriented community-based support for people with severe mental illness.

This contribution describes the implementation framework and evaluation protocol of the FACT pilot during its initial phase. The evaluation follows a prospective observational service evaluation design conducted over the first months of service delivery, using routinely collected clinical and service utilization data. Clinical severity and recovery are assessed through repeated measures of the Health of the Nation Outcome Scales (HoNOS) and the Individual Recovery Outcomes Counter (I.ROC). Additional indicators include, amongst others, hospitalization-related outcomes, trajectories of care within FACT (intensive and recovery-oriented follow-up), and continuity of outpatient care.

This study provides the first empirical evidence on the feasibility and early functioning of the FACT model in the Luxembourg context. The findings will inform service development, quality improvement, and policy decisions regarding the potential scaling of FACT services at the national level, particularly in small countries with rural regions and fragmented mental health service systems.

154. Early Learning About Pain and Illness: Physical Symptoms in German Children’s Picture Books
Steven Stelz | Johannes Gutenberg Universität Mainz, Psychologisches Institut | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Steven Stelz | Johannes Gutenberg Universität Mainz, Psychologisches Institut | Germany
Bella Makhlin | Johannes Gutenberg Universität Mainz, Psychologisches Institut | Germany
Bleona Smajli1 | Johannes Gutenberg Universität Mainz, Psychologisches Institut | Germany
Prof. Stefanie Maria Jungmann | Johannes Gutenberg Universität Mainz, Psychologisches Institut | Germany

Although picture books are among the most common early-childhood media for communicating information about pain, illness, and care, surprisingly little is known about how symptoms and responses to them are portrayed in contemporary books. As a result, we know far less about the “symptom scripts” children may learn from these shared narratives than from direct experience or parental talk. Therefore, the present study examined these “symptom scripts” in 49 German picture books for young children published between 2010 and 2025, identified through systematic searches of two public library catalogues and analyzed using structured content analysis. Caregiver responses were additionally coded using the Adults’ Responses to Children’s Symptoms framework (ARCS).
Across books, symptoms were mostly mild (40.8%) or moderate (46.9%), short-lived, and situated in everyday contexts, yet even minor complaints were depicted as disrupting daily routines and accompanied by withdrawal and fear. Accidents (36.7%) and infections (22.5%) were the most common causes, with accidents often framed as personally caused (61.1%). Social responses were almost uniformly supportive, emphasizing attention, comfort, and medical help. ARCS analyses revealed a strong predominance of protective caregiving (70.2%), whereas encourage/monitor responses (25.5%) were rare and minimizing responses (2.1%) virtually absent.
Overall, the books convey a relatively narrow script in which bodily symptoms disrupt everyday life and primarily elicit protection and medicalization. While such portrayals may foster feelings of safety, they rarely depict symptoms as transient experiences that resolve without professional intervention, thereby missing an opportunity to normalize everyday discomfort and model adaptive self-regulation.

155. Diverging Paths? Trajectories of Loneliness Among Older Migrants vs. Natives in Germany
Gabriela Christofoletti | Luxembourg University | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Gabriela Christofoletti | Luxembourg University | Luxembourg
Prof. Dr. Adrian Stanciu | Luxembourg University | Luxembourg

Loneliness is a subjective, developmental experience that evolves across the life course. For older migrants, loneliness may be chronic rather than transient, shaped by cultural transitions, migration history, and the imprints of emotional and psychological adaptation. Understanding the developmental aspects of loneliness in this group is essential, given their unique life trajectories and psychological challenges. While research suggests that the risks and course of loneliness differ for migrants compared with the native population, longitudinal evidence on migrants remains scarce. This study addresses this gap by utilizing longitudinal data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP-Core) and applying multilevel growth curve modeling to track trajectories of loneliness among migrants and native-born Germans. Moreover, by controlling for socioeconomic status, health, and relationship status, we aim to explore whether the discrepancies persist beyond objective factors. Our approach aims to provide data-driven evidence on how loneliness among migrants may emerge differently across the lifespan and persist due to enduring psychological and emotional pressures. These findings can guide future research seeking to address the unique needs of migrants. It contributes by moving beyond purely structural explanations to adopt a context-sensitive perspective—one that recognizes loneliness as a dynamic, developmental phenomenon. This approach can pave the way to age-appropriate, culturally sensitive strategies to mitigate loneliness among migrant populations.

156. Evaluating Institutional Mental Health Support for PhD Students: A Longitudinal Quasi-Experimental Study

Dr. Aljoscha Dreisoerner | Universität Wien, Fakultät für Psychologie

Depression and anxiety symptoms are highly prevalent among PhD students and occur at substantially higher rates than in the general population. Despite increasing recognition of these mental health issues and repeated calls for action, empirical evidence on the effectiveness of mental health support measures for PhD students remains limited. Addressing this gap, the present study evaluates a comprehensive institutional mental health support campaign using a longitudinal, quasi-experimental design. PhD students enrolled in the natural sciences at the University of Vienna (n = 1,533) will be offered limited slots of individual and group coaching, well-being seminars, self-help groups, networking events, and a mental health retreat, organized by their institutionalized student representatives orang, while PhD students in the social sciences (n = 651) will serve as a business-as-usual control group. Two online surveys administered before and after a four-month intervention period to these approximately 2,200 PhD students are used to examine whether additional institutional support is associated with reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms. Beyond hypothesis testing, the study provides a descriptive overview of PhD students’ mental health across disciplines, their awareness and use of mental health services, and their satisfaction with institutional support, complemented by qualitative feedback on unmet needs. By evaluating a multifaceted mental health campaign embedded in PhD students’ everyday academic context, this study adds empirical evidence on the effectiveness of institution-level support. If promising effects are found, the intervention may provide a blueprint for universities aiming to improve PhD students' mental health.

157. Attention Shapes Perception, Not Production: Task-Specific Influences on Rhythmic Development in Childhood
Katharina Schaaf | Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Katharina Schaaf | Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics | Germany
Franziska Degé | Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics | Germany

Evidence consistently supports a positive association between rhythmic timing abilities and attentional functioning. Individuals with ADHD show impairments in beat perception and rhythm processing, including reduced temporal sensitivity and disrupted neural entrainment (Marx et al., 2022), with similar associations observed in non-clinical samples (Khalil et al., 2013). Deficits are most pronounced in internal rhythm generation and beat tracking. However, the role of attention and working memory in sequence-based tasks—such as pattern reproduction and discrimination—remains unclear, particularly given their potential reliance on working memory, a domain often affected in ADHD.
To address this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study of 120 children aged 5–7 years. Participants completed pattern reproduction (Jungbluth & Hafen, 1997) and pattern discrimination (PMMA; Gordon, 1979), alongside assessments of auditory attention (NEPSY-II, Korkman et al., 2007) and auditory working memory (Mottier, 1951).
Multiple regression models revealed that only attention significantly predicted pattern perception accuracy (β = 0.003, p = .004), with working memory adding no significant explanatory power. In contrast, auditory working memory was the strongest predictor of pattern reproduction (β = –0.02, p = .009), indicating that higher working memory capacity was associated with lower reproduction error. Attention did not significantly predict reproduction when working memory was controlled for.
These findings suggest that attention plays a selective role in musical pattern perception, while working memory is critical for accurate production. This dissociation underscores the need for task-specific models of rhythmic development that account for distinct cognitive demands.

158. Between- and Within-Person Associations of Loneliness and Self-Perceptions of Aging in Middle and Older Age: The role of Gender and Age
Melania Prandi | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Melania Prandi | Luxembourg
Dr. Markus Wettstein
Prof. Dr. Anna E. Kornadt

Loneliness and self-perceptions of aging (SPA) are recognized as key social determinants of health in later life; however prior research has largely examined them in isolation or within unidirectional frameworks. We therefore investigate the longitudinal, reciprocal associations between loneliness and SPA among middle-aged and older adults and examine whether these associations vary by gender and chronological age. Using over 30,000 observations from more than 11,000 participants (Mage = 61.9 years; SDage = 11.5; 50% women) across six waves of the German Ageing Survey (2008–2023), we applied Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models (RI-CLPM) to disentangle stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations over time. Preliminary descriptive analyses indicate expected cross-sectional associations between loneliness and SPA, in that more negative SPA are associated with higher loneliness, as well as moderate stability of both constructs and their association across waves. Ongoing RI-CLPM analyses will assess whether within-person changes in loneliness and SPA prospectively predict one another, and whether these dynamic associations differ by gender and age. This study advances understanding of how social connectedness and aging perceptions develop across later life, with implications for interventions targeting psychosocial pathways to healthy aging.

159. Wenn die einzige Frau spricht: Stereotype Threat und Voice
Sophie Mahn | Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sophie Mahn | Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena | Germany
Courtney Von Hippel | The University of Queensland
Karoline Schubert | Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena
Mona Weiss | Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena

Obwohl Frauen weltweit rund 70% (in Europa ca. 50%) der Beschäftigten im Gesundheits- und Sozialwesen ausmachen, sind sie in klinischen Entscheidungspositionen weiterhin unterrepräsentiert. Gleichzeitig zeigen empirische Befunde, dass die Beteiligung von Frauen an Entscheidungsprozessen mit einer patientenzentrierteren und geschlechtersensibleren Versorgung sowie günstigeren Behandlungsergebnissen assoziiert ist. Effektive Teamarbeit hängt jedoch neben der personellen Zusammensetzung auch vom Ausmaß an Employee Voice ab, dem freiwilligen Ansprechen von Themen oder Verbesserungsvorschlägen, was den Informationsaustausch und die Patientensicherheit erhöht sowie Entscheidungsprozesse verbessert. Daraus ergibt sich ein strukturelles Paradox: Obwohl Frauen substanzielle Beiträge zur Qualität der Gesundheitsversorgung leisten, erhöht ihre Unterrepräsentation in Führungspositionen die Wahrscheinlichkeit von Token-Positionen in klinischen Entscheidungsteams. Zugleich zeigt klassische Forschung zu Tokenism, dass solche Positionen häufig mit verzerrten Bewertungen und stereotypbasierten Erwartungen seitens der Mehrheitsgruppe einhergehen, wobei bislang unklar bleibt, ob stereotypbasierte Dynamiken auch intrapersonal wirksam sind. Aufbauend auf der Stereotype-Threat-Forschung untersucht die vorliegende, präregistrierte, experimentelle Studie diesen Zusammenhang in einem Between-Subjects-Design mit einer Stichprobe von Ärztinnen. Als Stimulus dient eine videobasierte Fallvignette, die eine Diskussion zur Einführung einer Checkliste zur Patientensicherheit in einem rein männlichen oder gemischtgeschlechtlichen Team simuliert. Es wird angenommen, dass Ärztinnen in rein männlichen Teams geringere Voice-Intentionen berichten als in gemischtgeschlechtlichen Teams, vermittelt durch erhöhten Stereotype-Threat. Zudem wird erwartet, dass Beiträge unter Token-Bedingungen vorsichtiger und weniger direkt formuliert sind. Die Datenerhebung findet derzeit statt und Ergebnisse dieser werden zum Zeitpunkt der Konferenz präsentiert. Die Studie erweitert unsere Erkenntnisse der Voice- und Tokenismusforschung, indem sie Intragruppenprozesse und Stereotype-Threat als Hemmnisse von Voice in einem patientensicherheitskritischen medizinischen Kontext untersucht.

Dr. Gerald Weiher | Goethe University Frankfurt am Main | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ulrich Stangier | Goethe University Frankfurt am Main | Germany
Prof. Dr. Holger Horz | Goethe University Frankfurt am Main | Germany

Theoretical Background: With the growing use of digital technologies in psychotherapy, blended care psychotherapy (BCP) is gaining importance, expanding the range of competencies required of psychotherapists beyond clinical expertise. To address these demands, an online training program for licensed psychotherapists, psychotherapists in training (PiAs), and clinical psychology master’s students (KliPPS) was developed and evaluated.
Methods: The online training on competencies in BCP is conducted separately for three groups: licensed psychotherapists, PiAs, and KliPPS master’s students. A pre–post–follow-up study design is applied. Participants’ competencies are measured as comprised of attitudes, knowledge and skills. Attitudes toward technology use are assessed following the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). Knowledge and skills are assessed using a modified to the BCP context version of the Meta Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, covering the subscales Use & Apply, Know & Understand, Problem Solving, and Emotion Regulation. Additionally, the frequency of BCP application in clinical practice is measured.
Results: The data collection is still in progress, with an expected number of participants ranging from 20 to 30 per group. This presentation will report the results of the training evaluation, focusing on changes in attitudes toward digital technologies, self-reported knowledge relevant to BCP, and the application of blended care approaches over time.
Conclusions: The evaluated training represents an important contribution to preparing psychotherapists for the specific competency demands of BCP and supports the sustainable integration of digital components into routine clinical practice.

Show details

Aim of the study was to examine whether alcohol consumption among adolescents differs depending on school type (boarding vs. day school) and what role drinking motives, social context, and individual backgrounds play. In an anonymous online survey, 276 students in grades 9-13 from a boarding school and a day school (mean age = 16.6 years) were asked about alcohol consumption, drinking motives (DMQ-R), behavioral problems (SDQ), contexts of consumption, and reasons for attending boarding school and additional drug use (only students from boarding school). Boarding school students experienced their first intoxication significantly earlier than day school students (14.72 vs. 15.09 years; p < .05), but did not differ in terms of the amount or frequency of drinking or the proportion of risky consumption. They consumed alcohol significantly more often on school grounds (M = 2.41 vs. 1.13; p < .001) and drank more often with friends and schoolmates. Boarding school students scored higher on drinking for intoxication (p < .01), while social motives tended to differ only slightly. In the boarding school group, 66.4% of adolescents with alcohol experience reported having also used other drugs; this subgroup showed earlier and significantly more intensive alcohol consumption (p < .001). Family problems as a reason for attending boarding school correlated with younger age at first intoxication, higher alcohol consumption, and more frequent drunkenness. The findings point to specific risk patterns and underscore the need for school-specific prevention and support services in boarding schools.

Thermal comfort is a dynamic aspect of everyday environments. Prior work links thermal conditions to affect, although reported patterns are not uniform. Against this background, the present study examined whether different thermal comfort states are associated with distinct affective profiles in daily life. Eighty-eight participants completed ecological momentary assessments (EMA) multiple times per day over three to four consecutive weeks during summer (11,581 observations). At each prompt, participants reported thermal comfort (too hot, comfortable, too cold) and momentary affect, including negative affect (irritated, nervous), activated positive affect (arousal, enthusiasm), and deactivated positive affect (relaxation, satisfaction). Multilevel models revealed significant associations between thermal comfort categories and affective states. Moments rated as too hot were associated with higher negative affect (B = 0.11, p < .001), higher activated positive affect (B = 0.08, p < .001), and lower deactivated positive affect (B = −0.13, p < .001) compared to moments rated as comfortable. In contrast, moments rated as too cold were not significantly associated with higher negative affect (B = 0.03, p = .29) but were associated with lower activated positive affect (B = −0.08, p = .009) and lower deactivated positive affect (B = −0.07, p = .02). These distinct associations highlight thermal comfort as a meaningful situational and motivational factor in daily life and a key variable in research on everyday environmental influences on psychological experiences.

163. Reducing or Reinforcing Stigma? Digital Mental Health Interventions for Children and Adolescents
Elisabeth Höhne | Universitätsmedizin Rostock | Germany

Dr. Olaf Reis | Universitätsmedizin Rostock | Germany

Stigma is a key barrier to mental health service utilization among children and adolescents, affecting help-seeking and treatment adherence—yet research has primarily focused on adolescents, with evidence on children remaining scarce (Gulliver et al., 2010; Henderson et al., 2013; Rüsch et al., 2020; Vogel et al., 2007). Digital psychotherapeutic interventions offer new opportunities to reduce stigma—through improved access, anonymity, flexible use, and enhanced mental health literacy (Gkintoni et al., 2024; Ito-Jaeger et al., 2022; Kretzschmar et al., 2019; Lincke et al., 2022; Marcu et al., 2022). However, they may also unintentionally reinforce stigma—through frequent therapeutic use with increased self-focus, data tracking, or public visibility of symptoms and personal data (Huckvale et al., 2019; Oudin et al., 2023; Wies et al., 2021).
To investigate how digital interventions may reduce or reinforce stigma, a systematic review is being conducted within the “GamKi” project, synthesizing evidence regarding (i) technological solutions in the context of mental disorders and stigma, (ii) factors influencing positive and negative stigma effects of digital applications, and (iii) concepts and validated instruments measuring stigma in childhood and adolescence. Database searches are complete and title and abstract screening is ongoing. Full results will be presented at the congress following PRISMA guidelines, providing a systematic overview of key mechanisms, influencing factors, and existing measurement instruments.
Ultimately, this review aims to advance our understanding of how digital interventions influence stigma processes in childhood and adolescence, providing a foundation for stigma-sensitive research approaches, evaluation strategies, and measurement instruments.

It remains unclear whether ketamine-induced effects on emotional processing are primarily driven by acute changes in limbic activity or by delayed, plasticity-mediated reorganization of prefronto-limbic networks. Investigating healthy participants allows the characterization of primary ketamine-induced effects independent of disease-related alterations. Objective: This study investigates the temporal dynamics of ketamine-induced prefronto-limbic network mechanisms underlying emotional processing, assessed through amygdala reactivity, task-modulated dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC)–amygdala functional connectivity, and task-related modulation of the default mode network (DMN). A predominantly delayed effect profile at 24 hours post-infusion, compared to the acute phase, is expected. Methods: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 7T fMRI dataset comprising 81 healthy participants (ketamine: n = 41; placebo: n = 40) is being analyzed. Participants completed an Emotional Face Matching Task at three time points (baseline, 1–2 hours, and 24 hours post-infusion). Effects are tested using linear mixed-effects models with the factors group and time, including their interaction. Expected Results: At 24 hours post-infusion, reduced amygdala reactivity, enhanced dmPFC–amygdala connectivity, and stronger DMN deactivation are expected, whereas acute effects are expected to be more variable. This study provides novel insights into the temporal dynamics of ketamine-induced affective network mechanisms.

In complex contemporary work environments, effectively managing work demands is essential for employee well-being. Against this background, we examined the potential adaptive value of avoidance orientations and strategies. Avoidance goal orientations – striving for minimal workload (work avoidance; WA) or avoiding failure (performance avoidance; PAV) – are typically associated with detrimental organisational outcomes. However, prior findings point to potential short-term benefits for individual well-being when avoidance goal orientations are adopted in response to high demands, by temporarily reducing workload and facilitating recovery (e.g., Ebert et al., 2024). Similarly, avoiding demands job crafting can be assumed to serve the same adaptive function.
To investigate the relationship between demands, avoidance goal orientation, avoidance crafting, and recovery experiences, we conducted a diary survey among N = 161 German employees over one workweek. Using moderated multilevel path analysis, we found that daily cognitive and behavioural avoidance demands crafting (Level 1) were highly stable across the workdays. Nevertheless, daily job demands (Level 1) negatively predicted avoidance cognitive demands crafting. PAV (Level 2) significantly moderated this relationship, such that participants with higher PAV reported more avoidance job crafting in response to higher demands. We found no significant effects of avoidance job crafting on recovery (Level 1). However, at the between-person level, both WA and avoidance cognitive demands crafting were positively associated with recovery experiences. Additionally, both WA and PAV were positively associated with avoidance behavioural demands crafting. These findings call for further research on potential positive effects of avoidance processes in daily work and employee well-being.

166. Not Every Stress Is Harmful: Personality Traits as Moderators of Chronic Stress and Executive Functioning in Young Adults

Show details
Authors:

Lilly Buhr
Prof. Dr. Caterina Gawrilow | Germany

Executive functions help us stay focused on our goals. They include abilities like holding information in mind (working memory), stopping automatic responses (response inhibition), and flexibly adjusting our thinking (cognitive flexibility). It is often assumed that chronic stress impairs these abilities. However, research findings are mixed, suggesting that individual differences, such as personality, might shape how stress affects cognition.
In this study, we examined whether personality traits influence the relationship between chronic stress and executive functioning in young adults. Participants were 273 university students aged 18 to 30 years. Chronic stress was measured with the workload scale of the Trier Inventory for Chronic Stress (TICS). Personality was assessed using the NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (NEO-PI-R), focusing on neuroticism, openness, and extraversion. Executive functions were measured with three tasks: a 3-back task for working memory, a Stroop task for response inhibition, and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test for cognitive flexibility.
We conducted moderation analyses to test whether personality traits changed the way chronic stress related to executive performance. Preliminary results suggest that the link between stress and working memory depends on personality. Among individuals with lower levels of neuroticism, higher stress was associated with faster reaction times in the 3-back task. No similar effects emerged for openness, extraversion, or other executive functions.
These findings indicate that stress does not uniformly impair executive functions. Instead, personality differences shape how stress affects cognition. Emotionally stable students may process academic stress as energizing rather than overwhelming. Understanding these individual differences could help identify which students need stress interventions versus those who naturally thrive under pressure. Final analyses will aim to confirm and expand these results.

Suicide represents a global public health challenge, claiming over 700 000 lives each year and leaving profound psychological, social, and economic repercussions. In recent years, media-based awareness campaigns have emerged as a prominent strategy within suicide prevention efforts, aiming to improve suicide literacy, reduce stigma, and encourage help-seeking behavior. Despite their growing presence, the effectiveness of such campaigns remains insufficiently understood. Through a controlled experimental study, using a between-subjects design (N = 158), this study evaluated their impact across the three key domains. Participants were randomly assigned to view one of two suicide awareness campaigns or a control campaign unrelated to mental health. Changes in suicide literacy, stigma, and help-seeking intentions were assessed using validated pre- and post-intervention measures (LOSS-SF, SOSS-SF & GHSQ). Results showed that participants exposed to suicide-related content demonstrated a statistically significant increase in help-seeking intentions. However, no significant improvement in suicide literacy or stigma reduction was observed, likely due to ceiling effects and the limited impact of brief, single exposures. These findings highlight both the promise and the limitations of media campaigns: while they may foster short-term attitudinal openness, they are insufficient on their own to drive deeper cognitive or behavioral change. The study advocates for integrating emotionally resonant messaging with targeted educational content, and embedding such campaigns within broader, multi-level suicide prevention frameworks to enhance their reach and effectiveness.

168. Managing Exam-Related Stress in University Students: A Multimethod Experience Sampling Study
Dr. Esther Moszeik | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Esther Moszeik | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Prof. Dr. Karl-Heinz Renner

Students in their early academic semesters face substantial performance-related and social adjustment stressors, which are closely linked to mental health outcomes such as perceived stress, affective well-being, and physiological stress regulation. This multimethod research project at the University of the Bundeswehr Munich accompanied 74 students across two consecutive exam periods. The aim was to investigate changes in exam-related stress, patterns in psychological and physiological mental health indicators, and the effects of positive interventions under real-life academic conditions. In addition, exploratory analyses examined whether personality traits were associated with individual differences in stress responses and intervention-related changes. The study combined psychological questionnaires assessing stress, coping, and affect, diurnal salivary cortisol sampling, and experience sampling via smartwatches and mobile applications. Prior to the main study, 20 students were accompanied during a preceding exam period without any intervention as part of a pilot phase. The final sample of 74 participants were then randomly assigned to one of two intervention conditions: a structured meditation group practicing an 11-minute Yoga Nidra protocol, and a comparison group engaging in weekly changing, self-selected positive interventions (e.g., gratitude journaling, guided imagery, physical activity). Both formats were implemented over a three-week period preceding and during exam phases. The findings provide a differentiated picture of short-term and mid-term effects of mindfulness-based and resource-oriented interventions on mental health indicators in a university setting. Preliminary results indicate significant group differences primarily in cortisol dynamics, favoring the self-selection group. The poster highlights implications for exam-related stress and mental health in higher education.

169. The TYDES Study - A Longitudinal Investigation of Transdiagnostic Processes Using Passive Smartphone Sensing
Christian Ramelow | University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Christian Ramelow | University of Basel | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Nicholas C. Jacobson | Dartmouth College | United States
Prof. Dr. Ines Mürner-Lavanchy | University of Basel | Switzerland

Adolescence constitutes a critical period for mental health. Worldwide, one in seven 10-19-year-olds suffers from a mental illness, and 50% of mental disorders first emerge before age 18. Mental disorders that develop during adolescence carry a heightened risk of persistence or recurrence in adulthood, emphasizing the need for early prevention. However, low help-seeking rates and complex service pathways hinder delivery of preventive efforts to adolescents. Low-threshold digital solutions could address these barriers yet require further validation in youth.
Our study aims to improve understanding of digital signatures of mental health trajectories in adolescents. Leveraging the high smartphone-possession rates among youth, we will collect digital biobehavioral data from 250 individuals from the community aged 14 to 18 over one year. We will focus on transdiagnostic processes linked to emerging youth psychopathology, namely sleep, physical activity, social connection, and affective reactivity, which will be collected through passive smartphone sensing and digital self-reports. We will 1) analyze the data regarding its predictive value for emerging psychopathology, 2) assess the added value of passive sensing compared with self-report alone, and 3) examine temporal dynamics and interactions among the processes. Resulting insights may provide a foundation for early risk detection and the development of targeted prevention tools. The study’s accessible online design and minimal participant burden may, moreover, allow for scaling to larger youth populations in the future. Ethics approval has been obtained, and data collection started in early 2026.

170. Development and Validation of a German-Language Scale for Emotional Granularity
Laura Hirschel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Erko Martins
Show details
Authors:
Laura Hirschel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Erko Martins

Emotional granularity (EG) describes the ability to perceive emotional states in a differentiated way, label them with semantic precision, and interpret them appropriately within a given context. Based on a systematic synthesis of current theoretical and empirical research and grounded in Lisa Feldman Barrett’s Theory of Constructed Emotion, EG was conceptualized as a multidimensional construct. Despite increasing evidence linking EG to emotion regulation and mental health, validated self-report instruments for German-speaking populations remain scarce. The present study therefore aimed to develop and validate a theory-based German-language measure of emotional granularity.

Six subdimensions were defined: valence and arousal sensitivity, interoceptive differentiation, semantic-conceptual differentiation, context sensitivity, affective self- efficacy, and metacognitive emotion regulation. An initial pool of 144 items was deductively generated and reduced to 78 after pretesting. The questionnaire was administered online to N = 218 participants. Exploratory factor analysis extracted six factors with 62 retained items, and confirmatory factor analysis supported this structure. The six-factor model showed the best fit compared to alternative models. Subscales demonstrated good to excellent internal consistencies (α = .81-.90; total scale α = .94).
Construct validity was examined through theory-based correlations with external measures, including the SEK-27 (emotion clarity, body awareness), ERQ, the PHQ-8, WHO-5 Well-Being Index, and a German translation of the RDEES. Associations largely followed theoretical expectations.

Overall, the findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and validity of a multidimensional German self-report measure of emotional granularity and represent a first step toward a more systematic assessment of this construct in German-speaking contexts.

171. Development and Validation of the Black Humor Coping Scale (BHCS)
Jette Gläsel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Erko Martins | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jette Gläsel | Germany
Prof. Dr. Erko Martins | Germany

Background: Stress is an omnipresent phenomenon, and while various coping mechanisms exist, the use of humor—specifically black humor—remains under-researched. This study addresses this research gap by developing and validating a scale to measure how individuals use black humor as a strategy to manage stress.

Methodology: The research followed a quantitative approach. Initially, items were theoretically generated and evaluated for content validity by five psychology students using Lawshe’s Content Validity Index. In the next step, an online survey was conducted with a sample of N=116. To assess construct and criterion validity, the scale was correlated with established instruments measuring the Big Five personality traits, resilience, social desirability, and general stress-coping mechanisms.

Results: Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses confirmed that black humor as a coping strategy constitutes an independent psychological construct. The final scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency with a Cronbach’s alpha of .939. Statistical testing revealed a significant positive correlation with neuroticism and a significant negative correlation with social desirability. No significant correlations were found regarding resilience, general coping strategies, extraversion, and openness.

Conclusion: The results highlight that black humor is a relevant psychological mechanism for processing stressful traumatic experiences. This newly developed scale provides a reliable foundation for future research in stress management and potential therapeutic applications.

172. Resilienz im Übergang in den Ruhestand: Eine qualitative Analyse ruhestandsspezifischer Stressoren
Nelli Niemitz | Leibniz-Institut für Resilienzforschung (LIR) gGmbH | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nelli Niemitz | Leibniz-Institut für Resilienzforschung (LIR) gGmbH | Germany
Prof. Dr. Thomas Rigotti | Johannes Gutenberg - Universität Mainz; Leibniz-Institut für Resilienzforschung (LIR) gGmbH | Germany
Prof. Dr. Miriam Arnold | Leibniz-Institut für Resilienzforschung (LIR) gGmbH; University of Groningen | Germany

Hintergrund: Resilienz wird häufig als Prozess positiver Anpassung an Belastungen verstanden. Lebensübergänge sind hierfür besonders aufschlussreich, da sie mehrere Veränderungen mit sich bringen, Anpassung erfordern (z. B. neue Alltagsroutinen, Umgestaltung sozialer Aktivitäten) und als stressreich erlebt werden können. Der Übergang in den Ruhestand ist eine solche zentrale Transition: Während viele Personen sich gut anpassen, erleben andere den Ruhestand als herausfordernd und berichten Einbußen im Wohlbefinden. Bisherige Forschung zur Ruhestandsanpassung fokussierte vor allem Prädiktoren (z. B. finanzielle Lage, körperliche Gesundheit) sowie Ressourcen, die Anpassung unterstützen. Die psychologischen Stressoren während des Übergangs sind jedoch bislang nur unzureichend spezifiziert. Vorliegende Kategorisierungen sind entweder sehr breit oder beschränken sich auf alltägliche Ärgernisse, was ihren Nutzen für ein differenziertes Verständnis von Resilienz im Ruhestandsübergang begrenzt. Daher braucht es eine klarere Beschreibung ruhestandsspezifischer Stressoren, um sie systematisch mit bestehenden Ressourcenmodellen zu verknüpfen und Ansatzpunkte für wirksame Unterstützung zu identifizieren. Ziel und Methode: Ziel dieser qualitativen Studie ist es, (1) psychologische Stressoren im Übergang in den Ruhestand zu spezifizieren und zu kategorisieren sowie (2) sie mit bestehenden Ressourcenrahmen zu verbinden. Dazu werden leitfadengestützte Interviews mit Personen vor oder nach dem Ruhestand geführt (Ruhestandsdatum ± 1 Jahr; reguläres Rentenalter; ca. 20 Interviews geplant). Die Auswertung erfolgt mittels reflexiver thematischer Analyse nach Braun und Clarke; die Datenerhebung läuft derzeit. Erwarteter Beitrag: Erwartet wird eine Taxonomie ruhestandsspezifischer Stressoren und ein differenzierteres Verständnis des Resilienzprozesses. Die Ergebnisse sollen eine Grundlage für zukünftige Längsschnittstudien zu Resilienzverläufen liefern und praktisch Programme zur Ruhestandsvorbereitung und Intervention unterstützen.

174. Mapping social participation after transition to secondary school: Indegree, reciprocity, and classroom effects in Grade 5
Prof. Dr. Wolfram Rollett | Carl von Ossietzky University of Oldenburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Wolfram Rollett | Carl von Ossietzky University of Oldenburg | Germany
Prof. Dr. Katja Scharenberg | Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich | Germany
Dr. Anna Gieschen | University of Education Freiburg
Dr. Jan Henning-Kahmann | University of Education Freiburg | Germany

The transition to lower secondary education is a phase when peer networks (re-)organize within newly composed classrooms, shaping access to social recognition, belonging, and social participation. Although peer relations matter for students’ adjustment to this transition, less is known about how strongly the classroom environment structures these networks in the early stages and whether these patterns inform opportunities for improvement.
Using sociometric data from 379 students in 17 inclusive classrooms at the beginning of Grade 5, this study examines friendship networks using indegree, outdegree, and reciprocity to index social participation. We hypothesized meaningful between-classroom variation immediately after the transition as well as differences in social participation between student subgroups by gender, migration status and SEN. In addition, we expected a lower social participation indicated by mean indegree compared to reference data from Grades 6 and 7 (n=758, 36 inclusive classes).
Analyses reveal substantial between-class variation in social recognition, nomination behavior, and reciprocity, indicating that the classroom context plays an important role from the outset of secondary schooling. At student level, girls receive more nominations and are involved in more reciprocal ties, whereas students with SEN receive fewer nominations and have fewer reciprocal friendships. Comparisons with reference data from higher grades suggest lower indegrees in Grade 5, underscoring the transition as a sensitive period.
By identifying early differences in classroom networks, the study demonstrates peer relations as diagnostically relevant indicators of classroom social environments and highlights the beginning of secondary education as a promising leverage point for prevention and intervention.

175. Effective parental communication and children’s compliance
Stefanie Peykarjou | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Stefanie Peykarjou | Germany
Marta Giner Torréns
Maria Becker
Rebecca Rodemer
Joscha Kärtner

Effective parental communication is central for supporting preschoolers‘ compliance and promoting internalization of values, but the empirical foundation of guidelines (e.g., THAV, Görtz-Dorten & Döpfner, 2010; THOP, Döpfner et al., 2013) is questionable. Across two data-sets of natural interactions in home contexts, we analyzed relations between parents’ communicative means (use of questions, praise, reference to moral values…) and children’s compliance. Interactions were videotaped and coded based on a novel coding manual.
In a toy clean-up task with N = 54 2-6-year-olds (27f), arguments based on authority were related to longer discussions (p < .01), whereas explicit rather than implicit commands were met with more compliance (p < .001). If moral values were addressed, the majority of statements referred to positive moral values (>78%), in particular liberty (>48%). If parents mentioned prospective rewards, children showed higher contentment, Cramer’s V = .50.
In a mealtime context with N = 36 2-year-olds, data analysis is under way. First data indicate that parental questions compared to declarations are related to higher committed compliance, and explicit use of the child’s name is related to lower compliance. Moral values in this context still need to be analyzed.
Together, these data indicate that in natural interactions, explicit commands lead to higher compliance, whereas questions are related to first indicators of internalization of values (committed compliance). In contrast, in interactions where parents refer to their authority, children show less compliance and engage in longer discussions. Differences in findings may result from variations in task settings and participant age.
