Nico Ruhara | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nico Ruhara | Germany
Silvia Kube
Barbara Bergmann
Prof. Dr. Dr. h.c. Rainer Banse

Die Evaluation der Wirksamkeit therapeutischer Maßnahmen bei Personen mit Sexual- oder Gewaltstraftaten ist häufig durch heterogene Interventionen und unzureichend standardisierte Behandlungsdokumentation eingeschränkt. Zur Verbesserung der Datenqualität und Auswertbarkeit wurde ein strukturiertes Dokumentationskonzept auf Basis einer systematischen Stichwortnutzung entwickelt.
Dieses Konzept wurde von Februar 2023 bis November 2024 im Rahmen einer Prozessevaluation an der Psychotherapeutischen Fachambulanz Nürnberg/Regensburg mit 19 Therapeut:innen pilotiert. Die Ergebnisse zeigten signifikante Verbesserungen der Dokumentationsqualität und Nachvollziehbarkeit bei gleichzeitig hoher Anwenderakzeptanz. Die stichwortbasierte Struktur ermöglichte eine klarere Zuordnung therapeutischer Interventionen sowie der adressierten dynamischen Risikofaktoren.
Aufbauend auf diesen Befunden werden erste Ergebnisse aus weiteren forensisch-psychotherapeutischen Ambulanzen vorgestellt.
Ergänzend wurde ein Large Language Model auf Basis von 26.000 Sitzungsdokumentationen eingesetzt, um zu prüfen, inwieweit sich adressierte kriminogene Bedürfnisse identifizieren lassen und welches Potenzial forschungsfreundliche Dokumentationssysteme für die Evaluation forensischer Praxis besitzen.

207. How new media shapes youth political mindsets in democratic societies: A scoping review
Dr. Hannah Decker | Univerversity of Southern Denmark | Denmark
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Hannah Decker | Univerversity of Southern Denmark | Denmark
Dr. Lea Frentzel-Beyme | Universität Duisburg-Essen | Germany

Today's media landscape is characterised by rapid technological innovation, algorithmic curation and permanent connectivity. For young people, digital and social media have become important platforms for communication, learning and participation. These environments can broaden access to political content and participation, but they also expose young people to misinformation, polarised communication and increasingly AI-generated content that may appear credible even though it is false or misleading. This can affect what young people believe to be true, how they evaluate political issues, and whether they decide to participate in democratic processes. Although many studies address aspects of these developments, research across different disciplines and media types is fragmented. Therefore, this scoping literature review aims to synthesise international, cross disciplinary empirical findings on the relationship between new media (e.g., social networks, messaging apps, video platforms, podcasts, AI-based media) and the political mindset of adolescents in democratic societies. Using both deductive and inductive content analysis, the study examines (1) the status quo of research on digital media and its relation to young people’s political mindset focusing on political knowledge, orientation, and participation, (2) what differences can be found between different media types, (3) the role of media literacy and educational interventions, and (4) which contextual or individual factors moderate these effects. By mapping current evidence and identifying conceptual and methodological gaps, this review aims to inform civic education, media literacy programs, and future research on young people’s political mindset in increasingly developing media environments.

208. Central Versus Peripheral Routes to Digital Participation: An Experimental Study on Persuasion in a Mobile Citizen Participation App
Anna Rauh | Germany
Show details
Author:
Anna Rauh | Germany

The KoodiKo project aims to develop a mobile application for digital citizen participation to increase willingness to participate in informal engagement processes. A mixed between–within subjects experimental design based on the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986) was employed for investigating possible influencing factors of participation willingness. Participants were exposed to different informational cues within a three-stage scenario-based online survey, mimicking a fictious digital participation process. The selected variables were conceptualized as representing either the central or the peripheral route of persuasion of the ELM. It was assumed that higher personal relevance - such as the geographical proximity of one’s place of residence to the location of the participation process - would increase central processing and thereby participation willingness. To test for the influence of peripheral cues, the authority of the source and the social popularity of the process were additionally manipulated in the scenario. Participation willingness was measured five times: baseline, after each information exposure and after finishing the scenario all together. The analyses revealed a significant effect of location, while both cues, associated with the peripheral route of persuasion showed no significant effects. The findings provide valuable implications for the design of the digital participation application, particularly the possible location-matching of participation processes may increase the likelihood of participation. Future studies should address other operationalizations of the factors from the ELM, especially concerning the peripheral cues, to further investigate how persuasion effects can promote willingness to participate.

209. AI-supported systematization of views on ageing in everyday life across the lifespan: The KImAge project
Denise Künstler | Hochschule Furtwangen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Denise Künstler | Hochschule Furtwangen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Verena Klusmann-Weißkopf | Hochschule Furtwangen | Germany

Undifferentiated, negative age stereotypes lead to discrimination in different domains of everyday life (esp. work or health care). Views on ageing (VoA) also significantly influence people's health behaviour and health. Still, we lack knowledge on how VoA develop across the life span and which issues prevail in which domain and life phase. Questionnaire-based assessments get biased when being used in different age groups. Hence, we use a Photovoice method validated in a pilot study to capture photographs to then assess which VoA prevail in which people and settings.
Participants (aged 18–80+ years) uploaded their photographs on what are their VoA in everyday life together with a written comment. The photograph database was analysed using a mixed method approach: An artificial intelligence (AI) model (BERT) was trained by a category system developed by an expert panel to then provide a satisfactory solution for analysing the large-scale qualitative data. The AI uses a multi-label classification approach (combining AI image description and participant’s comment) to identify thematic categories and valence of the depicted VoA.
Categories on functional changes, family and friends, and cultural activities achieved acceptable fit: precision > .83, recall > .50, and F1-scores > .67. Appearance changes, mobility, death and dying, or wisdom were less precisely coded, precision < .51. More heterogeneity and complexity of the images, including a larger number of hard-to-classify cases might explain the differences.
The study provides a proof-of-principle that AI can be used to upscale qualitative research to larger samples. Re-training using data augmentation could enhance model refinement.

210. Personalisierte Ernährungsempfehlungen: Ein Online-Vignettenexperiment
Louisa Albermann | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Louisa Albermann | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christel Salewski | FernUniversität in Hagen | Germany

Hintergrund: Ungesunde Ernährungsgewohnheiten stellen einen zentralen Risikofaktor für die Entstehung chronischer Erkrankungen dar. Vielen Menschen gelingt es trotz des vorhandenen Wissens darüber und einem guten Zugang zu hochwertigen Informationsquellen nicht, sich dauerhaft gesund und ausgewogen zu ernähren. Ein möglicher Grund ist die fehlende Anpassung von Interventionen und Empfehlungen an die individuellen Bedürfnisse der Nutzenden. Dabei könnten neue Technologien und die Anwendung Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) die Möglichkeit eröffnen, skalierbare, individualisierte Interventionen und personalisierte Ernährungsempfehlungen in Echtzeit bereitzustellen.

Ziel: Ziel der vorliegenden Studie war es, den Effekt von personalisierten gegenüber generischen Ernährungsempfehlungen auf die Verhaltensintention einer gesunden Ernährung zu untersuchen. Ergänzend wurden die ernährungsspezifische Selbstwirksamkeit und Technikaffinität als potenzielle Mediatoren bzw. Moderatoren berücksichtigt.

Methode: In einem Online-Vignettenexperiment im Within-Subjects-Design (N = 96, 67.7 % weiblich) wurden die Intention und ernährungsspezifische Selbstwirksamkeit jeweils vor und nach der randomisierten Präsentation einer fiktiven App mit personalisierten sowie generischen Ernährungsempfehlungen erhoben. Die Technikaffinität wurde einmalig erfasst. Die Analyse erfolgte mittels linearer gemischter Modelle.

Ergebnisse: Personalisierte Empfehlungen führten zu einem signifikanten Anstieg der Intention (b = 0.28, p < .001, 95 %-KI [0.17, 0.39]). Die Mediationsanalyse bestätigte einen signifikanten indirekten Effekt der personalisierten Bedingung auf die Intention über die ernährungsspezifische Selbstwirksamkeit (b = 0.16, p < .05, 95 %-KI [0.09, 0.24]). Technikaffinität moderierte den Effekt nicht signifikant.

Schlussfolgerungen: Personalisierte Ernährungsempfehlungen in Echtzeit können die Intention und die ernährungsspezifische Selbstwirksamkeit hinsichtlich einer gesunden Ernährung fördern. Ob diese motivationalen Veränderungen zu nachhaltigen Verhaltensänderungen führen, sollte in zukünftigen längsschnittlichen Studien mit objektiven Verhaltensindikatoren geprüft werden.


211. Families and Automated Vehicles: A Systematic Literature Review
Greta Valentina Seitz | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Greta Valentina Seitz | TU Braunschweig | Germany
Dr. Vanessa Schmidt | TU Braunschweig

A growing body of research investigates families' perspectives (including parents and children) on automated mobility. In recent years, particular attention has been paid to the potential of highly and fully automated vehicles (SAE Levels 4 and 5) to enhance mobility for families with children. This systematic literature review synthesizes key findings from existing empirical studies and identifies gaps for future research. Following the PRISMA guidelines, we screened empirical publications (quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods), including journal articles and full-text conference proceedings published in English between 2017 and 2025. Searches were conducted in three databases and complemented by cross-referencing. A three-stage screening process resulted in the inclusion of N = 41 relevant publications. The majority of studies focused on parental perspectives on child transportation using automated vehicles and predominantly employed quantitative online surveys. Across the literature, five central research themes emerged: (1) attitudes toward and willingness to use automated vehicles for family mobility, (2) factors influencing this willingness, (3) perceived benefits and concerns related to automated vehicle use, (4) design implications, including usability and user experience, and (5) specific use cases for child transportation. Overall, parents remain cautious about using automated vehicles for child transport, whereas children and teenagers show more positive attitudes and higher willingness to use such services for everyday travel. Future research should more strongly incorporate children’s perspectives, address regulatory aspects of unaccompanied child transportation, and examine real-world applications to better understand the integration of automated vehicles into everyday family mobility.

212. Wer nutzt Dashboards? Technologische und pädagogische Kompetenzen von Lehrkräften als Prädiktoren für die Nutzung von Dashboards und die Leistung der Schüler:innen
Katharina M. Bach | University of Potsdam | Germany
Sarah I. Hofer | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU)
Show details
Authors:
Katharina M. Bach | University of Potsdam | Germany
Natalia Revenga | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU)
Karina E. Avila | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU)
Stefan Küchemann | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU)
Steffen Steinert | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU)
Jochen Kuhn | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU)
Sarah I. Hofer | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU)

Dashboards sammeln Daten zum Fortschritt, zur Leistung und zum Verhalten von Schüler:innen und stellen diese Lehrkräften in übersichtlicher Form zur Verfügung, um den individualisierten Unterricht zu unterstützen. Trotz dieser Potenziale werden Dashboards bislang selten genutzt. Zudem ist wenig darüber bekannt, wie pädagogische und technologische Kompetenzen von Lehrkräften die Nutzung beeinflussen und wie sich diese Kompetenzen sowie die Nutzungshäufigkeit auf das Lernen der Schüler:innen auswirken. Auf Basis von Daten von Physiklehrkräften der Sekundarstufe (N = 17) und ihren jeweiligen Schüler:innen untersuchen wir (1) wie Lehrkräfte hinsichtlich ihrer pädagogischen und technologischen Kompetenzen gruppiert werden können, (2) wie diese Kompetenzen mit der Nutzungshäufigkeit von Dashboards zusammenhängen und (3) ob die Leistung der Schüler:innen durch die Nutzungshäufigkeit oder durch die Kompetenzen der Lehrkräfte beeinflusst wird. Zunächst wurden die Lehrkräfte qualitativ in vier Kompetenzprofile eingeordnet, die unterschiedliche Kombinationen pädagogischer und technologischer Expertise abbilden und von Anfänger:innen bis zu Expert:innen in einem oder beiden Bereichen reichen. Anschließend wurden die Lehrkräfte anhand von Logdaten und der Anzahl der Klicks (zwischen 10 und 80) in Gruppen mit geringer, mittlerer und hoher Nutzung zugeordnet. Die z-standardisierte Nutzungshäufigkeit erwies sich nicht als signifikanter Prädiktor der Schüler:innenleistung im Post-Test. Schüler:innen von Lehrkräften mit hoher pädagogischer und technologischer Kompetenz erzielten jedoch signifikant bessere Leistungen als Schüler:innen von Lehrkräften mit geringerer Kompetenz. Dies deutet darauf hin, dass die reine Nutzungshäufigkeit, die von technologischer Kompetenz geprägt scheint, nicht ausreicht, um Lernprozesse positiv zu beeinflussen. Vielmehr scheint pädagogische Kompetenz entscheidend dafür zu sein, wie Dashboard-Daten interpretiert und zur Individualisierung des Unterrichts genutzt werden.

213. Playing a linear number board game promotes basic numerical skills more than nursery rhymes involving fingers in preschool children
Joël Kohler | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt (KUEI) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Joël Kohler | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt (KUEI) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Korbinian Moeller | UMIT-Tirol Private University for Health Science and Technology | Austria
Maria-Aikaterini Chatzaki | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt (KUEI) | Germany
Dr. Valérie-D. Berner | Katholische Universität Eichstätt-Ingolstadt (KUEI) | Germany

Linear number board games as well as finger-based activities were found to promote the acquisition of basic numeracy skills (e.g. Elofsson et al., 2016; Frey et al., 2024). This study therefore compared effects of playing a linear number board game and doing nursery rhymes involving finger activities on the acquisition of basic numerical skills in preschool children (N=43, 17 girls, M=5.90 years, SD=0.05). Each experimental group (board-game-group n=21; finger-based-activity-group n=22) attended six intervention sessions. Basic numerical skills were assessed using MARKO-D (Ricken et al., 2013) in a pre-post-design differentiating performance on 5 levels of numerical development (i.e., i) count number, ii) mental number line, iii) cardinality, iv) class inclusion, and v) relationality). Results of an ANCOVA evaluating differences in post-test performance while controlling for pre-test scores indicated a significant difference for increases of performance on level iv) only with better post-test performance (meaning higher learning gains) for the group playing the board game compared to the nursery rhymes. This finding suggests that children benefitted significantly more from playing linear number board games when it comes to learning about class inclusion, embeddedness and the part-whole concept. This seems feasible as basic numerical skills associated with level iv) were specifically addressed by the board game but not the nursery rhyme finger-based intervention. This indicates that directly addressing specific basic numerical skills in the intervention may be more important than the actual intervention mode.

214. Complexity Through Technology: The Impact of Information and Communication Technologies on Integrative Complexity
Anika Motzkus | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Anika Motzkus | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München | Germany
PD Dr. Katharina G. Kugler | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München | Germany

Organizations must increasingly rely on employees to collaborate effectively using technological tools. When exploring conditions and modes of effective collaboration via technological tools, research has mainly focused on comparing technology-mediated with face-to-face collaboration. But often the question is not whether, but which technological tool to use. In the present study we compared different information and communication technologies (ICTs) with respect to the complexity in communication, a prerequisite for effective collaboration on complex matters. We drew on integrative complexity (IC), a concept that captures the level of differentiation and integration of different perspectives as manifested in expression. We proposed that different ICTs foster different levels of IC in communication due to their technical features and affordances. Specifically, we compared email with chat, hypothesizing that email fosters higher levels of IC given its greater affordances for structuring, rehearsing, and reprocessing information, which should be beneficial for higher levels of IC. In an online experiment with between-subjects design, we asked participants (N = 187) to express their individual thoughts on a work-related controversy, and manipulated the ICT (email vs. chat) while holding the device used constant. Supporting our hypotheses, individuals in the email condition, compared to individuals in the chat condition, showed significantly higher levels of IC in expression of their thoughts. Moreover, this effect of different ICTs on IC remained significant when controlling for individual need for cognition (a personality trait associated with expressing oneself in a complex manner). Overall, this study showed that ICTs impact the level of complexity in communication.

215. Psychological requirements for AI-supported stress training for emergency personnel: User expectations of automated stress diagnostics and feedback design in virtual training environments
René Frenz | University of the Bundeswehr Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:

PD Dr. Silja Meyer-Nieberg | University of the Bundeswehr Munich | Germany

Prof. Dr. Marko Hofmann | University of the Bundeswehr Munich | Germany
Monika Eder | University of the Bundeswehr Munich | Germany
Dr. Cornelia Küsel | University of the Bundeswehr Munich | Germany

Background: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in stress training is becoming increasingly important for preparing emergency personnel for possible scenarios through personalized training. This study aims to identify the requirements for AI-supported digital stress training for operational preparation and relate them to participants' individual risk competence. Theoretically, this study lies at the intersection of stress and coping models (e.g., Lazarus & Folkman), risk competence concepts, and AI model applications.

Method: Data will be collected via an online, cross-sectional survey of German military personnel and civilian emergency personnel from June 2, 2025, to January 31, 2026. The survey will cover expectations and acceptance of AI-based stress training, perceived deployment scenarios, transparency requirements, and aspects of risk competence.

Results: The sample consists of N = 704 fully completed questionnaires. Preliminary descriptive analyses indicate differentiated requirement profiles depending on professional context and previous experience. Fifty-seven percent of the study participants stated that it is important (26% said it is very important) that a trainer receives an assessment of the stress level of the person being trained. Seventy-one percent of the participants stated that, when using AI, the system should provide transparency regarding the factors and information underlying its assessment. This study provides an important empirical basis for the user-centered development of AI-supported stress training for emergency personnel, while also critically examining the concept of risk competence as part of operational preparation.

216. Feedback Timing in XR-Based Procedural Training: A Multimodal Study of Performance and Cognitive Processes in Surgeons
Kathrin Adamietz | University Hospital, University Bonn | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Kathrin Adamietz | University Hospital, University Bonn | Germany
philipp Stefan | Medability GmbH | Germany
Diana Oullette | Medability GmbH
Dr. Mohammed Banat | University Hospital Bonn (UKB) | Germany
Dr. Thaer Ali | University Hospital Bonn (UKB) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Matthias Weigl | University Hospital, University Bonn | Germany

Background
Feedback is central to skill acquisition in simulation training during medical training. Research in traditional simulation setups showed that immediate feedback enhances performance while concurrently increasing cognitive load. Novel extended-reality (XR) simulators enable precise, context-sensitive feedback during training. However, empirical evidence on how feedback timing in XR-based surgical training influences cognitive and behavioural learning processes remains limited.
Aim
We examined the effects of immediate XR simulator–generated feedback on performance, cognitive workload, and visual attention during simulated spine procedures.
Methods
A within-subject XR simulation study was conducted. Junior surgeons performed two distinct injection procedures: lumbar facet joint injections with delayed feedback provided after task completion, and cervical injections with immediate feedback following each needle insertion. Outcome measures included needle placement accuracy, procedure duration, fluoroscopy time, and OSATS ratings. Visual attention was assessed using eye-tracking, and subjective workload was measured using standardized scales. Learning-related changes across sessions were examined descriptively and through MANOVAs.
Results
20 simulations were conducted with surgeons of varying level of experience. Preliminary analyses indicate improvements in selected performance measures following feedback exposure. Changes in attentional patterns and perceived workload are currently under analysis. XR simulation allowed fine-grained tracking of behavioural and cognitive processes across learning trials.
Discussion
The preliminary findings support the feasibility of XR simulators to study feedback effects in complex skill acquisition. Multimodal assessment contributes valuable insights into cognitive load and feedback processing and informs the development of evidence-based training interventions for surgical training.

217. Zwischen Realität und Künstlichkeit: Schützen KI-Labels vor negativen Effekten KI-generierter Körperdarstellungen auf Instagram?
Jasmin Malzahn | Hochschule für angewandte Wissenschaften Ansbach | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jasmin Malzahn | Hochschule für angewandte Wissenschaften Ansbach | Germany
Prof. Dr. Marion Händel | Hochschule für angewandte Wissenschaften Ansbach | Germany

Influencerinnen und auch deren virtuelle (KI-generierte) Pendants verbreiten auf Social Media häufig übersteigerte Schönheitsideale, welche sich negativ auf das Körperbild junger Frauen auswirken. Unklar ist bislang, ob eine Kennzeichnung KI-generierter Körperdarstellungen durch ein KI-Label als Schutzmechanismus gegenüber negativen Effekten auf das Körperbild wirken kann. In einem 3 (between) * 2 (within) mixed Online-Experiment mit 147 Instagram-Nutzerinnen im Alter von 18 bis 35 Jahren sahen Teilnehmerinnen entweder Beiträge einer virtuellen Influencerin ohne KI-Label, dieselben Beiträge mit KI-Label oder vergleichbare Beiträge einer realen Influencerin und wurden vorher und nachher zu ihrem Körperbild und sozialen Vergleichen befragt. Zunächst ließ sich replizieren, dass das Betrachten von Bildern der realen Influencerin zu einer deutlichen Verringerung der Körperzufriedenheit führte, η² = .14. Gleichzeitig transferierte dieser negative Effekt auch auf das Betrachten KI-genierter Influencerinnenbilder, η² = .18. Entgegen den Erwartungen konnte das KI-Label diese Effekte weder auf die Körperzufriedenheit noch auf soziale Vergleiche signifikant abmildern. Zusätzliche Moderatoranalysen zur Intensität und Häufigkeit bisheriger Instagram-Nutzung und der persönlichen Einstellung gegenüber KI erbrachten keine differenziellen Effekte des KI-Labels. Explorative Analysen deuten jedoch darauf hin, dass bei häufiger und längerer Betrachtung der virtuellen Influencerin inkl. des KI-Labels eine potenzielle Schutzwirkung des Labels auftreten könnte. Aufgrund der recht kurzen Expositionsdauer im durchgeführten Experiment (unter fünf Minuten) ist die Übertragbarkeit der Befunde auf die natürliche Social-Media-Nutzung eingeschränkt. Entsprechend bedarf es weiterer Untersuchungen mit längerer und alltagsnäherer Exposition oder auch anderen oder prominenteren KI-Labels, um die Wirksamkeit von KI-Labels unter realistischen Nutzungsbedingungen zu überprüfen.

218. Strengthening Emotional Labor Competencies for Customer Interactions: Concept and Evaluation of a Digital Training Program for Retail Workers
Louisa Schuettke | Ruhr-Universität Bochum, Fakultät für Psychologie | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Louisa Schuettke | Ruhr-Universität Bochum, Fakultät für Psychologie | Germany
Prof. Dr. Marcel Kern | Georg-August-Universität Göttingen, Georg-Elias-Müller-Institut für Psychologie | Germany

Background: Emotional labor is a core element of daily work in retail. However, few theory-based and empirically proven training programs exist to support employees in managing demanding customer interactions. To address this gap, we developed an evidence-based digital training program to strengthen emotional labor competencies among service employees, accompanied by a comprehensive evaluation.

Method: The training was developed in co-creation with several retail companies. Training methods include psychoeducation, video-based examples, and interactive exercises, all aimed at promoting emotional and social competencies. Its self-paced and smartphone-compatible design allows for easy integration into daily work routines.

Training effectiveness is evaluated in a longitudinal study with a waiting control group. The evaluation includes theory-based performance tests developed and validated for this study, short diary entries, and self-report questionnaires. Data from 150–200 employees will be collected before, during, and after the training to assess changes over time and intervention effects.

Expected Results: Initial analyses from the evaluation can be presented at the conference. We expect that the training enhances emotional competencies, promotes the use of adaptive emotion regulation strategies in daily customer interactions, and yields positive organizational outcomes, including improved well-being and job satisfaction.

Conclusion: This study examines the effectiveness of a digital emotional competence training program in the retail sector and demonstrates how training development and evaluation can be integrated from the outset. The participatory design ensures practical relevance and supports implementation in real workplace settings.

219. Is Blended Psychotherapy the Future of Mental Health Care? Evidence from a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Lena Sophia Steubl | Ulm University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lena Sophia Steubl | Ulm University | Germany
Dr. Laura Luisa Bielinski | University of Bern | Switzerland
Dr. Rebekka Büscher | University of Freiburg | Germany
Dr. Carmen Schäuffele | Freie Universitaet Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Harald Baumeister | Ulm University | Germany

Background:
Blended psychotherapy - the structured integration of digital and face-to-face components within one treatment protocol - has been proposed as a future-oriented model of mental health care. While previous reviews suggest promising effects, conclusions are limited by heterogeneous intervention formats and frequent comparisons with inactive control conditions. The added value of blended psychotherapy compared to established active treatments remains unclear, particularly regarding patient-centered outcomes such as quality of life.

Objective:
This systematic review and meta-analysis examines (1) the efficacy of blended psychotherapy compared to active control conditions (e.g., face-to-face psychotherapy alone) with respect to symptom severity and quality of life, and (2) differences in treatment adherence. A secondary aim is to descriptively analyze structural implementation characteristics. The projected is registered on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/T2Y8W).

Methods:
A systematic literature search was conducted in February 2026 in EMBASE, MEDLINE, and PsycINFO. Eligible studies are randomized controlled trials in clinical populations comparing blended psychotherapy with at least one active treatment condition and reporting validated mental health outcomes. Screening is currently ongoing using Rayyan, with independent review by two researchers. Risk of bias is assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool. Random-effects meta-analyses (Hedges’ g) will be conducted where sufficient data are available.

Results & Conclusions:
Preliminary findings will be presented. By focusing on active comparators and quality of life, this review aims to clarify whether blended psychotherapy represents meaningful innovation.

220. Validation of a German Questionnaire for Assessing AI-Anxiety (AIAS-G)
Dr. Mona Leonhardt | Goethe - Universität Frankfurt am Main | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Mona Leonhardt | Goethe - Universität Frankfurt am Main | Germany
Lena Surlan | Goethe - Universität Frankfurt am Main
Prof. Dr. Sonja Rohrmann | Goethe - Universität Frankfurt am Main

The accelerated development and diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) in recent years has fundamentally transformed educational and occupational contexts. In contrast to earlier waves of information technology, contemporary AI systems are increasingly characterized by autonomy, learning capability, and opaque decision-making processes. On the one hand, AI offers substantial opportunities for individuals and organizations. On the other hand, the rapid and pervasive integration of AI into everyday life and professional environments is accompanied by growing concerns and affective responses. Individuals increasingly express fears related to job displacement, loss of professional autonomy, and growing dependence on algorithmic systems. Empirical evidence suggests that AI anxiety negatively affects individuals’ interactions with AI systems, reduces acceptance, and may hinder the development of future-relevant skills. To date, no validated instrument for assessing AI anxiety exists for German-speaking populations. Building on the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS), we develop and validate a German-language measure of AI-related anxiety in a sample of university students and working professionals (N = 582). Using descriptive item statistics, reliability estimates, and confirmatory factor analyses, we examine the factorial structure and psychometric properties of the German Questionnaire for Assessing AI Anxiety (AIAS-G). The poster presents the scale development, validation results, and implications for research on AI-related anxiety in educational and occupational contexts.

221. Shared Spaces, Shared Norms? The Influence of Social Norms on Digital Privacy Decisions of Adolescents and Young Adults Across Social Media and Smart Speakers
Ann-Sophie L. Schenk | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Ann-Sophie L. Schenk | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Mia Maurer | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Sophie Würger | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Jennifer Klütsch | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Anja Poppe | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Sabine J. Schlittmeier | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Astrid M. Rosenthal-von der Pütten | RWTH Aachen University | Germany

Due to their intensive use of digital media, adolescents and young adults (“digital natives”; aged 16–25), face numerous privacy-related choices across shared digital (e.g., social media) and physical environments (e.g., smart speakers). Strong social needs and Fear-of-Missing-Out make these decisions demanding, leading to resignation and increased self-disclosure. To manage this complex decision-making, individuals rely on heuristics. Given the importance of peer influence in this age group, social norms represent a central driver of privacy-related behavior. The present study investigates how descriptive social norms influence digital privacy decisions across two use cases: social media and smart speaker interaction using a preregistered 2×2 mixed, scenario-based online vignette design, manipulating descriptive peer norms of self-disclosure (low vs. high; within-subjects) and digital context (social media vs. smart speaker; between-subjects). The planned sample comprises N = 150 German-speaking participants aged 16–25 years. Outcome measures include hypothetical privacy decisions, such as the amount of personal data disclosed, context-specific information sharing, and privacy settings. We expect higher descriptive social norms of disclosure to be associated with increased self-disclosure across both contexts. Exploratory analyses will examine how usage motives, perceived social norms (descriptive, injunctive, subjective), and context-specific privacy concerns differ between contexts and shape privacy decisions. The study has received ethical approval, data collection is ongoing, and results will be presented and discussed at the conference. These findings will inform the development of educational materials and a serious game to support informed and reflective privacy decision-making among young people.

222. Between Aspiration and Actuality: Self-Perception in the Age of AR Beauty Filters
Nicole Haerter | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nicole Haerter | Germany
Vanessa Gabriela Yarza Navarro-Schär | Ludwig-Maximilian-Universität München | Germany
Prof. Dr. Eric Eller | Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christine Hennighausen | Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt | Germany

In recent years, Augmented Reality (AR) beauty filters have become widely available across various social media platforms, allowing users to easily modify their appearance in real-time and project idealised versions of themselves directly onto their faces, thus introducing an interactive and effortlessly playful form of photo manipulation. Although previous research has linked appearance-focused social media usage, traditional photo editing and AR beauty filter usage to negative body image outcomes, the role of discrepancies between users’ actual appearance and the filtered self-depiction still needs to be explored further. Building on self-discrepancy theory, which links gaps between the actual and ideal self-image to feelings of dissatisfaction, this study examines whether frequent use of AR beauty filters is associated with higher actual-ideal self-discrepancy and lower body satisfaction, and whether self-discrepancy moderates the relationship between filter usage and body satisfaction. A standardised online survey of N = 206 participants assessed the frequency of AR beauty filter usage, body satisfaction and actual-ideal self-discrepancy. Results of regression analyses indicate that more frequent filter usage is associated with lower body satisfaction and greater self-discrepancy. A moderation analysis revealed significant negative associations between filter usage and body satisfaction for individuals with low and moderate actual-ideal discrepancy, while no significant association was found for those with high self-discrepancy. These findings extend prior research, suggesting that associations between AR beauty filter usage and lower body satisfaction vary across users and may be influenced by individual factors such as internalised ideals.

223. KI zur Bewertung im internationalen Assessment? Automatisches Kodieren über Sprachgrenzen hinweg
Dr. Nico Andersen | DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Nico Andersen | DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education | Germany
Dr. Fabian Zehner | DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education | Germany

Die automatische Kodierung offener Textantworten (Automatic Short Answer Scoring, ASAS) bietet einen potenziell effizienten Ansatz, Antworten in internationalen Large-Scale Assessments automatisch zu bewerten. Für einen verantwortungsvollen Einsatz automatischer Kodiersysteme im internationalen Kontext ist jedoch entscheidend, ob diese fair und frei von Verzerrungen auf der Basis linguistischer Merkmale arbeiten.

Die vorliegende Studie untersucht sprach- und modellabhängige Bewertungsverzerrungen auf Basis von n = 1.217.886 Textantworten aus jeweils 50 Items der electronic Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (ePIRLS) 2016. Es wurden sprachübergreifende und monolinguale Kodiermodelle in 14 Testsprachen trainiert und verglichen, darunter Englisch, traditionelles Chinesisch, Französisch, Hebräisch und Norwegisch. Als möglicher mechanischer Einflussfaktor wurde zudem die modell- und sprachabhängige Subword-Segmentierung analysiert.

Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass vollständig sprachübergreifend trainierte Modelle im Mittel die höchste Übereinstimmung mit menschlichen Bewertungen erreichen (κ = .776 gegenüber κ = .683 beim monolingualen Modell) und zugleich die geringsten Bewertungsverzerrungen (D = .025 gegenüber D = .060 für das monolinguale Modell) aufweisen. Besonders deutlich profitieren Sprachen mit kleinen Stichproben durch sprachübergreifenden Transfer. Monolinguales Training zeigt dagegen stärkere und systematisch leistungsabhängige Bewertungsabweichungen. Unterschiede in der Subword-Segmentierung stehen in keinem signifikanten Zusammenhang mit der Bewertungsverzerrung.

Zusammenfassend lässt sich ableiten, dass es sprachbedingte Unterschiede gibt, die jedoch nicht per se auf die Sprache selbst zurückzuführen sind, sondern auf mehrere Faktoren wie die Größe der bereitgestellten Trainingsdaten und damit auch auf eine Abhängigkeit von der Menge erhobener Tests pro Sprache. Sprachübergreifend trainierte Kodiermodelle profitieren von den resultierend größeren Trainingsdatensätzen und sprachübergreifendem Transfer bei der Modelloptimierung, wodurch Verzerrungen reduziert werden können.

224. Licht ins Dunkel der Shadow AI tragen: Mixed-Methods-Studie zu GenAI Literacy und Nutzungsmustern im Zusammenhang mit arbeitsbezogener Kreativleistung
Elisabeth Liedmann | Ruhr-Universität Bochum | Germany
Show details
Author:
Elisabeth Liedmann | Ruhr-Universität Bochum | Germany

Während sich bisherige Forschung zu Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) im Arbeitskontext vorwiegend auf organisationale Top-Down-Implementierungen bezieht, nimmt zeitgleich der dezentrale, nicht formal gesteuerte Einsatz von (generativer) KI (GenAI) für kreative Problemlösetätigkeiten zu. Ein solcher Einsatz durch Mitarbeitende ohne ausdrückliche Befürwortung oder Verwaltung durch das Management sowie IT- und Cybersicherheitsabteilungen wird als Shadow AI (Puthal et al., 2025) bezeichnet. Neben Risiken hinsichtlich Compliance und Cybersicherheit ist nicht nur unklar, inwiefern GenAI tatsächliche kreative Leistungsgewinne ermöglicht oder potentiell auch qualitative Einbußen mit sich bringt, sondern auch, wie sich diese Effekte insbesondere in nicht organisational gestalteten Nutzungskontexten entfalten (Puthal et al., 2025).

Untersuchungsgegenstand ist somit die selbstgesteuerte GenAI-Nutzung bei arbeitsbezogenen Kreativaufgaben zur Problemlösung sowie deren Auswirkungen auf die kreative Leistung. Analysiert wird, ob und unter welchen Bedingungen die selbstgesteuerte Nutzung eines GenAI-Systems die Qualität kreativer Arbeitsergebnisse beeinflusst.

Die für Frühjahr 2026 geplante Studie folgt einem zweiteiligen Mixed-Methods-Design. In Teil 1 bearbeiten Teilnehmende (N = 311) einen Performanztest zu GenAI Literacy (Jin et al., 2025) sowie zwei arbeitsbezogene Kreativaufgaben. Die zweite Aufgabe erfolgt dabei unter randomisierter Between-Subject-Variation (Kontrollbedingung ohne GenAI, Experimentalbedingung mit ChatGPT). Dabei werden sowohl individuelle Voraussetzungen (Kreative Basisleistung, GenAI Literacy) als auch funktionale Nutzungsmuster der Mensch-GenAI-Interaktion berücksichtigt. Die Mensch-GenAI-Interaktionen der Experimentalgruppe werden dokumentiert und qualitativ inhaltsanalytisch ausgewertet (Kuckartz, 2018). In Teil 2 bewerten unabhängige Rater:innen die anonymisierten Arbeitsergebnisse beider arbeitsbezogener Kreativaufgaben anhand von Kreativitätskriterien, um die kreative Leistungsqualität statt bloßer Ideenquantität zu erfassen.

Langfristig sollen die Ergebnisse als empirische Grundlage für Empfehlungen zum verantwortungsvollen und kompetenzförderlichen Umgang mit GenAI in arbeitsbezogenen Kreativprozessen dienen

225. Digitale Transformation und Kompetenzerwerb im höheren Erwachsenenalter: Intergenerationale Lernprozesse im familiären Kontext
David Seistock | Sigmund Freud Privat Universität | Austria
Show details
Authors:
David Seistock | Sigmund Freud Privat Universität | Austria
Elisabeth Ponocny-Seliger | Austria

Hintergrund:
Bedingt durch digitale Transformationsprozesse gewinnen digitale Technologien zunehmend an Bedeutung für die Bewältigung zentraler Lebensanforderungen. Ihr effizienter Einsatz setzt jedoch digitale Kompetenzen voraus, deren Erwerb für Personen im hohen/höheren Erwachsenenalter aufgrund historisch eingeschränkter Lernmöglichkeiten und veränderter Ressourcenlage erschwert sein kann. Jüngere Familienmitglieder fungieren hierbei häufig als Unterstützungsressource, wodurch intergenerationale innerfamiliäre Lehr-Lern-Dyaden entstehen, die Chancen/Herausforderungen für beide Seiten beinhalten. Während bisherige Forschung primär die Perspektive der Unterstützten (älteres Familienmitglied) fokussiert, untersucht die vorliegende Studie diesen Lernkontext aus beiden Perspektiven. Der Fokus liegt auf Unterstützungsschwerpunkten, Lernbedingungen, motivationalen und interaktionalen Prozessen sowie Prädiktoren subjektiven Lernerfolgs, zur Ableitung von Optimierungsansätzen.
Methode: Quantitative Befragung jüngerer unterstützender (n=176) und älterer unterstützter Familienmitglieder (n=155) zu Unterstützungspraktiken, Lernbedingungen und Lern-/Unterstützungsmotiven (explorativ/faktorenanalytisch validiert), reziprokem intergenerationalen Lernen, altersbezogenen stereotypen Kognitionen (Age-Based-Stereotype-Threat; ABST) und subjektivem Lernerfolg. Zusätzlich wurden ein heuristisches Pfadmodell zu personenbezogenen Prädiktoren konstruktiver Lernbedingungen sowie hierarchische Regressionsanalysen zur Vorhersage des Lernerfolgs durchgeführt.
Ergebnisse: Unterstützung erfolgt überwiegend spontan, face-to-face und primär in der Kernfamilie mit Fokus auf Kommunikationstechnologien. Lernbedingungen werden als eher konstruktiv beschrieben, zeigen jedoch Optimierungspotenzial hinsichtlich einer Förderung selbstständigen Weiterlernens und Feedbackprozessen. Funktional-instrumentelle Motivationen dominieren; reziprokes intergenerationales Lernen tritt hingegen selten auf. Geduld und Perspektivenübernahme fördern konstruktive Lernbedingungen, jedoch ohne substanzielle Effekte auf den Lernerfolg. ABST erweist sich als stabiler negativer Prädiktor, während autonomere Lernmotivation und Selbstwirksamkeit positive Effekte für den Lernerfolg zeigen.
Konklusion: Innerfamiliäre Lerndyaden stellen einen zentralen alltagsnahen Kontext für den Erwerb digitaler Basiskompetenzen dar. Eine Verbesserung des Lernprozesses kann beispielsweise durch einen Ausbau konstruktiver Feedbackprozesse sowie selbstständigen Lernens und Adressierung negativer Altersstereotype erreicht werden.

Dr. Christian Böffel | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Astrid M. Rosenthal-von der Pütten | RWTH Aachen University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Sabine J. Schlittmeier | RWTH Aachen University | Germany

Friends are of particular importance to adolescents and young adults (aged 16-25), who express a strong need to belong to their peer group, coupled with a pronounced Fear of Missing Out (FoMO). Previous research has highlighted the behavior of friends and embedded social cues in digital environments as main risks to young adults’ privacy by encouraging them to share more personal data online. However, security research suggests that friends’ experiences could also be promising way of promoting online privacy protection. Building upon this work, we will examine whether social risk communication from friends can increase risk perception and reduce intended data sharing when using technologies in shared spaces (e.g. social media or a smart speaker in a shared apartment). In an online vignette study (Nplanned = 300), we will systematically examine how the decision target (deciding for oneself vs. having others decide on one's behalf) and risk specificity (abstract vs. specific vs. firsthand experienced) in simulated online chat messages from friends affect risk perception, reactance, and the intention to protect one’s data. Based on our findings, we aim to develop recommendations for educational training programs and privacy nudges to raise risk awareness and protection motivation in shared technologies. The study is ethically approved, and data collection is ongoing. The results will be presented and discussed at the conference.

227. What drives the fast perception of the mind?
Nele Bögemann | University of Münster | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nele Bögemann | University of Münster | Germany
Maike Berten | University of Münster
Prof. Dr. Steffen Nestler | University of Münster

According to a prominent framework by Gray et al. (2007), two dimensions govern the social perception of other minds: Agency, describing others’ capacity to intend and act, and Experience, describing others’ capacity to perceive and feel. Since the Agency-Experience framework was identified and replicated in studies using rating formats only, it builds on reflective and controlled judgments of mind, which may occur less in everyday contexts. Here, we investigated whether the framework also applies to more intuitive and fast judgments of other minds. To this end, we collected RT data in an experimental paradigm that asked subjects to make speeded, intuitive decisions about the presence of mental capacities in a range of social targets. We conceptualized decision-making as a process of bounded evidence accumulation, which we estimated via hierarchical Bayesian drift diffusion modeling. Within the model, we tested whether target levels of Agency and Experience, identified in an independent rating study, predicted the drift diffusion process. This is, to the best of our knowledge, the first time a drift diffusion model is applied to the mind perception context. It provides novel insights into the cognitive components of mind perception and shows how Agency and Experience shape them.

228. Effects of math ability-self-concept, math competence, and their discrepancy on math grades mediated by expectancy of success and subjective task values
Dr. Patrick Paschke | Ruhr Univeristy of Bochum | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Patrick Paschke | Ruhr Univeristy of Bochum | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ricarda Steinmayr | Technische Universität Dortmund | Germany

While the positive influence of high ability self-concepts (ASCs) on academic achievement is empirically well-established, there are still gaps in our understanding of the responsible mechanisms. According to situated expectancy-value theory, ASCs affect academic achievement through pathways of expectancy of success and subjective task values. However, this proposition has not been tested longitudinally. Additionally, some authors propose that the discrepancy between a person’s ASC and their actual competence in a certain field (self-evaluation bias) is involved in affecting academic achievement. Various theories and hypotheses include positive effects of accurate self-evaluation, self-overestimation, or even self-underestimation. Like ASCs themselves, self-evaluation biases are theorized to affect academic achievement, at least partially, via mediation by motivational factors (e.g., self-overestimation increasing students’ intrinsic motivation). In a longitudinal study with 504 10th grade students (264 female, 240 male; M = 15.28 years (SD = 0.60); t0: second term 9th grade, t1: first term 10th grade, t2: first term 11th grade, t3: second term 11th grade), we tested whether math ASC, math competence (assessed at t1 with standardized tests), and the self-evaluation bias affect subsequent math academic achievement (operationalized as math report card grades assessed at t0 and t3) directly and via mediation by expectancy of success and subjective task values in math (assessed at t2). For this purpose, we employed response surface analysis. Results indicate that competence but not ASC affected subsequent grades. The effect of competence is partially mediated by expectancy of success. There are no effects of self-evaluation bias on grades.

229. Zwischen Einblick und Eingriff: Privatsphäre, Boundary Flexibility und Cybervetting
Stefan Kenst | Saarland University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Stefan Kenst | Saarland University | Germany
Dr. Nida ul Habib Bajwa | Saarland University

Die Nutzung von Social-Media-Inhalten zur Beurteilung von Bewerber:innen und Beschäftigten hat sich in vielen Organisationen als informelle Praxis etabliert, wirft jedoch grundlegende Fragen zum Schutz der Privatsphäre auf. Die vorliegende Studie untersucht dieses als Cybervetting bezeichnete Phänomen und analysiert, inwiefern die wahrgenommene Invasivität davon abhängt, ob online geteilte Inhalte kontextkongruent oder kontextinkongruent für Personalentscheidungen verwendet werden, sowie welche Rolle individuelle Unterschiede in der Boundary Flexibility spielen. Boundary Flexibility beschreibt dabei die Bereitschaft und Möglichkeit, private Zeit, Aktivitäten und Verpflichtungen zugunsten beruflicher Anforderungen anzupassen. In einem experimentellen Between-Subjects-Design bewerteten erwerbstätige Personen in Deutschland Social-Media-Profile mit privaten oder arbeitsbezogenen Inhalten hinsichtlich der wahrgenommenen Invasivität ihrer Nutzung in Personalauswahlverfahren. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass die Nutzung privater Inhalte signifikant invasiver wahrgenommen wird als die Verwendung arbeitsbezogener Inhalte. Zudem zeigte sich ein signifikanter Haupteffekt der Boundary Flexibility: Unabhängig vom Nutzungskontext nahmen Personen mit höherer Grenzflexibilität Cybervetting insgesamt als weniger invasiv wahr. Die Befunde verdeutlichen, dass die Wahrnehmung von Privatsphäre-Eingriffen im Cybervetting nicht nur von der Art der verwendeten Inhalte, sondern wesentlich von individuellen Unterschieden im Umgang mit der Grenze zwischen Arbeit und Privatleben abhängt.

230. Social milieus in Germany: A Typological Approach to Inter-Individual Differences in Values and Socioeconomic Position
Dr. Anne Speer
Show details
Author:
Dr. Anne Speer

Social milieu typologies allow for the analysis of different ‘types of people’: large latent groups in society with similarities in various characteristics. Existing typologies, such as the SINUS® milieus, lack transparency or focus on specific domains (e.g., work or lifestyle). We therefore developed a novel typology based on similarities in Basic Human Values and socioeconomic positions: The RISC model of social milieus (Research Institute Social Cohesion). RISC milieu typologies can be estimated for different datasets (e.g., countries, subpopulations, etc.) using Latent Class Analysis. This talk presents a RISC milieu typology for Germany along with validation efforts, and illustrates various applications to advance psychological research. The RISC milieu typology for Germany is based on the German Social Cohesion Panel (N = 9,218) and identified eight social milieus, each with unique combinations of value orientations and socioeconomic positions. Extensive quantitative validation efforts and qualitative focus groups with milieu members (N = 48) supported the robustness of the typology. It can be applied to study whether interventions work for different types of people and to analyze conflicts between groups in society, among others. We make the typology accessible to researchers by providing replication code and online applications for identifying milieu memberships and for exploring milieu differences in attitudes.

Belkis Ezgi Arikan | University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Belkis Ezgi Arikan | University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen | Germany
Katharina Schmidt | University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen
Helena Hartmann | University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen
Livia Asan | University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen
Lieven Schenk | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf
Maren-Isabel Wolf | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf
Christoph Wittkamp | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf
Frederik Schlitt-Nguyen | University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen
Christian Büchel | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf
Michael Rose | University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf
Dagmar Timmann | University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen
Katja Wiech | University of Oxford, John Radcliffe Hospital
Ulrike Bingel | University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen

Treatment expectations can significantly impact treatment outcomes. In the context of pain, positive and negative expectations can result in pain relief (placebo analgesia) and pain exacerbation (nocebo hyperalgesia). Despite their fundamental translational potential, only few studies have examined whether and how pain-related placebo and nocebo effects persist over time. In this preregistered study, we combined datasets from five studies. All studies used an established experimental paradigm to induce expectations of pain relief or pain exacerbation regarding a sham treatment. Expectation induction was achieved through verbal instructions and a conditioning procedure that covertly manipulated the intensity of the applied heat pain stimulation depending on the condition. The effects of these procedures on pain perception were tested subsequently and approximately one week after, by comparing pain perception of the same heat pain application in the placebo/nocebo condition with a control condition. Placebo analgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia were still evident after one week, with nocebo hyperalgesia being stronger than placebo analgesia. Furthermore, the magnitude of the placebo/nocebo effects immediately after conditioning predicted the persistence of these effects. Together, these results demonstrate the maintenance of placebo and nocebo effects, with stronger persistence of nocebo effects after one week, which is in line with the 'better safe than sorry' strategy. Clinically, these findings underscore the need to systematically assess and modulate treatment-related expectations in pain management, as negatively induced expectations may exert more durable and pronounced effects on pain perception than positively induced expectations.

232. Personal development, personal growth, or both? Lay understandings of developmental concepts in Positive Psychology
Stefan Dressler-Stross | University of Applied Sciences Wiener Neustadt | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Stefan Dressler-Stross | University of Applied Sciences Wiener Neustadt | Austria
Dr. Kathrin Gärtner
Dr. Michael Penkler

Concepts such as personality development, personal development, and growth take a central position in Positive Psychology. Despite their prominent use, there is still no conceptual consensus regarding how these terms can be clearly distinguished or which psychological processes they are intended to describe. Existing research repeatedly points to overlaps and ambiguities, particularly concerning the distinction between subjective experiences of development and long-term structural changes in personality, as well as between normatively charged assumptions about growth and empirically describable developmental processes (e.g., Bringmann, Elmer & Eronen, 2022; Ryff, 2022; van Zyl et al., 2024).

Against this background, the present contribution adopts an exploratory, concept-clarifying approach and examines how people outside academic discourse understand these concepts. As these constructs are closely tied to everyday experience and subjective meaning, a qualitative research design was chosen. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 24 participants and analyzed using thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke.

The results indicate that personality development and growth are conceptualized both as active, conscious, goal-directed processes (e.g., goal setting and intentional self-change) and as passive, inevitable processes arising through social relationships or challenging life events. The environment was described partly as actively shapeable and partly as an external force beyond individual control. Across all concepts, self-reflection and self-awareness emerged as central unifying elements influencing the subjectively perceived process of development.

The findings point to the conceptual ambiguity of development-related terms in Positive Psychology and highlight the potential of psychological research to contribute to conceptual clarification through empirical and theoretical refinement.

233. Parental Educational Aspirations, Socioeconomic Status, and Migration Background in Germany: A Preregistered Integrated Data Analysis
Lena Hofbauer | Humbold-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lena Hofbauer | Humbold-Universität zu Berlin | Germany
Maximilian Brinkmann | TU Dortmund
Dr. Kristin Schotte | Humbold-Universität zu Berlin
Prof. Michael Becker | TU Dortmund
Prof. Aileen Edele | Humbold-Universität zu Berlin

Accounting for socioeconomic status and child academic achievement, immigrant parents often report higher educational aspirations for their children than non-immigrant parents (e.g. Cebolla-Boado et al., 2021). This applies to idealistic aspirations (wishes) and realistic aspirations (expectations). High educational aspirations of immigrant parents are attributed to transgenerational upward-mobility-goals (Kao & Tienda, 1995). It is therefore conceivable that the observed difference in educational aspirations is particularly pronounced in low-SES immigrant vs. non-immigrant parents. Still, few studies to date have explicitly modelled the joint role of SES and migration background. Immigrant parents may also be less influenced by child academic performance in their (realistic) aspirations, as they may perceive performance as reflecting temporary hurdles only (Becker & Gresch, 2016). Further, immigrant parents constitute a highly heterogeneous group with respect to their origin, migration motive, and socioeconomic selectivity. Previous single-study analyses have typically lacked the power to address this. This pre-registered study will analyse data from multiple German large-scale educational studies (e.g. NEPS, PISA, TIMSS). Using an Integrated Data Analysis (IDA) approach, parallel regression models will be estimated separately within each study-grade and synthesised using random-effects meta-analyses. We present results. The preregistered hypotheses include that (i) low-SES immigrant vs. non-immigrant parents have particularly high aspirations as reflected in an SES x migration background interaction, (ii) realistic educational aspirations in immigrant vs. non-immigrant parents are less strongly shaped by child performance than idealistic aspirations, and (iii) aspiration patterns differ across immigrant origin groups. All hypotheses were pre-registered on the OSF (registration is embargoed).

234. Zur Rolle kommunikativer Subjektaffirmation: Relationalität als Faktor der Ideological Bias Expression
Julius Weiske | FSU Jena | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julius Weiske | FSU Jena | Germany
Dr. Christine Finn | FSU Jena
Arne Stolp | FSU Jena | Germany
Prof. Dr. Tobias Rothmund | FSU Jena

Die Ideological Bias Expression (IBE)-Skala misst ideologische Verzerrung daran, ob Menschen identische Fakten je nach politischer Passung unterschiedlich bewerten, selbst dann, wenn sie über vergleichbares Wissen verfügen. Forschung zu ideologischen Verzerrungen betrachtet Bias überwiegend als kognitives Phänomen, etwa im Sinne motivierter Kognition oder asymmetrischer Informationsverarbeitung. Entsprechend zielen viele Interventionen auf kognitive Mechanismen wie Perspektivwechsel oder analytisches Denken ab, zeigen jedoch insbesondere in politisch stark polarisierten Kontexten häufig begrenzte oder instabile Effekte. Daraus ergibt sich die Frage, inwiefern der Ausdruck ideologischer Verzerrung auch situations- und kontextabhängig variiert.
Der vorliegende Beitrag verfolgt eine ergänzende Perspektive und versteht Ideological Bias Expression als relationale und kommunikative Praxis, die durch soziale Bedingungen des Urteilens mitgeprägt wird. Untersucht wird, ob sich der Ausdruck ideologischer Verzerrung bereits dann verändert, wenn Individuen kommunikativ als urteilsfähige Subjekte adressiert werden, unabhängig von inhaltlicher Überzeugungsarbeit oder kognitiver Umstrukturierung.
Theoretisch knüpft die Studie an sozialpsychologische Arbeiten zu Identitätsbedrohung, sozialer Anerkennung und Self-Affirmation an. Es wird angenommen, dass die Bestätigung der Urteilskraft des Individuums defensive Abwehrreaktionen reduziert und damit ideologische Bias-Expression abschwächt, ohne konkrete politische Überzeugungen zu beeinflussen.
Diese Annahme wird in einer vignettenbasierten Studie geprüft. Teilnehmende interagieren mit einem kurzen Pseudodialog, der sich ausschließlich in der kommunikativen Ansprache unterscheidet: Eine Bedingung affirmiert die Urteilskompetenz der Teilnehmenden, die Vergleichsbedingung nutzt eine disaffirmative, funktionale Anrufung. Ideologische Bias-Expression wird mit einer etablierten Skala (Stolp et al.) erfasst.
Erwartet wird, dass subjektaffirmative Kommunikation mit geringerer Bias-Expression einhergeht. Die Ergebnisse werden im Hinblick auf soziale Bedingungen epistemischer Urteilsbildung sowie die Gestaltung zukünftiger dialogischer und digitaler Interventionsformate diskutiert.

235. Geklickt. Gehandelt. Riskiert? Beeinflussen Kontext und Nutzen sicherheitskritisches Verhalten?
Niklas George | Saarland University | Germany
Show details
Author:
Niklas George | Saarland University | Germany

Social-Engineering-Angriffe stellen eine zunehmende Bedrohung für Organisationen dar, da sie gezielt menschliche Schwachstellen ausnutzen, um an sensible Daten zu gelangen. Viele Aufklärungsmaßnahmen zielen darauf ab, Endnutzer:innen den Wert ihrer Daten im Sinne einer Kosten–Nutzen-Abwägung bewusst zu machen. Die Theorie der kontextuellen Integrität hingegen geht davon aus, dass Daten keinen absoluten Wert besitzen, sondern dass deren Weitergabe vom jeweiligen Kommunikationskontext abhängt. Vor diesem Hintergrund untersucht die vorliegende Studie, ob Kosten–Nutzen-Abwägungen von Opfern telefonischen Betrugs durch einen als passend wahrgenommenen Kontext überlagert werden. In einem 2x2-Zwischen-Versuchspersonen-Design wurden 52 Mitarbeitende der Universität des Saarlandes mit simulierten Vishing-Anrufen konfrontiert, wobei sowohl die wahrgenommenen Kosten der Datenpreisgabe als auch die kontextuelle Integrität experimentell variiert wurden. Als abhängige Variable wurde die Anzahl während des Anrufs ausgeführter sensibler Handlungen erfasst, darunter das Weitergeben eines Codes, das Einrichten einer PIN sowie das Ausführen eines vermeintlichen Diagnosetools. Die Ergebnisse zeigten weder signifikante Haupteffekte der Kosten–Nutzen-Manipulation noch der kontextuellen Integrität, ebenso wenig einen Interaktionseffekt. Auffällig war jedoch ein stark polarisiertes Entscheidungsverhalten: Rund 50 % der Teilnehmenden führten alle abgefragten Handlungen aus, während etwa 30 % keinerlei sensible Handlungen vornahmen. Explorative Analysen zeigten zudem, dass ein höheres selbsteingeschätztes IT-Wissen mit einer geringeren Bereitschaft zur Durchführung sensibler Handlungen einherging.

236. From Hyperactivity to Peer Problems: How Do Behavioural Dimensions Relate to Early Language?
Dr. Katharina Repnik | University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Katharina Repnik | University of Basel | Switzerland
Marina Jambreus | University of Basel
Prof. Dr. Alexander Grob | University of Basel

Language development in early childhood is closely intertwined with children’s self-regulation, emotional functioning, and social behaviour. In large-scale studies of early language outcomes, behavioural measures are often treated as global composites or control variables; thus, limiting insight into how distinct behavioural dimensions may differentially relate to language development. This ongoing pilot study explores whether sub-scales of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) show such differentiated associations with preschool children’s language and communication abilities.

Adopting a dimensional and exploratory approach, we examine how emotional symptoms, hyperactivity/inattention, conduct problems, prosocial behaviour and peer relationship difficulties relate to both structural and functional aspects of language. Rather than assuming a unitary behaviour–language link, the study aims to identify which behavioural dimensions appear most relevant for specific language outcomes, including indicators of pragmatic communication. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Developmental Language Disorder (DLD) are referenced as clinically well-described conditions in which such behaviour–language intersections are particularly evident, while the present work itself remains non-diagnostic.

Using an existing population-based dataset, this pilot study maps patterns of co-occurrence between SDQ subscales and multiple language measures. The focus lies on descriptive profiling, preliminary association analyses, and the evaluation of analytic feasibility, with particular attention to subclinical variability and overlapping risk profiles in linguistically diverse preschool populations.

The goal of this pilot is to generate hypotheses, refine conceptual models, and inform subsequent confirmatory analyses on the interplay between behavioural regulation and language development in early childhood.

237. Admiration, Not Rivalry, Predicts Self-Enhancement in a Performance Task
Simona Florescu | University of Bucharest | Romania
Ilinca Bercaru | University of Bucharest | Romania
Show details
Authors:
Simona Florescu | University of Bucharest | Romania
Ilinca Bercaru | University of Bucharest | Romania
Prof. Dr. Klaus Moser | Friedrich Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) | Germany
Prof. George Gunnesch-Luca | University of Bucharest | Germany

Narcissism has been linked to self-enhancement (favorable self-views exceeding objective evidence) to the extent that it has been described as the “self-enhancer personality” (Morf et al., 2011). However, modern theoretical developments suggest this characterization may be overly broad. The Narcissistic Admiration and Rivalry Concept (Back et al., 2013) differentiates between admiration (agentic self-promotion) and rivalry (defensiveness and antagonism). The model predicts that self-enhancement should be specific to admiration rather than a general feature of narcissism. We tested this prediction using performance-based tasks with objective accuracy criteria, allowing statistical control of actual performance for ruling out the possibility that associations between narcissism and self-evaluations reflect true performance differences.

An initial study using a dot-estimation task (N = 86) provided moderate evidence that admiration predicted more favorable relative self-evaluations (b = 0.73, 95% CrI [0.13, 1.34], BF ≈ 5), whereas rivalry showed no reliable relation. In an extension study, psychology undergraduates (N = 172) counted virtual bacterial colonies on agar plates under time constraints and evaluated their performance relative to peers (worse than, same as, or better). Bayesian cumulative logit models revealed extreme evidence that admiration improved prediction over rivalry alone (BF₁₀ = 7,079). Admiration positively predicted more favorable self-evaluations (b = 0.47, 95% CrI [0.11, 0.86]), whereas rivalry showed no association. In both studies, predicted probabilities show that admiration primarily reduced the likelihood of self-categorizing as worse than peers and increased the likelihood of reporting performance at least as good as average, suggesting status maintenance rather than overt superiority claims.

238. Physiological correlates of performance fluctuations and cognitive load in mental-rotation tasks – A multimodal pupillometry, heart rate, and electrodermal study
Dr. Mirko Saunders | University Koblenz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Mirko Saunders | University Koblenz | Germany
Maya Kirsch | University Koblenz | Germany
Amelie Tietz | University Koblenz | Germany
Prof. Dr. Claudia Quaiser-Pohl | University Koblenz | Germany

Mental rotation performance varies as a function of rotation axis (picture-plane vs. in-depth) and stimulus type (concrete vs. abstract). In the present study, rotation axis was experimentally manipulated and assumed to vary cognitive load, understood as task-related cognitive demands during problem solving. We examined which physiological measures are sensitive to cognitive load. N = 69 students completed a 2 × 2 within-subjects mental rotation task while pupil dilation, heart rate (HR), and phasic electrodermal activity (EDA) were recorded. Data were analyzed using linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models with within-subject centering and random slopes.
Behavioral results revealed a strong interaction between rotation axis and stimulus type (p < .001). In-depth rotation impaired accuracy and increased response times for concrete stimuli, whereas this effect was absent for abstract stimuli, indicating that the impact of experimentally varied task demands depended on stimulus characteristics.
HR and phasic EDA showed no effects of the experimental factors; HR exhibited a habituation trend across trial order (p = .005). Pupil dilation showed a small but significant main effect of rotation (p = .002) and increased across item position (p < .001), but no interaction between rotation and stimulus type.
Within-person increases in pupil dilation were associated with a lower probability of correct responses (p < .001 in the fixed-slope model). When allowing random slope variation, this association remained comparable in magnitude but was marginally significant (p = .056).
Pupil dilation emerges as the most performance-relevant physiological correlate of experimentally varied cognitive load in mental rotation.

239. The operationalization of the socio-economic status matters: Contrasting different strategies and their effect on child educational outcomes in a large panel study
Dr. Christoph H. Klatzka | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Christoph H. Klatzka | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Lena Paulus | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Marie Peitz | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany
Prof. Dr. Frank M. Spinath | Universität des Saarlandes | Germany

Socio-economic status (SES) is a central construct in research on inequality, yet there is no clear consensus on how it should be operationalized. Common approaches rely on parental education, occupational status, and household income, while alternative strategies focus on material and cultural resources (e.g., books at home, household possessions) or subjective self-assessments of social standing. This plurality of operationalizations raises the question whether conceptual and analytical choices systematically affect estimated associations between SES and empirical outcomes.
Using data from TwinLife, a large German twin family panel study, this paper examines how different SES operationalizations and analytical decisions influence effect sizes in models predicting children’s educational outcomes. Multiple SES measures are constructed and compared within the same sample and their associations with (a) school grades and (b) cognitive abilities are assessed.
By systematically contrasting alternative SES operationalizations, this study aims to contribute in two ways. First, it provides a structured nomenclature for categorizing SES measurement strategies. Second, it demonstrates that seemingly technical measurement decisions can have substantive consequences for the magnitude of SES effects on educational outcomes. These findings underscore the importance of transparency and comparability in SES measurement in educational research.

240. Liking Others and Perceiving Others’ Liking in Initial Social Encounters: First Insights from the TRIAD-Project
Jana Bruns | University of Münster | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jana Bruns | University of Münster | Germany
Prof. Dr. Steffen Nestler | University of Münster

In social interactions, people frequently form judgments about one another. One of the most central judgments concerns how much they like others. At the same time, individuals estimate how much they are liked by others, which is relevant for self-esteem and behavior. Beyond that, people also form perceptions of their surrounding social networks, such as how much others like each other. In a pre-registered study, we examined the components, accuracy, correlates, and longitudinal development of these liking, meta-liking and triadic liking judgments. To this end, we conducted TRIAD, a large round-robin study in which previously unacquainted participants interacted across three 60-minute group laboratory sessions. During these sessions, participants completed seven tasks (e.g., self-introductions, lost-on-the-moon task, moral dilemma discussions) and repeatedly judged one another. They indicated how much they liked each group member and how much they believed each member liked them. Additionally, participants judged how much they thought other group members liked each other. In this talk, we introduce the TRIAD study, its unique dataset, and present first findings on the accuracy of meta-liking judgments.

Jannis Augustin-Zschocke | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jannis Augustin-Zschocke | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stefanie Peykarjou | Germany
Yizhou Yang
